manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Demonstration of Nasal Consonant /m/ Using Visible Breath VaporI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Visualization of Nasal Consonant /m/ AirflowSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)Objective: To demonstrate that during the nasal consonant /m/, the lips are closed while airflow exits through the nose, visualized by breath vapor in a cold environment.II. Equipment and ConditionsCold room or outdoor cold environment (visible breath vapor); camera with tripod; fixed-focus setting; timer or time-lapse mode; participant seated or standing still.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the camera on a tripod facing the participant’s face; adjust framing to include nose and lips; lock focus and exposure.2. Environment Check: Ensure ambient temperature is low enough for breath vapor to be visible.3. Articulation Setup: Ask the participant to relax, keep lips gently but fully closed.4. Core Operation: The participant sustains the nasal consonant /m/ continuously for several seconds while breathing out.5. Recording: Capture the process using fixed-focus time-lapse or continuous recording.6. समाप्त: Stop recording and review footage.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: No vapor before phonation.During /m/: Continuous white vapor visibly exits from the nostrils while lips remain closed; no vapor exits the mouth.End: Vapor dissipates after phonation stops.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe nasal consonant /m/ is produced with complete lip closure and a lowered velum, blocking oral airflow and directing exhaled air through the nasal cavity. In cold conditions, the moist exhaled air condenses, forming visible vapor at the nostrils, visually confirming nasal airflow during /m/ articulation.VI. PrecautionsMaintain fixed camera focus; avoid head movement; ensure lips remain closed; limit recording to core steps for clarity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: nasal consonant /m/ articulation requiring lip closure and nasal airflow due to lowered velum. Minimum assumptions: cold air produces visible vapor; sustained phonation is possible without mouth opening.Phased storyline: (1) Cold setting established with fixed camera; (2) lips close and phonation begins; (3) continuous nasal vapor appears as causal result of /m/ articulation; (4) vapor ceases when phonation stops. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Stop vs Fricative Using Incense SmokeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visualizing Stop vs Fricative Consonants with Incense SmokeSubject: Linguistics - PhoneticsObjective: To visually demonstrate the difference between stop consonants and fricative consonants by observing burst versus continuous airflow using incense smoke at the mouth.II. Experimental EquipmentLit incense stick (1), lighter or matches, stable incense holder, well-lit indoor space with minimal air disturbance.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Light the incense and place it in the holder. Ensure the room is still so smoke rises steadily.2. Positioning: The demonstrator holds or positions the incense directly below the mouth, about 10–15 cm, so smoke rises in front of the lips.3. Stop Consonant Production: Close the lips or relevant articulators fully, then release to produce a stop consonant (e.g., p or t) once.4. Fricative Production: Immediately after, produce a sustained fricative (e.g., s or f) for 2–3 seconds.5. Observation: Keep the camera focused on the mouth and smoke throughout the sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Smoke rises vertically in a thin, steady stream.2. Stop Consonant: At release, the smoke shows a brief, sudden burst or rapid dispersion.3. Fricative: During sustained articulation, the smoke is continuously deflected or spread by steady airflow.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleStop consonants involve complete closure of the vocal tract followed by a sudden release, producing a short burst of airflow. Fricative consonants involve a narrow constriction that creates continuous turbulent airflow. Incense smoke visualizes these airflow differences: a momentary burst for stops versus continuous disturbance for fricatives.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual differentiation of stop and fricative consonants via airflow patterns. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Demonstrating the Relationship Between Frequency and Pitch Using an OscilloscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstrating the Relationship Between Frequency and Pitch Using an Oscilloscope2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the relationship between sound frequency and pitch by inputting sound signals of different frequencies into an oscilloscope, keeping amplitude constant, and observing waveform changes.II. Experimental EquipmentSignal generator or electronic sound source (sine wave), microphone or direct audio input cable, oscilloscope, connecting cables, speaker or headphones (optional for auditory comparison).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the oscilloscope and signal generator. Set the oscilloscope to time-domain display. Adjust vertical scale to clearly show waveform amplitude.2. Initial Input: Set the signal generator to output a low-frequency sine wave (e.g., 100 Hz) with fixed amplitude. Input the signal into the oscilloscope and stabilize the waveform on the screen.3. Core Operation: While keeping the amplitude constant, gradually increase the signal frequency in small steps.4. Observation: Observe the waveform on the oscilloscope as frequency increases, focusing on changes in the number of cycles displayed within the same time window.5. Completion: Stop increasing frequency once clear differences in waveform periodicity are observed. Turn off equipment after observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low frequency, the waveform has a long period with fewer cycles displayed on the screen.2. As frequency increases, the waveform cycles become denser, and the period shortens while amplitude remains unchanged.3. Correspondingly, the perceived pitch of the sound becomes higher.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPitch perception in linguistics is primarily related to the frequency of sound waves. Frequency refers to the number of vibrations per second. When frequency increases, the waveform period decreases, resulting in a higher perceived pitch. The oscilloscope visually represents this relationship by showing more waveform cycles within the same time interval at higher frequencies, while constant amplitude indicates unchanged loudness.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: The relationship between sound frequency and pitch, assuming basic knowledge that frequency determines pitch while amplitude relates to loudness.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: A sound signal can be represented as a periodic waveform; increasing frequency increases the number of cycles per unit time without altering amplitude.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial low-frequency waveform appears with long periods; (2) frequency control is adjusted upward while amplitude remains stable; (3) waveform cycles compress horizontally, showing shorter periods; (4) higher pitch is implied by denser waveform. Visibility Requirements: Clear view of oscilloscope screen and control adjustments; stable camera angle to verify continuous temporal changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Voice Tones Vibrating Thin Plastic Wrap Over WaterI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Voice-Induced Vibration of Plastic Wrap Over WaterSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Acoustic Phonetics)Objective: To demonstrate that sustained human voice tones produce sound waves that mechanically vibrate a thin membrane and transfer energy to water, making sound-induced vibration visible.II. EquipmentClear bowl; clean water; thin transparent plastic wrap; rubber band or tape; camera or smartphone with tripod; quiet room; optional marker light for reflections.III. Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the clear bowl with water to about 2/3 full. Stretch thin plastic wrap tightly over the bowl opening and seal with a rubber band or tape so the surface is taut and smooth.2. Camera Setup: Place the camera facing the bowl at a slight angle to capture reflections on the plastic wrap and water. Fix focus and exposure. Enable time-lapse or accelerated recording.3. Core Operation: Stand close to the bowl without touching it. Speak or sing a sustained steady tone toward the plastic wrap for several seconds. Optionally vary pitch after the first tone.4. Recording: Continue recording while maintaining the tone; then stop speaking and recording.5. End: Review the footage; clean and store equipment.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial State: Plastic wrap is still; water surface is calm and flat.During Speaking: The plastic wrap visibly vibrates; small ripples or shimmering patterns appear on the water surface. Changes in pitch or loudness alter vibration patterns.After Speaking: Vibrations cease; water surface gradually returns to calm.V. Experimental PrincipleHuman voice produces sound waves that propagate through air. When these waves strike a taut plastic wrap, they cause the membrane to vibrate at corresponding frequencies. The vibrating membrane transfers mechanical energy to the water below, producing visible ripples. This demonstrates the physical basis of speech acoustics: sound as pressure waves capable of causing mechanical vibration.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Human voice tones generate acoustic pressure waves that mechanically vibrate a thin membrane and transmit energy to water. Minimum assumptions: sound propagates through air; a taut plastic wrap behaves as a membrane; vibration transfers to water.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with calm water and taut wrap; fixed camera view. (2) Sustained speaking begins, causing immediate membrane vibration. (3) Visible ripples/shimmering appear on water, modulated by tone. (4) Speaking stops and motion dissipates. Visibility constraints: clear bowl, taut transparent wrap, stable camera focus, reflections or ripples visible to verify vibration-causation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop ConsonantI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Spectrogram Visualization of Sustained Vowel versus Stop Consonant2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare spectrogram characteristics of a sustained vowel and a stop consonant, and to understand the acoustic differences between continuous and transient speech sounds using live phonetic analysis software.II. Experimental EquipmentComputer with phonetic analysis software capable of live spectrogram display (e.g., Praat), external microphone, microphone stand, quiet room, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse or continuous recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the microphone on a stand about 15–20 cm from the speaker’s mouth. Open the phonetic analysis software and enable the live spectrogram view. Fix the camera focus and framing on the screen and speaker.2. Calibration: Ask the speaker to remain silent for 1–2 seconds to observe the baseline spectrogram (low background noise).3. Sustained Vowel Production: The speaker sustains a steady vowel (e.g., /a/) for about 3–4 seconds at a comfortable pitch and loudness while observing the live spectrogram.4. Pause: The speaker stops phonation and remains silent for about 1 second, keeping posture unchanged.5. Stop Consonant Production: The speaker produces a single stop consonant (e.g., /p/ or /t/) once into the microphone.6. End: Stop recording and save the spectrogram display if needed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. During the sustained vowel, the spectrogram shows continuous energy with clear horizontal formant bands.2. During the pause, overall energy decreases, showing near-silence on the spectrogram.3. During the stop consonant, the spectrogram shows a brief closure (low or no energy) followed by a sudden burst of energy.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesVowels are produced with an open vocal tract, resulting in continuous acoustic energy and stable formant structures on the spectrogram. Stop consonants involve complete closure of the vocal tract, causing a momentary silence, followed by a rapid release that appears as a transient burst. The spectrogram visually represents these acoustic differences over time, allowing direct comparison of sustained versus transient speech sounds.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: acoustic contrast between sustained vowels and stop consonants as visualized on a live spectrogram. Minimum assumptions: a functioning microphone, live spectrogram software, and a speaker producing controlled speech sounds. Phased storyline: (1) baseline silence with minimal spectral energy; (2) sustained vowel causing continuous, stable formant bands; (3) brief pause with reduced energy; (4) stop consonant showing closure then burst. Verification requires a fixed camera view of the speaker and spectrogram, with clear temporal alignment between speech actions and visual changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Demonstrating the Relationship Between Amplitude and Loudness Using an OscilloscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Relationship Between Amplitude and Loudness Using an Oscilloscope2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Speech Acoustics)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that loudness is related to the amplitude of a sound wave by observing real-time waveform changes on an oscilloscope while keeping pitch (frequency) constant.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrophone (dynamic or condenser), oscilloscope, signal cable (microphone to oscilloscope or via audio interface), power supply, quiet indoor environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the oscilloscope on a stable surface and turn it on. Connect the microphone output to the oscilloscope input. Adjust the time base and voltage scale so a clear waveform is visible.2. Calibration: Ask the experimenter to produce a steady vowel sound (e.g., ‘ah’) at a comfortable pitch. Adjust oscilloscope settings to stabilize the waveform display.3. Core Operation (Soft Voice): The experimenter speaks softly into the microphone while maintaining the same pitch. Observe and note the waveform amplitude on the oscilloscope screen.4. Core Operation (Loud Voice): Without changing pitch, the experimenter speaks louder into the microphone. Observe and compare the waveform amplitude in real time.5. Completion: Stop speaking, freeze or reset the oscilloscope display if needed, and turn off the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: A stable waveform is displayed on the oscilloscope.2. Soft Speech: The waveform has a relatively small vertical height (small amplitude).3. Loud Speech: The waveform height increases significantly (larger amplitude), while the horizontal spacing between wave cycles (frequency) remains nearly unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSound is a mechanical wave. Loudness is related to the amplitude of the sound wave, which represents the magnitude of air pressure variation. Pitch is related to frequency. In this experiment, keeping pitch constant keeps frequency constant. When the speaker increases loudness, the energy of vibration increases, causing a larger amplitude on the oscilloscope display, while frequency remains the same.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Loudness corresponds to waveform amplitude, while pitch corresponds to frequency. Minimum assumptions: a working microphone–oscilloscope connection and a human speaker capable of controlling loudness while keeping pitch stable.Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial stable waveform appears on the oscilloscope; (2) Soft speech produces a small-amplitude waveform; (3) Louder speech produces a visibly larger amplitude; (4) Frequency spacing remains visually constant across phases. The camera should clearly show the oscilloscope screen and the speaking action, with real-time response enabling causal verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Tissue Strip Airflow Demonstration in SpeechI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Airflow During Vowel and Stop Consonant Articulation Using a Tissue Strip2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate continuous airflow during vowel articulation and airflow blockage during stop consonant articulation using a thin tissue paper strip.II. Experimental MaterialsThin tissue paper strip (approximately 1 cm wide, 5–8 cm long), skin-safe tape, quiet indoor environment, mirror or camera (optional for observation).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut a thin, lightweight tissue strip. Tape one end of the strip just below the nose or in front of the lips so that the free end hangs directly in front of the mouth.2. Initial Vowel Articulation: Open the mouth naturally and sustain an open vowel (such as ‘aaa’) for 2–3 seconds, keeping the head steady.3. Stop Consonant Articulation: While maintaining the setup, briefly switch to a voiceless stop consonant (such as ‘p’ or ‘t’), fully closing the oral airflow for a short moment.4. Return to Vowel: Immediately return to the same sustained vowel for another 2–3 seconds.5. Completion: Stop speaking and observe the final position of the tissue strip.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. During the sustained vowel, the tissue strip moves steadily outward or flutters smoothly due to continuous exhaled airflow.2. When the stop consonant is articulated, the tissue strip briefly stops moving or falls limp because airflow is blocked by oral closure.3. Upon returning to the vowel, the tissue strip resumes steady movement, similar to the initial vowel phase.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVowels are produced with an open vocal tract that allows continuous airflow from the lungs through the mouth, which can be observed as steady movement of a lightweight tissue strip. Stop consonants involve a complete closure in the vocal tract that temporarily blocks airflow, causing the tissue strip to stop moving. This experiment visually demonstrates the phonetic distinction between continuous airflow sounds (vowels) and airflow-blocking sounds (stop consonants).
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is the relationship between speech sound articulation and airflow, specifically continuous airflow for vowels and blocked airflow for stop consonants, visualized by tissue movement. Minimum assumptions include a lightweight tissue responsive to airflow, correct placement in front of the mouth, and basic human speech articulation.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 (Vowel): Open mouth, sustained vowel, continuous exhaled airflow causes the tissue to extend or flutter steadily. Phase 2 (Stop): Brief oral closure for a stop consonant blocks airflow, causing the tissue to halt or drop. Phase 3 (Return to Vowel): Oral opening resumes, airflow restarts, and tissue movement returns. Visibility Requirements: Close frontal view of mouth and tissue; clear view of tissue motion changes synchronized with articulation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Acoustic Performance Comparison of Architectural Materials2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: Using sound wave ripples (wave graphics) to represent sound propagation, visually demonstrate the acoustic differences between sound-absorbing materials (sponge) and sound-reflective materials (glass), and help learners understand basic architectural acoustic principles.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Sound source model (represented by a point or speaker icon)2. Sponge block (porous, matte appearance, labeled Sound-Absorbing Material)3. Glass panel (smooth, transparent, labeled Reflective Material)4. Visualization medium or simulation interface capable of displaying sound wave ripples5. Flat reference surface or simplified room section diagramIII. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Scene Setup: Place the sound source at one side of the scene. Position the sponge block directly in front of the sound source at a fixed distance.2. Sound Propagation to Sponge: Activate the sound source. Display concentric sound wave ripples propagating toward the sponge.3. Observation at Sponge: Allow the waves to reach the sponge and visually attenuate, showing reduced amplitude and fading ripples.4. Material Replacement: Replace the sponge with a glass panel at the same position and distance from the sound source.5. Sound Propagation to Glass: Reactivate the sound source. Display sound wave ripples propagating toward the glass.6. Observation at Glass: Show strong reflection, with wave ripples bouncing back toward the source, maintaining higher amplitude.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sound wave ripples spread evenly from the sound source in all directions.2. Sponge Interaction: When waves reach the sponge, ripple amplitude decreases rapidly, and waves visually fade, indicating sound absorption.3. Glass Interaction: When waves reach the glass, ripples reflect clearly, forming returning wave patterns, indicating sound reflection.4. Comparative Result: Sponge shows weak or no reflected waves, while glass shows strong, visible reflected ripples.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on architectural acoustics principles. Porous materials such as sponge contain internal air cavities that convert sound energy into heat through friction, leading to sound absorption and reduced reflection. In contrast, dense and smooth materials like glass have high acoustic impedance and reflect most incident sound waves. By visualizing sound as wave ripples, differences in absorption and reflection become intuitive and comparable.VI. Experimental Notes1. Keep the distance between sound source and materials constant for fair comparison.2. Focus on relative wave amplitude and reflection direction rather than exact physical scale.3. The visualization is qualitative and intended for conceptual understanding, not precise acoustic measurement.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visual comparison of acoustic absorption versus reflection in architectural materials using wave graphics. Minimum assumptions: sound propagates as waves; sponge absorbs sound; glass reflects sound.Phased Storyline: (1) Sound source emits concentric wave ripples. (2) Waves reach sponge and visibly weaken and fade, showing absorption. (3) Scene resets with glass. (4) Waves reach glass and clearly reflect back, maintaining strength. Key causal transition: material type determines wave attenuation or reflection. Visibility constraints: wave direction, amplitude change, and interaction at material surface must be clearly observable from a fixed viewpoint.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualizing Dynamic Changes of Speech Amplitude (Intensity) in the Time DomainI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualizing Dynamic Changes of Speech Amplitude in the Time Domain2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Experimental Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how changes in speech loudness affect amplitude in the time-domain waveform, and to understand the relationship between speech intensity and acoustic amplitude.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrophone (connected to computer), computer with audio recording/visualization software (e.g., waveform display), quiet room environment, display screen.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Connect the microphone to the computer and open the audio visualization software. Set the display to show a real-time time-domain waveform. Ensure the input level is appropriate and background noise is minimal.Initial Recording: Position the speaker close to the microphone at a fixed distance. Begin recording or monitoring so that the waveform appears on the screen.Core Operation: The speaker repeatedly pronounces short syllables /t/ at a steady rhythm. First, speak softly for several syllables, then gradually increase loudness to a clearly loud level while maintaining the same syllable and tempo.Observation and Recording: Keep the camera focused on the computer screen showing the waveform. Use continuous or time-lapse recording to capture the dynamic waveform changes as loudness increases.Completion: Stop speaking and end the recording. Save the waveform display if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: When the speaker produces soft /t/ syllables, the waveform shows small-amplitude, brief bursts over time.2. Loudness Increase: As the speaker increases loudness, each /t/ syllable corresponds to a waveform with progressively larger peak-to-peak amplitude.3. Time-Domain Representation: The horizontal axis represents time, while the vertical axis shows amplitude; louder speech results in taller waveform peaks.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSpeech intensity is acoustically represented by waveform amplitude in the time domain. Louder speech produces greater air pressure variations at the microphone, which are converted into electrical signals with larger amplitudes. The real-time waveform visualization directly reflects these amplitude changes over time, allowing observation of the relationship between speech loudness and acoustic intensity.VI. Experimental PrecautionsMaintain a constant mouth-to-microphone distance to avoid confounding amplitude changes. Avoid clipping by keeping input levels within range. Conduct the experiment in a quiet environment to reduce noise interference.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visualization of speech amplitude (intensity) changes in the time domain using real-time waveform display. Minimum assumptions include basic acoustics: speech produces pressure variations, louder speech yields larger amplitude, and software displays amplitude versus time.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase: microphone connected, waveform visible but minimal activity. (2) Soft speech phase: speaker produces soft /t/ syllables, resulting in small, regular waveform bursts. (3) Loud speech phase: speaker increases loudness while keeping syllables constant, causing clearly larger waveform amplitudes. (4) Verification constraint: camera/view must clearly show the screen so amplitude changes over time can be visually confirmed, with smooth temporal transitions and direct causal linkage between speech and waveform.

Display: Stop recording and display the waveform. Zoom in so that each syllable waveform can be clearly observed in sequence.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Visually Distinguishing the Acoustic Features of Monophthongs and DiphthongsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Identification of Acoustic Features of Monophthongs and Diphthongs2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the acoustic characteristics of a monophthong and a diphthong using a spectrogram, understand the concepts of stable and changing formant patterns, and master basic spectrogram-based phonetic analysis.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrophone (1), computer with spectrogram software (e.g., Praat), audio interface (optional), quiet recording environment, display screen showing a split spectrogram interface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Connect the microphone to the computer and open the spectrogram software. Set the display to show real-time spectrograms with formant tracking enabled.2. Interface Setup: Configure the interface so that the left panel is designated for the monophthong display and the right panel for the diphthong display.3. Monophthong Production: The speaker faces the microphone and produces a sustained, stable monophthong /e/ for about 2–3 seconds. Observe the left spectrogram panel updating in real time.4. Diphthong Production: After a brief pause, the speaker produces the diphthong /ei/, smoothly transitioning from /e/ to /i/. Observe the right spectrogram panel updating in real time.5. Identification: The operator points out and labels the stable formant bands in the monophthong and the changing formant trajectories in the diphthong.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Monophthong /e/: The spectrogram shows relatively stable, horizontal formant bands (especially F1 and F2) over time.2. Diphthong /ei/: The spectrogram shows clear movement of formant trajectories, especially a rising or shifting F2, reflecting the vowel transition.3. Comparison: The left panel appears temporally stable, while the right panel shows dynamic change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSpeech sounds can be analyzed acoustically using spectrograms, which display frequency, time, and intensity. Monophthongs are produced with a relatively fixed vocal tract configuration, resulting in stable formant frequencies. Diphthongs involve a continuous change in vocal tract shape, causing formant frequencies to shift over time. Visualizing these patterns allows clear differentiation between monophthongs and diphthongs.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure a quiet environment to avoid noise interference; maintain consistent mouth-to-microphone distance; produce vowels steadily and clearly; avoid exaggerated movements that may distort formant tracking.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: visual and acoustic differentiation between monophthongs and diphthongs using spectrograms. Minimum assumptions: a functioning microphone–software system, real-time spectrogram with formant display, and a speaker capable of producing /e/ and /ei/.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – microphone connected and spectrogram interface visible with left/right panels; (2) Action phase – speaker produces sustained /e/, causing stable formant bands to appear; (3) Transition phase – speaker produces /ei/, leading to visible formant movement over time; (4) Identification phase – operator highlights stable versus changing patterns. Visibility constraints: spectrogram labels and formant trajectories must be clearly visible; timing must show real-time cause–effect between speech and visual change.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Microphone Windscreen Reducing Wind-Induced Mic Movement OutdoorsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of a Foam Windscreen on Wind-Induced Microphone Movement2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Speech and Acoustic Data Collection)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that a foam windscreen reduces wind-induced mechanical movement and disturbance of a microphone in outdoor recording conditions, improving recording stability.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical microphones, one thick foam windscreen, two identical microphone mounts or stands, outdoor location with natural breeze, fixed-position camera capable of time-lapse recording, mounting bar or clamp (to keep microphones side by side).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Choose an outdoor location on a breezy day. Mount two identical microphones side by side on the same support so they share the same height and orientation.2. Setup: Leave one microphone bare and cover the other microphone with a thick foam windscreen. Ensure both microphones face the same direction as the incoming wind.3. Camera Setup: Place the camera in front of the microphones. Fix focus, framing, and exposure. Enable time-lapse recording to compress observation time.4. Core Operation: Begin time-lapse recording. Allow natural wind gusts to pass over the microphones without manual interference.5. Completion: Stop recording after sufficient gusts have occurred. Ensure microphones and mounts remain unchanged during the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both microphones are stationary, mounted side by side, with no visible movement in calm moments.2. During Wind Gusts: The bare microphone exhibits more visible shaking or vibration in response to gusts, while the microphone with the foam windscreen shows noticeably reduced movement.3. Comparative Result: Over time-lapse playback, the difference in movement amplitude between the two microphones becomes clear and repeatable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWind gusts exert fluctuating air pressure and turbulence on microphone surfaces, causing mechanical movement and vibration. A foam windscreen diffuses airflow, reducing sudden pressure changes and turbulence acting directly on the microphone body. As a result, the screened microphone experiences less wind-induced movement, demonstrating the practical role of windscreens in stabilizing outdoor acoustic data collection.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both microphones are identical and firmly mounted; do not manually touch or adjust equipment during recording; maintain fixed camera focus and position to ensure fair visual comparison.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plotting and Analyzing the Dynamic Trajectory of Fundamental Frequency (F0) of Speech2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Experimental Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To understand the concept of fundamental frequency (F0) in voiced speech, master basic pitch analysis operations, and observe how F0 changes dynamically over time during vowel production.II. Experimental Equipment and Software1. Microphone (headset or desktop, properly connected)2. Computer3. Speech analysis software with pitch extraction function (e.g., Praat or equivalent)4. Quiet recording environmentIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Connect and test the microphone; open the speech analysis software and select the pitch analysis module.2. Recording: The speaker produces a short, steady vowel /e/ into the microphone. Stop recording after about 1–2 seconds.3. Display: Observe that the recorded audio waveform appears on the screen as an amplitude–time plot.4. F0 Extraction: Use the software pitch function to extract F0; display the F0 contour overlaid on or aligned with the waveform.5. Parameter Adjustment: Adjust pitch analysis settings (e.g., pitch range, smoothing). Note changes in the F0 contour shape.6. Replay Observation: Replay the recorded sound. Observe that the F0 contour updates dynamically and synchronously with playback.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The vowel /e/ produces a clear periodic waveform, indicating voiced speech.2. The extracted F0 contour appears as a relatively smooth curve over time.3. Adjusting pitch parameters changes the smoothness or stability of the F0 contour.4. During replay, the F0 curve moves in real time, corresponding to the temporal progression of the sound.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Fundamental frequency (F0) corresponds to the vibration rate of the vocal folds in voiced speech.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Scale Scaling for Architectural Physical ModelsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Scale Scaling for Architectural Physical Model2. Subject: Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To understand architectural scale concepts by visually comparing the same architectural physical model at 1:100 and 1:50 scales, and to recognize how scale affects perceived size and level of detail.II. Experimental MaterialsArchitectural physical model A (scale 1:100); Architectural physical model B (scale 1:50, same design as model A); Flat display table; Scale labels or cards (1:100, 1:50); Fixed light source; Camera or observer viewpoint.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Preparation: Place the display table under uniform lighting. Ensure both models represent the same architectural design, materials, and proportions.2. Placement: Position the 1:100 model on the left and the 1:50 model on the right, aligned along the same baseline. Attach clear scale labels in front of each model.3. Observation Setup: Adjust the camera or observer viewpoint to a frontal, eye-level angle that can capture both models simultaneously.4. Core Operation: Observe both models side by side without changing distance or viewpoint, focusing on overall size, proportions, and visible details such as windows, doors, and structural elements.5. Comparison Focus: Note that the 1:50 model appears larger and shows more visible details than the 1:100 model, while maintaining the same proportions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both models are static, with identical shapes, colors, and materials.2. Comparative Observation: The 1:50 scale model is clearly larger than the 1:100 scale model; details such as openings and facade elements are easier to distinguish in the 1:50 model.3. Visual Contrast: When viewed together, the difference in scale creates a strong contrast in size and detail clarity while preserving proportional consistency.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleArchitectural scale represents the ratio between the physical model and the real building. A 1:50 scale means 1 unit on the model equals 50 units in reality, while 1:100 means 1 unit equals 100 units. Therefore, for the same design, the 1:50 model has double the linear dimensions of the 1:100 model, resulting in a larger physical size and higher detail visibility. Visual comparison helps learners intuitively understand scale scaling principles in architectural design.VI. Experimental Notes1. Ensure both models are based on the same design to avoid misleading comparisons.2. Keep lighting and viewpoint consistent to maintain fair visual contrast.3. Focus on relative size and detail differences rather than absolute measurements.

Phase 2 (Comparison): The viewer observes that the 1:50 model is visibly larger than the 1:100 model. Phase 3 (Causal Understanding): Increased size leads to clearer and richer details in the 1:50 model. Visibility Constraints: Both models must remain in the same frame with a stable perspective to verify proportional consistency and scale contrast.

Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Sound and Pitch Perception)3. Experiment Objective: To observe how tuning forks of different pitches vibrate and interact with water, and to understand that pitch is related to vibration frequency, as shown by differences in water splash rate.II. Experimental EquipmentMetal tuning forks of two different sizes (one larger, one smaller), rubber or wooden mallet, shallow transparent water tray, clean water, stable tabletop, paper towels (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the shallow transparent tray on a stable tabletop and pour in clean water to a shallow, even depth. Ensure the water surface is calm and clear.2. Setup: Hold the two metal tuning forks upright above the tray. Confirm that the forks are different in size, representing different pitches.3. Striking the Forks: Use the same mallet to strike each tuning fork with similar force to ensure comparable vibration intensity.4. Core Operation: Immediately after striking, dip the tips of both tuning forks into the water at the same depth, keeping them steady and not touching the tray bottom.5. Observation: Observe the water surface around each tuning fork tip while the forks are vibrating.6. Completion: Remove the tuning forks from the water after the vibrations weaken. Wipe the forks dry and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water surface is smooth and still before the tuning forks are dipped.2. During Vibration: When the vibrating tuning forks touch the water, splashes and ripples appear around each fork tip.3. Comparative Phenomenon: The smaller, higher-pitch tuning fork produces more frequent and finer splashes, while the larger, lower-pitch tuning fork produces slower and fewer splashes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSound is produced by vibrations. Pitch is determined by vibration frequency: higher pitch corresponds to higher frequency, and lower pitch corresponds to lower frequency. When tuning forks vibrate in water, their vibrations transfer energy to the water. A higher-frequency vibration causes the water surface to be disturbed more frequently, resulting in a faster splash rate. Thus, differences in splash rate visually demonstrate differences in pitch.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both tuning forks are struck with similar force.2. Splicing Combination – Interlocking: Slightly offset one volume so that two volumes partially penetrate each other, clearly showing an interlocking relationship while maintaining geometric clarity.6. Dynamic Adjustment: Slowly adjust positions (sliding, lifting, rotating minimally) to show alternative classic combinations such as linear extension and stepped composition.7. Final State: Multiple white volumes form a coherent architectural mass, demonstrating classic massing combination logic with clear hierarchy, balance, and proportion.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Architectural Massing Principle: Architectural form can be understood as the combination of simple geometric volumes through addition, stacking, and interlocking.2. Visual Abstraction Principle: Using uniform white volumes removes material and functional distractions, allowing focus on pure spatial and formal relationships.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Granular Material Sliding on Steep vs Shallow RoofsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Granular Sliding on Steep and Shallow Roofs2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how roof slope affects the sliding behavior of snow or granular materials and to understand the architectural principle of slope design for snow shedding.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo roof models of identical material and surface texture; left roof with a gentle slope, right roof with a steep slope; white granular material (simulated snow); tray or base; camera.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place the two roof models side by side on the same base, ensuring identical orientation and surface conditions.2. Adjust the camera to clearly capture both roofs, with emphasis on the roof surfaces.3. Simultaneously or sequentially sprinkle the same amount of white granular material from the same height onto both roofs.4. Do not disturb the roofs; allow gravity to act naturally while recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Granular material rests on both roof surfaces.2. During Sliding: On the steep roof, granules quickly begin to slide downward and accumulate at the base; on the gentle roof, granules slide slowly, partially, or remain in place.3. Final State: The steep roof becomes largely clear, while more material remains on the gentle roof.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe component of gravitational force parallel to the roof surface increases with slope angle. When this force exceeds friction, granular material slides. Steeper roofs have a larger downslope force, promoting faster and more complete sliding, which is why steep roofs are effective for snow shedding in architectural design.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both roofs have the same material and surface roughness; apply equal amounts of granules; keep camera stable and lighting consistent.

manual: Experiment Title: Visualization of Thermal Conductivity Coefficient Comparison of Construction MaterialsSubject: Architecture & Urban Planning – Building PhysicsExperiment Objective: To visually compare the relative thermal conductivity of common construction materials by observing the speed of heat transfer, and to understand how material properties influence heat flow in buildings.Experimental Materials and Setup: Three large solid samples are prepared: rock wool (light yellow, porous texture), steel (silver gray, smooth metallic surface), and wood (brown, fibrous texture). Heat flow is represented by dynamic red arrows.Experimental Procedure: (1) Arrange the three samples side-by-side in the order of rock wool, steel, and wood, ensuring equal size and equal distance from the heat source. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Membrane Panel Vibration under Low-Frequency Sound ExcitationI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Membrane Panel Visibly Vibrating under Low-Frequency Sound ExcitationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning (Architectural Acoustics)Objective: To visually demonstrate how low-frequency sound waves excite a stretched membrane panel, causing observable vibration, and to understand the relationship between sound frequency and membrane response.II. Experimental EquipmentStretched membrane panel (thin elastic membrane mounted in a rigid rectangular frame), subwoofer capable of producing low-frequency tones (20–200 Hz), audio signal generator or sweep track, power amplifier (if required), tripod-mounted camera with fixed-focus capability, stable indoor space with minimal airflow.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the membrane tightly and uniformly in the rigid frame; place the frame vertically. Position the subwoofer directly facing the membrane at a short distance (about 0.3–0.5 m).2. Camera Setup: Place the camera on a tripod facing the membrane panel; fix the focus manually and ensure the entire membrane surface is in frame. Do not adjust focus during recording.3. Sound Setup: Connect the subwoofer to the signal generator or playback device. Set the volume to a safe but clearly effective level for visible vibration.4. Core Operation: Play a low-frequency tone sweep that gradually increases from low to higher frequency and then decreases. Keep all equipment stationary during playback.5. Recording: Record continuously (or using time-lapse) while the frequency sweeps up and down, ensuring stable framing.6. Completion: Stop the sound playback, end recording, and power off equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The membrane appears flat and stationary when no sound is playing.2. During Low-Frequency Excitation: As the subwoofer emits low-frequency sound, the membrane begins to vibrate visibly, with larger and slower oscillations at lower frequencies.3. Frequency Sweep Effect: As frequency increases, the vibration pattern and amplitude change; during the downward sweep, the vibration correspondingly returns to larger, slower motions.V. Experimental Principle SummaryLow-frequency sound waves produce periodic air pressure fluctuations. When these pressure variations reach the stretched membrane, they apply alternating forces that cause the membrane to oscillate. The vibration amplitude depends on sound frequency, membrane tension, and boundary conditions. This experiment demonstrates sound–structure interaction, a key concept in architectural acoustics and building envelope design.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Sedimentation Gradually Burying Objects in a JarSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyObjective: To demonstrate how sediments carried by water settle as water energy decreases, gradually burying objects, illustrating a basic archaeological formation process.II. MaterialsClear glass jar with lid, clean water, mixed sediment (sand, silt, clay), small stones or beads, table, camera or phone fixed on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place small stones at the bottom of the clear jar. Add mixed sediment and fill the jar with water, leaving a small air gap. Seal the lid.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Foam or Cardboard Ribbed Vault Model under Incremental LoadI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Incremental Loading of a Ribbed Vault Model2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how ribbed vaults carry and distribute loads through ribs and supports by incrementally adding identical weights and observing deformation.II. Experimental EquipmentFoam or cardboard ribbed vault model (self-made or prefabricated), flat base board, identical small weights (coins or metal washers, 10–20 pieces), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable lighting, marker (optional for reference points).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the ribbed vault model on a flat, stable base. Ensure ribs, crown, and supports are clearly visible. Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing the model; lock focus and framing.2. Initial Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording with no load applied. Observe and record the undeformed initial state.3. Incremental Loading: Place identical small weights one by one across the top of the vault, starting at the crown and then symmetrically along adjacent rib intersections. Pause briefly between each addition to allow visible response.4. Continued Loading: Continue adding weights evenly until slight deformation, rib emphasis, or partial instability becomes visible.5. Completion: Stop adding weights before total collapse (if possible). End recording and remove weights after documentation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The vault maintains its shape with no visible deformation.2. Early Loading: As initial weights are added, the structure remains stable, with load visually aligned along the ribs.3. High Load (Optional): Concentrated deformation or local buckling may occur, indicating structural limits.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRibbed vaults work by concentrating loads along ribs rather than distributing them uniformly across the entire surface. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure weights are identical to maintain controlled loading; add weights symmetrically; keep camera fixed; avoid sudden impacts that may cause premature collapse.

manual: Experiment Title: Observation of Wood Surface Before and After Progressive SandingSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyExperiment Objective: To observe and understand how progressive sanding with different grit sandpapers alters the surface texture of wood, and to demonstrate standard hand-sanding procedures used in archaeological wood analysis and conservation.Equipment and Materials: Wooden board (flat, untreated), workbench, clamp or vise, coarse grit sandpaper (e.g., 80 grit), medium grit sandpaper (e.g., 150 grit), fine grit sandpaper (e.g., 320 grit), soft brush or cloth, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Place the wooden board flat on the workbench and secure it firmly with a clamp to prevent movement. Set up the camera facing the board, fix the focus and frame, and start time-lapse recording.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the unsanded wood surface, noting visible roughness, tool marks, or uneven texture.3. Coarse Sanding: Using coarse grit sandpaper, sand the wood surface evenly along the grain with steady hand pressure. Continue until major roughness and tool marks are reduced. Brush off dust.4. Medium Sanding: Switch to medium grit sandpaper. Sand along the grain to remove scratches left by the coarse grit and further smooth the surface. Clean the surface again.5. Fine Sanding: Switch to fine grit sandpaper. Lightly sand to refine the surface, producing a smooth and even texture. Remove remaining dust.6. Final Observation: Observe and record the final sanded surface for comparison with the initial state. Stop recording and release the clamp.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- Before sanding: The wood surface appears rough, with visible grain irregularities and tool marks.- After coarse sanding: Surface becomes flatter but shows deep, uniform scratches from coarse grit.- After medium sanding: Scratches become finer and less visible; surface feels smoother.- After fine sanding: Surface appears smooth and uniform, with minimal visible scratches and a slight sheen.Summary of Experimental Principle:Progressive sanding works by gradually reducing surface irregularities through abrasion. Coarse grit removes material quickly to level the surface, while successive finer grits remove the scratches left by previous stages. This principle is important in archaeological wood analysis and conservation, where controlled surface preparation reveals manufacturing traces and material characteristics without damaging the artifact.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Acidic vs Alkaline Soil on Shell or Limestone PreservationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Acidic and Alkaline Soil on Shell or Limestone Fragments2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that shell or limestone fragments remain relatively intact in alkaline soil but gradually erode in acidic soil, helping explain differential preservation of calcareous materials in archaeological contexts.II. Experimental Materials- Two identical shell or limestone fragments (similar size, thickness, and color)- Two transparent containers or beakers- Acidic soil slurry (soil mixed with water; acidity adjusted with weak acid such as vinegar)- Alkaline soil slurry (soil mixed with water; alkalinity adjusted with lime or baking soda)- Stirring rods or spoons- Labels or markers- Camera or smartphone with fixed support for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Label the two containers as Acidic Soil and Alkaline Soil. Pour equal volumes of the prepared soil slurries into their respective containers.2. Placement: Place one identical shell or limestone fragment into each container, ensuring both fragments are fully submerged.3. Stirring: Gently stir each container for the same duration to ensure uniform contact between the fragment and soil slurry.4. Positioning: Place the two containers side by side on a stable surface under the same lighting conditions.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and angle so that both containers are clearly visible. Start time-lapse recording.6. Observation Period: Leave the setup undisturbed. For demonstration purposes, time may be accelerated to show changes within seconds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both shell or limestone fragments appear solid, with clear edges and similar surface texture.2. Over Time: In the acidic soil slurry, the fragment gradually shows surface dulling, pitting, or thinning. In the alkaline soil slurry, the fragment shows little to no visible change.3. Comparative Result: The difference in preservation between the two fragments becomes increasingly obvious when viewed side by side.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleShells and limestone are primarily composed of calcium carbonate. In acidic conditions, hydrogen ions react with calcium carbonate, causing it to dissolve and leading to erosion. In alkaline soils, this reaction is inhibited, allowing calcareous materials to remain relatively intact. This principle explains why shells and limestone artifacts are better preserved in alkaline archaeological contexts than in acidic ones.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Ice Blocks in Insulated vs Bare Containers Melting Over TimeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Ice Melting in Insulated and Bare Containers2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the effect of thermal insulation on heat transfer by visually comparing the melting rates of ice blocks placed in an insulated container and a bare container at room temperature, and to understand the basic principle of insulation used in architectural and urban environmental design.II. Experimental Equipment1. Two identical clear containers (same size, shape, and material)2. Two equal-sized ice blocks (same mass and shape)3. Foam insulation material (sufficient to wrap one container)4. Tabletop in an indoor room at stable room temperature5. Camera or smartphone with time-lapse photography function6. Tripod or fixed camera stand7. Timer or clock (optional, for reference)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the two identical clear containers side by side on a flat tabletop. Ensure the surrounding environment is stable, with no direct sunlight, airflow, or external heat sources.2. Container Setup: Leave the left container bare. Wrap the right container evenly with foam insulation, ensuring the insulation covers the sides without obstructing the camera view of the ice.3. Ice Placement: Place one ice block of equal size into each container at the same time. Ensure both ice blocks initially appear solid, transparent-white, and unmelted.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing the two containers. Adjust the framing so both containers are fully visible, and lock the focus, exposure, and white balance to keep visual conditions consistent.5. Recording: Start time-lapse recording immediately after placing the ice blocks. Allow the experiment to proceed at room temperature without interference.6. Completion: Continue recording until a clear difference in melting degree between the two containers is observed. Stop recording and save the footage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both containers contain solid ice blocks of similar size and shape, with no visible liquid water.2. Early Stage: After a short time, a thin layer of water appears at the bottom of both containers. The ice in the bare container begins shrinking slightly faster.3. Middle Stage: The ice block in the bare container becomes noticeably smaller, surrounded by more liquid water. The ice in the insulated container remains larger and melts more slowly.4. Later Stage: The bare container may contain mostly water with a small remaining ice piece, while the insulated container still retains a larger portion of solid ice.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the principle of heat transfer and thermal insulation. At room temperature, heat flows from the surrounding air into the containers and then into the ice. The bare container allows heat to transfer more quickly through conduction and convection, causing the ice to melt faster. The foam-insulated container reduces heat transfer by providing a barrier with low thermal conductivity, slowing the melting process. This principle is widely applied in architecture and urban planning to improve building energy efficiency by reducing unwanted heat gain or loss.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical containers and ice blocks to ensure a fair comparison.2. Avoid touching or moving the containers during recording.3. Keep environmental conditions consistent throughout the experiment.4. Ensure the camera focus and position remain fixed during time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Thermal insulation reduces heat transfer, slowing ice melting compared to an uninsulated condition. Minimum assumptions: identical containers and ice blocks, stable room temperature, and insulation with low thermal conductivity. Phased storyline: (1) Initial state—two identical ice blocks placed simultaneously in side-by-side clear containers, one insulated; (2) Early melting—both ice blocks begin to melt, with visible water forming first in the bare container; (3) Divergence—bare container ice shrinks noticeably faster while insulated container retains more solid ice; (4) Outcome—clear contrast in remaining ice volume. Visibility constraints: fixed camera focus, full view of both containers at all times, and no camera movement to allow direct visual comparison and causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Ductile and Brittle Failure Form Comparison of Structural MaterialsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Ductile and Brittle Failure Form Comparison of Structural Materials2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare ductile failure and brittle failure of structural materials under tensile load, understand their different deformation and fracture characteristics, and recognize their implications for architectural structural design and safety.II. Experimental Equipment1. Steel specimen (ductile material), silver-gray, prismatic or cylindrical, standard size.2. Stone specimen (brittle material), beige, same shape and dimensions as the steel specimen.3. Tensile testing device or simulated tensile loading frame.4. Clamps or grips for fixing both ends of the specimens.5. Measuring scale or visual markers (optional, for observing elongation).6. Safety shield or protective barrier.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the steel specimen on the left and the stone specimen on the right, ensuring both have identical dimensions and are aligned along the same tensile axis. Fix both ends of each specimen securely in the tensile device.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial shape, color, and surface condition of both specimens. Confirm no visible cracks or defects.3. Tensile Loading: Gradually apply tensile force to both specimens at a controlled and similar rate.4. Steel Specimen Observation: Continue loading while closely observing the steel specimen. Note the gradual elongation, visible thinning (necking), and significant plastic deformation before fracture.5. Stone Specimen Observation: Continue loading the stone specimen. Observe that it shows little to no visible deformation and fractures suddenly once its tensile strength is exceeded.6. Fracture Completion: Stop loading after both specimens have fractured. Maintain the fractured pieces in place for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Steel (Ductile) Component: Before fracture, the steel specimen becomes longer and thinner, showing clear plastic deformation. The fracture occurs after noticeable necking, and the fracture surface appears uneven and fibrous.2. Stone (Brittle) Component: The stone specimen remains almost unchanged in shape until fracture. It breaks suddenly without obvious elongation, producing a relatively flat and clean fracture surface.3. Comparative Observation: Under the same tensile conditions, steel absorbs more energy through deformation, while stone fails abruptly.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Ductile Failure Principle: Ductile materials like steel can undergo significant plastic deformation under tensile stress. This deformation redistributes stress and provides warning before failure.2. Brittle Failure Principle: Brittle materials like stone have limited ability to deform plastically. When tensile stress exceeds their strength, they fracture suddenly.3. Architectural Significance: Understanding ductile versus brittle failure is critical in structural design, as ductile behavior improves safety by providing visible deformation and energy dissipation before collapse.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure specimens are securely fixed to avoid slippage.2. Apply load gradually to clearly observe deformation and fracture processes.3. Use protective barriers to prevent injury from sudden brittle fracture.4. After the experiment, safely dispose of fractured materials and clean the equipment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is the visual and mechanistic comparison between ductile and brittle failure of structural materials under tensile load. Minimum assumptions include identical specimen geometry, uniaxial tension, and correct material behavior (steel exhibits plastic deformation; stone does not).Phased Storyline Summary: Phase 1 – Initial state: two identical columns, steel on the left (silver-gray) and stone on the right (beige), intact and fixed in tension. Phase 2 – Loading: tensile force increases; steel begins to elongate while stone remains unchanged. Phase 3 – Pre-failure: steel shows necking and visible thinning; stone still shows no deformation. Phase 4 – Failure: steel fractures after significant deformation with an uneven fracture surface; stone fractures suddenly with a clean interface. Visibility Constraints: The camera should maintain a clear frontal or slightly angled view, keeping both specimens in frame and focusing on deformation and fracture interfaces for verification.

Experiment Title: Visual Documentation of the Athenian Owl Quadrachma in a Museum Display Case2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Numismatics)3. Experiment Objective: Through controlled camera movement around a museum display case, to visually document and observe the material, iconography, and craftsmanship of the Athenian Owl Quadrachma, and to understand how systematic visual recording supports archaeological interpretation and public presentation of ancient coins.II. Experimental Equipment1. Museum display case containing one or more authentic or replica Athenian Owl Quadrachma coins.2. Camera (handheld or stabilized, e.g., gimbal-supported) capable of continuous video recording.3. Controlled lighting environment (museum ambient lighting; no direct glare).4. Tripod or stabilizer (optional, recommended for smooth motion).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Ensure the display case is clean, the coins are clearly visible, and lighting evenly illuminates both obverse and reverse surfaces without reflections. Set the camera to continuous recording mode.2. Initial Framing: Position the camera at eye level in front of the display case, capturing a clear frontal view of the Athenian Owl Quadrachma, including its silver surface and engraved details.3. Core Operation – Circling Movement: Slowly move the camera in a smooth circular path around the display case (approximately 180–360 degrees), maintaining a constant distance. Keep the coin centered in the frame while changing perspective to show depth, relief, and edge thickness.4. Detail Capture: During the circling motion, briefly slow down at key angles to emphasize the obverse (Athena’s helmeted head) and the reverse (owl, olive sprig, and incuse square).5. Conclusion: Complete the circular movement and gently stop recording, ensuring the final frame remains stable and focused on the coin.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The coin appears stationary inside the display case, silver-gray in color, with visible engraved imagery under stable lighting.2. During Camera Movement: As the camera circles, highlights and shadows shift across the coin’s surface, revealing relief depth, wear patterns, and fine engraving lines. The owl and Athena motifs become clearer from different angles.3. Final State: The coin remains unchanged physically, but the viewer gains a comprehensive visual understanding of its three-dimensional form and iconographic details.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on archaeological visual documentation principles. By systematically changing the camera’s spatial relationship to the object, parallax, light reflection, and shadow variation reveal physical properties such as relief, thickness, and craftsmanship. For numismatics, this method supports accurate interpretation of iconography, production techniques, and preservation state, demonstrating how controlled observation enhances understanding of ancient material culture.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Porosity-Related Water Absorption of a Pottery FragmentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Porosity-Related Water Absorption of a Pottery Fragment2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the porosity of unglazed pottery by observing air bubbles released during water absorption.II. Experimental EquipmentUnglazed pottery fragment (completely dry, with visible pores), clear glass tank or aquarium, clean still water (room temperature), stable support surface, camera with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Ensure the pottery fragment is completely dry. Fill the glass tank with clear water and allow it to settle until no movement is visible. Fix the camera position and focus on the central area of the tank.Core Operation: Gently place the dry, unglazed pottery fragment into the water, fully submerging it without splashing or stirring the water.Observation: Leave the fragment undisturbed for several minutes while recording with time-lapse photography. Do not touch or move the tank.Conclusion: After observation, stop recording and remove the fragment if needed; dry equipment and restore the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Water is clear and still; pottery fragment shows no surface bubbles before immersion.2. After Immersion: Small air bubbles emerge from the surface pores of the pottery fragment and rise to the water surface.3. Over Time: The number of bubbles gradually decreases as water fills the internal pores of the fragment.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnglazed pottery contains microscopic pores formed during shaping and firing. When a dry fragment is submerged, trapped air within these pores is displaced by water and escapes as visible bubbles. This process demonstrates the porosity and water absorption characteristics of archaeological ceramics, which are important indicators of manufacturing technique and functional use.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Shaping a Carthaginian-Style Pottery Vessel on a Simple TurntableI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Shaping Carthaginian Pottery with a Short Neck and Bulging Belly2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To reproduce the characteristic form of Carthaginian pottery (short neck, bulging belly) using traditional North African pottery-making techniques, and to observe shape evolution through time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentPlastic or wooden simple turntable, prepared clay (medium plasticity, reddish-brown), small bowl of water, hands (no modern tools), cloth base, fixed camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clay lump at the center of the simple turntable; moisten hands lightly; start fixed camera recording.2. Centering: Rotate the turntable by hand while pressing clay inward and upward to form a centered cone, then compress into a dome.3. Opening: Press thumbs into the center while rotating to create an internal cavity, keeping the base thick.4. Pulling Walls: Gradually pull the walls upward while rotating, maintaining even thickness.5. Belly Shaping: Apply outward pressure at the mid-body while supporting from inside to create a rounded, bulging belly.6. Neck Shaping: Compress the upper section inward to form a short, slightly constricted neck.7. Finishing: Smooth the surface with wet hands; stop rotation; allow the form to stabilize. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Clay is amorphous and centered on the turntable.2. During Shaping: Walls rise evenly; mid-section expands outward into a rounded belly.3. Final State: Finished vessel clearly shows a bulging belly and a short neck, typical of Carthaginian pottery.4. Time-lapse Effect: Gradual transformations appear accelerated, highlighting shape evolution.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTraditional North African pottery relies on manual rotation and hand pressure rather than high-speed wheels. Centrifugal force from rotation, combined with controlled hand pressure and moisture, allows expansion of the vessel’s belly and compression of the neck. The characteristic Carthaginian form reflects functional storage needs and cultural aesthetics, achieved through sequential shaping rather than tools.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Traditional Carthaginian pottery-making emphasizes hand-shaped vessels with a short neck and bulging belly formed on a simple turntable.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Clay is plastic and responsive to hand pressure; rotation provides centrifugal force; hand placement causally determines vessel geometry.Phased Storyline: (1) Centering clay on a rotating turntable; (2) opening and pulling walls upward; (3) deliberate outward shaping to form a bulging belly; (4) inward compression to create a short neck; (5) stabilized finished form shown via time-lapse. Visibility Constraints: Camera remains fixed, focused on the vessel; time-lapse acceleration preserves order but not real-time duration.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Differential Water Erosion of Sandstone and GraniteI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Water Erosion Differences Between Sandstone and GraniteSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyObjective: To demonstrate how water erosion affects soft sandstone more rapidly than hard granite through controlled visual comparison.II. Materials and EquipmentTan sandstone block (1, similar size), speckled granite block (1, similar size), two shallow trays, water source (bottle or tubing), support to create a narrow steady stream, camera with tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Place the two shallow trays side by side on a level surface.2. Position the tan sandstone block in the left tray and the speckled granite block in the right tray, ensuring similar orientation and exposure.3. Adjust the camera on a tripod facing both trays; fix focus, framing, and exposure for time-lapse recording.4. Pour or drip a narrow, steady stream of water onto the upper surface of each rock simultaneously, keeping flow rate similar.5. Continue water flow for an extended period; record using time-lapse to compress the process.6. Stop water flow and recording after visible surface changes appear.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Both rocks appear solid and intact, with clear color and texture.During erosion: Sandstone gradually develops small grooves, rounded edges, or sediment accumulation; water may appear slightly cloudy.Granite shows little to no visible surface change, maintaining sharp texture and clarity.Final: Clear contrast between worn sandstone and relatively unchanged granite.V. Experimental Principle SummarySandstone is composed of loosely cemented grains and has lower hardness, making it more susceptible to mechanical erosion by flowing water. Granite is a hard, crystalline igneous rock with tightly interlocked minerals, resisting abrasion. In archaeology, such differential erosion explains why certain stone structures or tools degrade faster in water-rich environments.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Fatty Residue on Ceramic Shards Causing Water BeadingI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Water Beading on Used Ceramic Shard Due to Fatty ResidueSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how fatty residues from long-term use alter ceramic surface properties, causing a hydrophobic effect observable through water beading and motion during tilting.II. Experimental MaterialsCeramic shard A (used, darker surface);Ceramic shard B (freshly cleaned, lighter surface);Dropper or pipette;Clear water;Flat table or board;Camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the table on a stable surface. Position the two ceramic shards side by side, with shard A (used, darker) on one side and shard B (clean) on the other. Ensure both shards lie flat.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera above or at a shallow angle facing the shards. Fix focus and exposure; start time-lapse recording.3. Water Application: Using the dropper, drip an equal amount of clear water onto the surface of shard A, then onto shard B.4. Tilting Operation: Gently tilt the table back and forth at a small angle, keeping motion slow and consistent.5. Completion: Stop tilting after clear differences in water behavior are observed. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both shards appear dry; shard A is darker and more polished from use, shard B is lighter and matte.After Dripping Water: On shard A, water forms rounded droplets that bead up; on shard B, water spreads or flattens against the surface.During Tilting: Water droplets on shard A roll or slide easily with tilting, while water on shard B moves slowly or remains spread.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLong-term use of ceramic vessels can leave fatty organic residues embedded in surface pores. These residues reduce surface energy, making the surface hydrophobic. When water contacts such a surface, cohesive forces within the water exceed adhesive forces with the ceramic, producing beading and easy movement. A freshly cleaned ceramic lacks these residues, remains hydrophilic, and allows water to spread. This contrast helps archaeologists infer past usage of ceramic artifacts.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate hydrophobic water-beading caused by fatty residues on used ceramic surfaces compared with clean ceramics. Minimum assumptions: one shard visibly darker from use indicating residue presence; clean shard free of residue; water behavior reflects surface energy differences.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup shows two contrasting shards side by side under fixed camera; (2) Water droplets applied to both surfaces; (3) Immediate contrast appears as beading on used shard versus spreading on clean shard; (4) Gentle tilting amplifies contrast as droplets roll on hydrophobic surface and lag on hydrophilic surface. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly capture droplet shape and motion; focus and framing remain fixed to verify causal sequence.
