manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Femur Side Determination Using Femoral Head Orientation and CondylesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Femur Side Determination Using Femoral Head Orientation and Condyles2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Osteology)3. Experiment Objective: To determine whether a single human femur belongs to the left or right side of the body by observing the orientation of the femoral head and the morphology of the distal condyles through systematic rotation and multi-angle observation.II. Experimental EquipmentSingle adult human femur (dry bone or teaching model), flat lab table with neutral background, disposable gloves (optional), fixed-position camera or tripod, overhead light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the lab table under uniform lighting. Position the camera above or at an oblique angle to the table and fix the focus for time-lapse photography. Ensure no zoom or refocusing occurs during recording.2. Initial Placement: Lay the femur flat on the lab table with the shaft horizontal. Ensure the entire bone is visible within the camera frame.3. Observation of Femoral Head: Slowly rotate the femur by hand to identify the spherical femoral head. Observe the direction it projects relative to the shaft, noting that it always faces medially toward the body midline.4. Observation of Distal Condyles: Continue rotating the femur to view the distal end. Observe the medial and lateral condyles, noting asymmetry in size and extension; the medial condyle typically extends further distally.5. Integrated Judgment: Rotate the femur through multiple angles, alternating views of the proximal and distal ends, to confirm consistency between femoral head orientation and condylar morphology.6. Completion: Return the femur to a neutral position on the table and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The femoral head appears as a smooth, rounded structure projecting to one side of the shaft.2. During rotation, the femoral head consistently points medially.3. The distal condyles are uneven; the medial condyle is larger and extends lower than the lateral condyle.4. Combining these observations allows clear identification of the femur as left or right.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe principle of femur side determination is based on human bilateral symmetry and functional anatomy. The femoral head articulates with the acetabulum and therefore always faces medially. The distal femur shows asymmetrical condyles adapted to knee mechanics, with the medial condyle extending further. By aligning femoral head orientation with condylar asymmetry, the anatomical side of the femur can be reliably determined.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle the bone carefully to avoid damage.2. Do not change camera focus or position during recording.3. Ensure lighting remains constant to avoid visual misinterpretation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Visual Features of Polished Surfaces on Ground Stone ToolsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Grinding and Polishing of a Ground Stone ToolSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how grinding produces polished stone tool surfaces that are delicate, smooth, and free of flake scars, through visual observation of the grinding process using time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsStone blank (hard stone such as basalt or sandstone), grinding slab or abrasive stone, water (as lubricant, optional), hands or simple holding tool, fixed camera or tripod, time-lapse recording device.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the stone blank on the grinding slab. Adjust the camera to focus closely on the stone surface, ensuring stable framing for time-lapse capture.2. Initial Polishing Stage: Rub the stone blank against the abrasive surface using steady, repeated motions. Apply consistent pressure, optionally adding water to reduce dust and enhance abrasion.3. Intermediate Shaping Stage: Continue grinding while slightly adjusting angles to refine edges and contours. Maintain repetitive motion to ensure even abrasion.4. Final Polishing Stage: Focus on smoothing the entire surface with lighter, more uniform strokes until the surface appears fine and even.5. Recording: Capture the entire process using time-lapse photography to compress long grinding durations into a short visual sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The stone surface appears rough, uneven, and matte, with visible irregularities.2. During Grinding: The surface gradually becomes flatter and smoother; rough textures diminish as grinding continues.3. Final State: The stone tool shows a delicate, smooth surface with a uniform texture and no visible flake scars, indicating polishing rather than knapping.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe principle of this experiment is mechanical abrasion. Repeated grinding causes friction between the stone blank and abrasive surface, gradually wearing down protrusions and irregularities. Unlike flaking, grinding removes material evenly, producing smooth, polished surfaces without flake scars. This process explains the characteristic visual features of ground stone tools in archaeology.VI. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Stop-Motion Animation on a TabletopI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Stop-Motion Animation Using a Clay Character2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Communication & Media Studies3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic stop-motion animation process by setting up objects, capturing frames one by one with a fixed camera, and assembling them into a continuous motion sequence; to master the importance of fixed focus, stable lighting, and incremental movement.II. Experimental EquipmentTabletop or flat desk surface; clay character (simple handmade figure); stable background board; fixed light sources (desk lamps); tripod; digital camera or smartphone with camera app; frame capture or time-lapse/stop-motion app.III. Experimental Procedure1. Object Setup: Place the tabletop against a stable background. Position the clay character upright at the center of the tabletop. Arrange lights on both sides to ensure even and fixed illumination. Do not change lighting during the experiment.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the tabletop. Adjust framing so the clay character is fully visible. Set the camera to manual or fixed focus and lock exposure if possible to avoid changes between frames.3. Initial Capture: Ensure the clay character is still. Capture the first frame using the camera or stop-motion app.4. Frame-by-Frame Capture: Gently move one part of the clay character (such as an arm or head) a very small distance. Capture the next frame. Repeat this process, keeping movements minimal and consistent, and ensuring the camera and lights remain unmoved.5. Sequence Assembly: After capturing multiple frames, use the app or software to automatically arrange the frames in order and preview the animation sequence.6. Completion: Play back the assembled sequence to observe the motion effect. Save the animation file.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The clay character appears stationary in a single frame.2. During Capture: Each frame shows a slightly different position of the clay character while the background, lighting, and camera view remain unchanged.3. Final Sequence: When frames are played in order, the clay character appears to move smoothly, creating the illusion of continuous motion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesStop-motion animation works by exploiting persistence of vision. By capturing a series of still images in which an object is moved slightly between frames, and then playing them rapidly in sequence, the human eye perceives continuous motion. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Color Constancy Under Changing Illumination (Warm to Cool Lighting)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Color Constancy Under Changing Illumination (Warm to Cool Lighting)2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Communication & Media Studies (Visual Perception)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the phenomenon of color constancy, showing that human perception tends to perceive the color of an object (a red apple) as stable even when the illumination changes smoothly from warm yellow light to cool blue light; to understand the difference between physical color signals and perceptual color experience.II. Experimental EquipmentRed apple (fresh, matte surface preferred), white tablecloth (clean, neutral white), table, adjustable room lighting or LED light source capable of continuous color temperature change (warm yellow to cool blue), camera or smartphone with tripod, time-lapse photography function, fixed focal length and exposure settings, darkened room to minimize external light interference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Preparation: Place the white tablecloth flat on the table. Put the red apple at the center of the tablecloth. Ensure no other colored objects are visible in the frame.2. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod directly facing the apple. Fix focus, framing, white balance, and exposure manually to avoid automatic correction during shooting. Ensure the apple and tablecloth remain fully within the frame.3. Lighting Setup: Set the initial lighting to warm yellow illumination (simulating tungsten light). Confirm that the apple appears strongly warm-toned in raw camera capture.4. Core Operation (Time-Lapse Recording): Start time-lapse recording. Gradually and smoothly shift the room lighting from warm yellow to neutral white and then to cool blue over a continuous period. Do not move the apple, tablecloth, camera, or camera settings during this process.5. Completion: Stop recording once the lighting has fully transitioned to cool blue. Save the recorded time-lapse sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Under warm yellow lighting, the white tablecloth appears yellowish, and the apple reflects warm tones.2. During Lighting Transition: As the illumination shifts, the physical color of the light reflected from both the apple and tablecloth changes continuously. The tablecloth appears to shift noticeably from yellowish to bluish.3. Perceptual Outcome: Despite the changing illumination, observers tend to perceive the apple as consistently red throughout the sequence, while the tablecloth is perceived as adapting to the light color.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates color constancy, a key concept in visual perception and media studies. Color constancy refers to the ability of the human visual system to perceive the color of objects as relatively stable despite changes in illumination. Although the spectral composition of light reflected from the apple changes significantly from warm to cool lighting, the brain uses contextual cues (such as the white tablecloth and overall scene illumination) to discount the light source and maintain a stable perception of the apple’s color. This illustrates that perceived color is not solely determined by physical wavelengths but is a result of perceptual and cognitive processing.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Color constancy—the perceptual stability of object color under changing illumination. Minimum assumptions: a single constant object (red apple), a neutral reference surface (white tablecloth), fixed camera parameters, and a continuous change in illumination color temperature.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial warm-light phase—scene appears yellowish; (2) Transition phase—illumination smoothly shifts through neutral to cool; physical light on all objects changes; (3) Final cool-light phase—scene appears bluish. Key causal transition: change in illumination leads to global color shifts, while perceptual interpretation maintains apple redness. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed, apple always in view, lighting change is smooth and continuous to allow verification of perceptual stability.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Cross-continental Fiddler Crab Claw-Wave Signal ComparisonSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Gender & Sexuality Studies (Animal Signaling and Display)Objective: To visually compare and understand cross-continental differences in fiddler crab claw-wave signaling, focusing on European species left-right waving versus North American species up-down waving through controlled visual demonstration.II. Experimental Materials and Setup1. Video footage or live specimens of a European fiddler crab species and a North American fiddler crab species.2. Static camera mounted on a tripod.3. Split-screen or dual-frame composition (left panel: European species; right panel: North American species).4. Neutral background and sufficient lighting to clearly show claw motion.5. Time-lapse or accelerated playback software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Position the camera statically facing the crabs’ frontal or lateral view, ensuring the major claw is fully visible in both panels.2. Framing: Assign the European species to the left panel and the North American species to the right panel; ensure equal scale and perspective.3. Recording: Capture repeated claw-wave displays from both species without camera movement.4. Time-lapse Processing: Apply time-lapse or accelerated playback to condense repeated waving into a short demonstration while preserving motion direction.5. Presentation: Display the synchronized split-screen video for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. European species (left panel): The enlarged claw moves repeatedly in a horizontal left-right waving pattern.2. North American species (right panel): The enlarged claw moves repeatedly in a vertical up-down waving pattern.3. Both species show rhythmic, repeated motions characteristic of signaling behavior.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFiddler crab claw waving is a sexually selected signaling behavior used in courtship and territorial display. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: LED Light Sender and Camera Receiver with Increasing Blink RateI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of LED Blinking Rate Increase Using a Camera2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Communication & Media Studies3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a single LED transmitting light signals interacts with a camera receiver, and how increasing blink rate affects visual perception and recorded images under fixed-focus, continuous viewing conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentSingle LED light source (any visible color, e.g., red), LED driver or microcontroller capable of adjusting blink rate, power supply, digital camera or smartphone camera with video or time-lapse function, tripod or fixed mount for the camera, dark or semi-dark room to enhance visibility.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mount the camera on a tripod and fix the focus manually so it will not refocus during recording. Position the camera so the LED is centered in the frame.2. Setup: Place the LED directly facing the camera at a fixed distance. Turn off unnecessary ambient lights to improve contrast.3. Initial Operation: Set the LED to blink a simple repeating pattern (e.g., on–off) at a low frequency that is clearly distinguishable by the human eye.4. Core Operation: Start continuous video recording or time-lapse photography. Gradually increase the LED blink rate in small, regular steps while maintaining the same pattern and LED position.5. Completion: Continue increasing the blink rate until the blinking appears continuous, banded, or visually altered on the camera display. Stop recording and power off the LED.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low blink rates, the LED appears as distinct on–off flashes, clearly separated in time.2. As the blink rate increases, the flashes appear faster and may begin to blur or merge when viewed through the camera.3. At higher blink rates, the LED may appear continuously lit, flickering, or show striped/banded patterns due to interaction with the camera frame rate and sampling.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on principles of visual perception and media technology. Human vision has persistence of vision, causing rapidly blinking light to appear continuous beyond a certain frequency. Cameras sample light at discrete frame rates; when the LED blink rate approaches or exceeds the camera frame rate, aliasing effects such as flicker or banding occur. This demonstrates fundamental concepts in optical communication, signal transmission, and media reception.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the camera focus remains fixed throughout the experiment.2. Increase blink rate gradually to clearly observe transitional phenomena.3. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Preparation: Arrange the medieval castle courtyard. Position background knights and horses to allow continuous walking or riding paths.2. Subject Positioning: Place the main armored knight at the center of the courtyard. Ensure full armor is worn, including both gauntlets.3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera or smartphone on a stable support. Select time-lapse mode and manually fix the focus on the main knight.4. Core Operation: The knight stops walking, removes one gauntlet, and takes out a modern smartphone. The knight interacts with the screen while remaining mostly still.5. Background Motion: At the same time, other knights and horses continue moving naturally through the courtyard.6. Recording: Start time-lapse recording for a short, accelerated duration, then stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The knight and surroundings appear normal at the start.2. During Recording: The main knight remains sharp and stable, while surrounding knights and horses appear to move rapidly due to time-lapse compression.3. Visual Contrast: A clear contrast is observed between the static, focused knight using a smartphone and the accelerated medieval activity around him.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis demonstration relies on literary anachronism and visual storytelling. The modern smartphone contrasts with medieval armor to create temporal dissonance. Fixed-focus time-lapse photography compresses time, causing moving background elements to accelerate while the stationary subject remains clear, reinforcing the thematic contrast between stillness and motion, past and present.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Visual and narrative anachronism demonstrated through a medieval knight using modern technology, combined with the photographic principle of fixed-focus time-lapse.Minimum Assumptions: A recognizable medieval environment, a clearly armored knight, a visibly modern smartphone, and a camera capable of time-lapse with fixed focus.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish medieval courtyard and moving background figures; (2) Knight stops and removes a gauntlet; (3) Knight uses modern smartphone; (4) Time-lapse effect shows accelerated movement of others while the knight remains stable and in focus. The camera perspective must remain fixed to verify focus stability and time compression.

manual: Instructions for the Comparative Literature Demonstration Experiment: Same Café Encounter in Film Noir vs Romantic Comedy StylesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Split-Screen Performance of One Story in Two Genres2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Literature & Comparative Literature3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how cinematic style (lighting, music, performance) reshapes narrative meaning by presenting the same short café encounter simultaneously as film noir and as romantic comedy.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Single café set or simulated café space (table, two chairs, counter background).2. Two actors (one protagonist, one stranger).3. Camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus and fixed framing.4. Lighting equipment: low-key, high-contrast light for noir; soft, high-key light for romantic comedy.5. Audio tracks: tense jazz/ambient noir music; light, upbeat romantic comedy music.6. Video editing software capable of split-screen and time-lapse compression.III. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Preparation: Arrange one café set. Mark actor positions and movement paths to ensure identical blocking in both performances.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod; lock focus, zoom, and angle. Do not move the camera throughout recording.3. Performance Recording – Noir Version: Light the set with strong shadows and contrast. Costume the protagonist as a private investigator. Actors perform the café meeting with restrained, serious acting. Record the full scene.4. Performance Recording – Romantic Comedy Version: Keep camera and blocking identical. Change lighting to bright and even. Adjust costumes to casual/light tones. Actors perform the same actions and dialogue beats with playful, warm acting. Record the scene.5. Editing: Place the noir version on the left and the romantic comedy version on the right in split-screen. Synchronize actions precisely. Apply time-lapse compression if needed to fit within 10–15 seconds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both sides show the same café layout and camera perspective.2. During the Encounter: Actors enter, sit, and interact in matching timing and movement on both sides.3. Stylistic Contrast: The left side appears tense and mysterious due to lighting, music, and acting; the right side appears lighthearted and romantic with bright visuals and cheerful music.4. Overall Effect: Despite identical actions, viewers perceive two different stories and emotional tones.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment illustrates a core principle of comparative literature and film studies: narrative meaning is not fixed by plot alone but is co-created by stylistic systems. Lighting, music, performance, and genre conventions function as interpretive frameworks that causally shape audience perception, transforming the same sequence of events into distinct narrative experiences.VI. Experimental Notes1. Camera focus and framing must remain fixed to isolate style as the only variable.2. Blocking and timing must match to ensure comparability.3. Time-lapse is permitted only to compress duration, not to alter event order.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate how identical narrative actions acquire different meanings through genre-specific cinematic style. Minimum assumptions: one fixed café space, identical blocking, fixed camera, and two contrasting genre systems (film noir vs romantic comedy).Phased storyline: (1) Establish split-screen café with identical framing; (2) Characters enter and sit simultaneously; (3) Interaction unfolds with matched gestures; (4) Genre styles diverge through lighting, music, and acting; (5) Viewer perceives contrasting emotional narratives. Visibility constraints: both sides must remain continuously visible, synchronized, and shot from the same perspective to verify causal comparison.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Grease Crayon LithographyI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Grease Crayon Drawing on Limestone and Hand Lithography PrintingSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)Objective: To demonstrate the basic process and principle of stone lithography by drawing with grease crayon on limestone, using water and oily ink to create an image, and transferring it to paper with a hand press.II. Materials and ToolsLimestone lithography stone (flat and clean); grease crayon; clean water and sponge; oil-based lithography ink; ink roller (brayer); dampened printing paper; hand lithography press.III. Experimental Procedure1. Drawing: On a dry limestone surface, draw an image using a grease crayon, applying clear and continuous lines.2. Water Wash: Lightly sponge clean water over the stone so the non-greasy areas become wet while the greasy drawing remains water-repellent.3. Ink Rolling: Roll a thin, even layer of oily ink across the stone. The ink adheres to the greasy drawing and is repelled by the wet areas.4. Paper Placement: Place a sheet of damp paper carefully on top of the inked stone, aligning it evenly.5. Pressing: Run the stone and paper together through a hand lithography press with steady pressure.6. Reveal: Peel the paper from the stone to reveal the printed image.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the stone shows only the grease crayon drawing. After wetting, water evenly covers non-image areas. During ink rolling, ink sticks only to the greasy lines. After pressing, the paper displays a reversed printed image matching the original drawing.V. Experimental Principle SummaryLithography is based on the immiscibility of oil and water. Grease crayon creates oil-based image areas that attract oily ink. Water occupies non-image areas and repels ink. When damp paper is pressed against the inked stone, the ink transfers to the paper, producing the print.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: basic stone lithography using oil–water repulsion. Minimum assumptions: limestone surface is flat; grease crayon is oil-based; water and oil repel; press applies uniform pressure. Phased storyline: (1) image creation on stone with grease crayon; (2) water wets non-image areas; (3) oily ink selectively adheres to greasy drawing; (4) damp paper contacts inked stone; (5) pressure transfers ink, revealing the print. Visibility requirements: close-up views of stone during inking and a clear reveal of the printed paper; camera angle should maintain continuous spatial orientation through pressing.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Zooming a Vector Logo from Small to Huge without PixelationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Zooming a Vector Logo from Small to Huge without Pixelation2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Visual Communication Design)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare scaling behavior of vector graphics and raster graphics, demonstrating that vector logos can be zoomed continuously without pixelation while raster logos lose clarity when enlarged.II. Experimental EquipmentDesk surface, computer or tablet with a high-resolution screen, one vector-format logo (e.g., SVG), one raster-format logo (e.g., PNG), graphic display or editing software capable of zooming, camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod, fixed lighting environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the computer on the desk; open the software and load the same logo in two formats.2. Layout Setup: Arrange the screen to show the two logos side-by-side, left as vector and right as raster, starting at very small size.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera facing the screen; fix focus, angle, and distance; do not adjust during recording.4. Core Operation: Start recording or time-lapse capture; continuously zoom in on both logos at the same rate from tiny size to full screen.5. Completion: Stop zooming when the logos fill most of the screen; end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both logos appear equally clear at small size.2. During Zooming: As size increases, the vector logo remains smooth with clean edges, while the raster logo gradually shows pixel blocks and jagged edges.3. Final State: At large scale, the vector logo is still sharp, whereas the raster logo is visibly pixelated and blurry.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesVector graphics are defined by mathematical paths and equations, allowing infinite scaling without loss of quality. Raster graphics are composed of fixed pixels; enlarging them increases pixel size, causing visible pixelation and loss of detail. This experiment visually demonstrates the fundamental difference between resolution-independent and resolution-dependent images.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure both logos originate from the same design; keep camera focus fixed; maintain constant zoom speed; avoid screen glare or lighting changes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: resolution independence of vector graphics versus resolution dependence of raster graphics. Minimum assumptions: a stable desk scene, a fixed camera, identical logos in two formats, and synchronized zooming.Phased storyline: (1) Establish scene with desk, screen, and side-by-side logos at tiny size; (2) continuous zoom-in phase where scaling increases smoothly; (3) causal transition where raster logo develops visible pixelation while vector remains smooth; (4) final full-screen comparison confirming clarity difference. Visibility constraints: camera focus and angle must remain fixed so clarity changes are attributable only to scaling behavior.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Clay Portrait Bust Built by Adding Small Clay Coils and Smoothing by HandI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Building a Clay Portrait Bust Using Coil Addition and Hand Smoothing2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Sculpture)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the traditional sculptural method of constructing a portrait bust by adding small clay coils onto an armature, blending them by hand and rib tool, and observing how gradual rotation supports even form development.II. Experimental EquipmentPortrait bust armature (head and shoulders), water-based clay, small clay coils, sculpting rib tool, sculptor’s turntable, water container, cloth or sponge, fixed camera on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the portrait bust armature on the center of the turntable. Prepare small, uniform clay coils and slightly moisten hands and tools.2. Coil Addition: Start the slow rotation of the turntable. Add small clay coils onto the armature surface, pressing them gently to ensure adhesion.3. Hand Smoothing: Use fingers and palms to compress and blend the coils into the underlying clay, reducing visible seams as the bust rotates.4. Tool Refinement: Apply a rib tool to further smooth and refine the surface, maintaining even pressure while the turntable continues rotating.5. Observation and Adjustment: Continue alternating coil addition and smoothing until the form appears unified. Keep the camera focus fixed throughout for time-lapse capture.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The armature is rigid and partially covered with clay; coils are visibly separate.2. During the Process: As coils are added and smoothed, seams gradually disappear and surface continuity increases. Rotation allows uniform access to all sides.3. Final State: The bust shows a coherent, smooth clay surface with integrated volume and balanced proportions.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on additive sculptural construction. Small clay coils increase volume in a controlled manner, while hand pressure and rib tools compress particles, improving structural cohesion and surface smoothness. Continuous rotation ensures even shaping, consistent observation, and balanced form development.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add clay gradually to avoid collapse or uneven weight.2. Maintain consistent moisture to prevent cracking.3. Use light, even pressure when smoothing to preserve form.4. Keep the camera fixed to ensure accurate time-lapse documentation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate additive clay sculpture of a portrait bust using small coils, hand smoothing, and rib tool refinement on a rotating turntable, documented with a fixed camera.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Clay behaves as a malleable material responding to pressure; coils adhere when pressed; rotation provides continuous access; smoothing blends seams rather than removing volume.Phased Storyline: (1) Static armature on turntable; (2) Slow rotation begins; (3) Small coils are added incrementally; (4) Hands compress and blend coils; (5) Rib tool refines surface; (6) Bust appears progressively unified and smooth. manual: Instructions for the Arts Experiment: Pointillist Dots Viewed from Increasing DistanceI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visual Blending of Blue and Yellow Pointillist DotsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Visual Arts)Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how pointillist painting relies on human visual perception, showing that separate blue and yellow dots visually blend into unified colors when viewed from increasing distance.II. Experimental MaterialsCanvas or flat board, blue and yellow paint, fine-tipped brushes or dotting tools, easel or wall mount, camera with fixed-focus capability, tripod, controlled lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Secure the canvas vertically. Apply dense, evenly distributed blue and yellow dots across the canvas, ensuring dots remain distinct and do not physically mix.2. Camera Setup: Place the camera on a tripod directly facing the canvas. Fix the focus manually so it does not change during recording. Maintain constant lighting.3. Core Operation: Begin recording or time-lapse capture at close range, where individual dots are clearly visible. Gradually move the camera backward in several stages (or zoom out without refocusing), keeping the canvas centered.4. Completion: Stop recording after the canvas is viewed from a far distance where individual dots are difficult to distinguish.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial Stage: At close distance, blue and yellow dots appear clearly separated.Intermediate Stage: As distance increases, dots become harder to distinguish, and colors begin to visually mix.Final Stage: From far distance, the canvas appears to show blended or greenish hues rather than distinct dots.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of optical color mixing in pointillism. Instead of physically mixing pigments, artists place small dots of pure color close together. The human visual system integrates these dots at a distance, producing the perception of mixed colors. The effect depends on viewing distance and fixed focus, illustrating how perception completes the image rather than the paint itself.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Pointillism demonstrates optical color mixing through human visual perception rather than physical pigment blending. Minimum assumptions include a static canvas, distinct blue and yellow dots, fixed camera focus, and controlled distance change.Phased Storyline: (1) Close view shows clearly separated blue and yellow dots; (2) gradual camera withdrawal reduces dot distinguishability; (3) mid-distance reveals partial blending; (4) far view shows unified blended color impression. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – History3. Activity Objective: To understand the route of Christopher Columbus’s first voyage in 1492 by reading a historical map, identifying key departure points, islands, and landing locations, and connecting them along the voyage route to form a complete and coherent map. Students will learn how geographic routes support historical interpretation.II. Materials and Tools1. Base map of the Atlantic Ocean (including Europe, Africa, and the Americas)2. Reference map titled Map of Columbus’s Voyage to the Americas (1492)3. Pencil or marker (preferably a distinct color such as red or blue)4. Ruler or straightedge (optional)III. Activity Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the blank base map on a flat surface. Ensure that major geographic regions such as Spain, the Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean islands, and the Americas are visible.2. Identifying the Starting Point: Locate Spain on the map and mark it clearly as the departure point of Columbus’s voyage in 1492.3. Tracing the Voyage Route: Refer to the reference map and identify each island and location Columbus visited in sequence across the Atlantic. Using the pencil or marker, draw a continuous arc-like route from Spain westward, passing through the marked islands.4. Connecting Locations: Connect all identified islands and landing points in the correct historical order to form a single, continuous route. Ensure the line flows smoothly across the Atlantic Ocean.5. Completion and Review: Check that all major locations shown on the reference map are included and connected. Adjust the route if necessary to ensure completeness and clarity.IV. Observation of Activity Phenomena1. Initial State: The base map shows unconnected landmasses with no marked route.2. During the Activity: As points are marked and connected, a curved transatlantic route gradually appears from Spain to the Caribbean.3. Final Result: All islands and countries along Columbus’s 1492 route are connected, forming a complete and visually continuous map of the voyage.V. Summary of Activity PrincipleThis activity is based on the historical principle that maps visually represent spatial and chronological information. By connecting Columbus’s departure point, stopovers, and landing sites in sequence, learners can better understand the geographic scale, direction, and logic of the 1492 voyage. The completed route illustrates how maritime exploration linked Europe and the Americas and supports historical reasoning through spatial visualization.VI. Activity Precautions1. Follow the correct historical order of locations when connecting points.2. Use a single, consistent color for the route to maintain clarity.3. Avoid adding locations not present in the 1492 voyage reference map.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Sequential Repainting of the Same Portrait in Renaissance, Baroque, and Modernist StylesI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Sequential Repainting of One Portrait in Three Art StylesSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArtsObjective: To visually demonstrate how different historical art styles reinterpret the same subject by sequentially repainting one portrait on a single canvas, observing stylistic transformation through time-lapse photography.II. Materials and EquipmentArtist’s studio space; one stretched canvas mounted on an easel; oil or acrylic paints; brushes of varying sizes; palette; reference portrait subject; fixed camera on tripod; time-lapse recording setup; consistent studio lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a blank canvas on the easel in the studio. Fix the camera facing the canvas, ensuring stable framing and constant lighting.2. Renaissance Stage: The painter creates a realistic portrait emphasizing proportion, perspective, natural skin tones, and balanced composition. Record the process using time-lapse until the painting is complete.3. Baroque Stage: Without changing the canvas position, the painter repaints over the same portrait, adding dramatic lighting, stronger contrasts, dynamic shadows, and emotional intensity. Continue time-lapse recording until completion.4. Modernist Stage: The painter again repaints the same portrait, simplifying or abstracting forms, altering colors, and breaking realistic proportions according to Modernist principles. Record via time-lapse until finished.5. Completion: Stop recording and review the three completed stylistic stages in sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Blank canvas in a stable studio setting.Renaissance Phase: The portrait appears realistic, harmonious, and proportionally accurate.Baroque Phase: The same portrait becomes more dramatic, with intensified light, shadow, and movement.Modernist Phase: The portrait transforms into simplified or abstract forms with expressive or non-naturalistic colors.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe experiment demonstrates that artistic style functions as an interpretive system. Although the subject remains constant, changes in historical context, aesthetic goals, and visual principles cause systematic transformations in form, color, and composition. Sequential repainting on the same canvas visually reveals these stylistic principles and their causal relationship to artistic intention.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Artistic style as a rule-based visual system that transforms a constant subject. Minimum assumptions: one stable canvas, one portrait subject, three historically defined styles, sequential repainting, and time-lapse recording. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 shows realistic, balanced Renaissance depiction; Phase 2 shows heightened contrast and drama caused by Baroque repainting; Phase 3 shows abstraction or simplification caused by Modernist repainting. Causal transitions must be visible through repainting actions, with a fixed camera perspective and continuous temporal flow enabling verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparing Matte vs Glossy Balls Under the Same Directional LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparing Matte and Glossy Balls Under One Directional Light2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Visual Arts / Visual Perception)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how surface material properties (matte vs glossy) affect light reflection and visual appearance under identical lighting conditions, and to understand the artistic principle of specular reflection versus diffuse reflection.II. Experimental Materials1. Two identical spheres of the same size and color:   - One matte-finished ball (diffuse surface)   - One glossy-finished ball (smooth, reflective surface)2. One fixed directional light source (e.g., spotlight or desk lamp with focused beam)3. Neutral background (gray or white backdrop)4. Rotating platform or manual rotation setup ensuring both balls rotate together at the same speed5. Stable table or standIII. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the matte ball and the glossy ball side by side on the rotating platform, ensuring equal distance from the light source and identical orientation.2. Lighting Adjustment: Fix the directional light at a constant angle (e.g., 45° from the front-left) and do not change its position or intensity throughout the experiment.3. Initial Observation (Static): With the balls stationary, observe and compare the brightness, highlights, and shading on both surfaces.4. Core Operation (Rotation): Start rotating both balls together at a slow, constant speed, ensuring synchronized motion.5. Continuous Observation: Observe how the light patterns, highlights, and shadow transitions change on each ball during rotation.6. Completion: Stop the rotation and record the final observations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Matte Ball:   - Appears evenly lit with soft transitions between light and shadow.   - No sharp highlight; brightness changes gradually during rotation.2. Glossy Ball:   - Displays a bright, sharp specular highlight.   - The highlight moves clearly across the surface as the ball rotates.   - Strong contrast between highlight, mid-tones, and darker areas.3. Comparative Observation:   - Under identical lighting and motion, the glossy ball shows stronger visual cues of light direction, while the matte ball emphasizes form through gradual shading.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the artistic and physical principle of light reflection. Matte surfaces cause diffuse reflection, scattering incoming light evenly in many directions, resulting in soft shading and reduced highlights. Glossy surfaces produce specular reflection, reflecting light in a concentrated direction, creating sharp highlights that move with the object’s rotation. Artists use these differences to convey material properties, volume, and light direction in visual representation.VI. Experimental Notes1. Ensure both balls are identical in size and color to isolate surface material as the only variable.2. Keep the light source fixed to maintain experimental control.3. Rotation speed should be slow enough to clearly observe changing light effects.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate how surface material (matte vs glossy) affects light reflection under identical conditions. Minimum assumptions: two identical spheres, one fixed directional light, synchronized rotation, neutral background. Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – static comparison shows soft shading on matte and sharp highlight on glossy; Phase 2 – during rotation, glossy highlight travels clearly across the surface while matte shading changes gradually; Phase 3 – consistent lighting and motion confirm material-based visual differences. Visibility constraints: both balls and the light-facing surfaces must remain in frame to verify highlight movement and shading transitions.

manual: Experiment Title: Paint Application on Raw Wood vs Sealed Wood PanelSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Painting Materials and Techniques)I. Experiment ObjectiveTo demonstrate how surface preparation affects paint behavior by comparing paint absorption and spreading on raw wood versus sealed wood.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical wooden panels; one untreated raw wood panel and one sealed (primed or varnished) panel; liquid paint (single color, same batch); flat paintbrush; workbench; gloves or apron (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical wooden panels side by side on a flat workbench, with the raw wood panel on the left and the sealed panel on the right.2. Paint Loading: Dip the brush into the liquid paint, ensuring a consistent and moderate paint load.3. Core Operation: Starting from the left edge of the raw wood panel, apply one continuous horizontal brush stroke that passes across the raw wood panel and continues directly onto the sealed panel without stopping.4. Observation: Stop brushing immediately after the stroke and observe both panels for several seconds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Contact: Paint contacts both panels at the same time.2. Raw Wood Panel: Paint is quickly absorbed, appearing darker, with uneven edges and reduced surface gloss.3. Sealed Wood Panel: Paint remains more on the surface, spreads smoothly, retains clearer brush marks, and appears more uniform with slight sheen.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRaw wood is porous and absorbs liquid paint into its fibers, causing faster absorption, darker tone, and less uniform edges. A sealed wood panel has reduced porosity due to the sealing layer, preventing absorption and allowing paint to sit on the surface, resulting in smoother spread and more consistent appearance. This demonstrates the importance of surface preparation in painting and visual arts.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Surface porosity and sealing affect paint absorption and visual outcome in painting. Minimum assumptions: two identical wooden panels differ only by sealing; the same liquid paint and single brush stroke are used.Phased storyline: (1) Establish static scene with two side-by-side panels on a workbench, raw left and sealed right; (2) a single, continuous brush stroke applies paint across both panels simultaneously; (3) immediate divergence appears—raw wood absorbs paint and darkens unevenly, sealed wood shows smoother, more uniform paint sitting on the surface. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show textures, edges of paint spread, and timing of absorption to verify causal differences.

Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Arts (Material Perception and Texture)3. Experiment Objective: To compare tactile and visual effects when the same steel nail is dragged with similar force across a soft pine wood plank and a stone tile, and to understand how material hardness and texture affect surface marks.II. Experimental EquipmentSteel nail (one piece, clean and straight), soft pine wood plank (smooth surface), stone tile (ceramic or stone, smooth surface), workbench, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse), stable lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the pine wood plank and stone tile flat on the workbench, side by side. Fix the camera position and focus to cover both surfaces.2. Operation on Wood: Hold the steel nail at a consistent angle. Drag it across the pine wood plank in a straight line using steady, similar force.3. Recording: Capture the entire process with fixed-focus time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. PrecautionsEnsure similar force and angle for both scratches; keep the camera fixed; avoid excessive force that could damage equipment or cause injury.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sealed vs Unsealed Canvas Absorbing Paint WashI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Paint Wash Absorption on Sealed and Unsealed Canvas2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Painting Techniques)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare how a diluted paint wash behaves on gesso-sealed canvas versus raw canvas, and to understand how surface preparation affects paint absorption and flow.II. Experimental MaterialsStretched canvas (1), acrylic gesso, masking tape, diluted acrylic paint wash (same color and dilution), flat brush, palette or container, easel or flat surface, camera or smartphone with tripod (for time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the canvas flat. Apply masking tape vertically down the center to divide it into two equal halves.2. Sealing: Apply an even layer of gesso to the left half only; allow it to dry completely. Remove excess texture for a smooth surface.3. Setup: Keep the right half raw canvas. Reapply tape if needed to maintain a clean division.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the canvas. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Start time-lapse recording.5. Core Operation: Load the brush with the diluted paint wash. In one continuous horizontal or vertical pass, brush the wash evenly across both halves, crossing the tape line without stopping.6. Observation Period: Do not touch the canvas. Let the wash sit and absorb naturally while recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Immediately after application, the wash appears similar on both halves.2. Short-Term Change: The raw canvas side absorbs the wash quickly, darkening and spreading into the fibers; the sealed side shows slower absorption and lighter tone.3. Later Stage: The raw side appears matte and embedded with pigment; the sealed side retains more surface pooling or visible brush marks.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCanvas preparation alters surface absorbency. Gesso-sealed canvas creates a barrier that reduces capillary absorption, keeping paint on the surface. Raw canvas fibers absorb liquid rapidly through capillary action, pulling pigment inward and outward, resulting in darker, more diffused washes. This experiment demonstrates how material treatment directly influences visual outcomes in painting.VI. PrecautionsUse the same paint dilution and brush pressure for both halves. Ensure gesso is fully dry before painting. Do not adjust camera settings during recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Surface preparation (sealed vs unsealed canvas) causally affects paint wash absorption and visual outcome. Minimum assumptions: one canvas, clearly divided; one side sealed with gesso, the other raw; identical diluted wash applied once; static camera.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup shows taped, split canvas with different surface textures; (2) single continuous brush pass applies the same wash across both halves; (3) immediate divergence appears—raw side darkens and spreads faster; (4) over accelerated time-lapse, raw side soaks in while sealed side remains lighter and more uniform. Visibility constraints: fixed frontal view, stable lighting, and uninterrupted time-lapse to verify causal progression.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Impasto Palette-Knife Base Layer Followed by Transparent GlazingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Impasto Base Layer with Palette Knife and Transparent Oil Glazing2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Arts (Painting Techniques)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the classical oil painting technique in which thick impasto is applied with a palette knife to build texture, followed by the application of a transparent oil glaze with a brush to modify color and depth without destroying surface relief. The process is recorded using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentOil paints (opaque colors for impasto, transparent or glazing colors), palette knife, soft bristle brush (medium size), primed canvas or panel, painting palette, oil medium or glazing medium, easel or flat working surface, camera with tripod, stable lighting source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the canvas on a stable surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the canvas, lock focus and exposure, and set time-lapse recording. Prepare thick oil paint on the palette.2. Impasto Application: Use the palette knife to pick up thick oil paint. Apply paint firmly onto the canvas, spreading and pressing to create visible ridges and raised texture. Cover the main working area with uneven, sculptural strokes.3. Drying Interval (simplified): Allow the impasto layer to set briefly until it is touch-stable (for demonstration, this stage may be visually implied in time-lapse).4. Glaze Preparation: Mix a small amount of transparent oil paint with glazing medium until it becomes fluid and translucent.5. Transparent Glazing: Using a soft brush, slowly brush the transparent glaze over the impasto surface. Let the glaze flow over peaks and into recesses without flattening the texture.6. Completion: Stop recording after the glaze evenly modifies the color and sheen of the textured surface.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The canvas surface shows thick, opaque paint with strong texture and visible palette-knife marks.2. During Glazing: The transparent glaze spreads thinly over raised and recessed areas, subtly altering color and increasing depth while leaving the physical texture intact.3. Final State: The impasto remains clearly three-dimensional, with enhanced chromatic richness and unified surface appearance due to the glaze.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on oil painting material principles. Impasto relies on the physical thickness of oil paint to create texture and relief. Transparent glazing uses the optical property of thin oil paint layers, allowing light to pass through the glaze, reflect off underlying layers, and return to the viewer. The combination produces depth and luminosity without mechanically altering the impasto structure.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the oil painting technique of applying an impasto base layer with a palette knife followed by transparent glazing with a brush, captured in a fixed-focus time-lapse setup.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Oil paint can be applied thickly to retain texture; transparent glaze is fluid and optically modifies underlying color; camera position, focus, and lighting remain stable throughout recording.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase: canvas, tools, and fixed camera are visible and stable. (2) Texture-building phase: thick impasto is applied with a palette knife, forming raised ridges. (3) Optical modification phase: a transparent glaze is brushed slowly over the textured surface, flowing over relief without flattening it. Visibility Constraints: The camera must clearly show surface texture and color changes from a consistent frontal or slight oblique angle to verify depth and glazing effects.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Linocut Block Inking and Hand Pressing on PaperI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Linocut Block Inking and Hand Pressing on Paper2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic process of relief printmaking using a carved linoleum block, understand how ink is transferred from raised surfaces to paper through hand pressure, and record the process with a fixed-focus camera for time-lapse observation.II. Experimental EquipmentCarved linoleum block (relief design completed), water-based or oil-based printing ink, brayer (rubber roller), smooth flat table or printing surface, inking plate or glass sheet, printing paper, clean hands or baren/spoon for pressing (hand pressing emphasized), camera or smartphone with tripod, stable lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the carved linoleum block flat on the table. Set up the camera on a tripod directly above or at a fixed angle, lock focus and exposure, and ensure the frame includes the block, paper, and hands.2. Inking the Block: Squeeze a small amount of ink onto the inking plate. Roll the brayer back and forth until the ink is evenly distributed. Roll the brayer over the raised surface of the linoleum block repeatedly until the surface appears evenly coated with ink.3. Placing the Paper: Carefully lay a clean sheet of printing paper on top of the inked block, aligning it without shifting.4. Hand Pressing: Use hands (or a baren/spoon if needed) to press evenly across the back of the paper, applying consistent pressure from the center outward to ensure full contact.5. Lifting the Print: Slowly peel the paper from one corner and lift it completely to reveal the printed image.6. Completion: Place the finished print aside to dry. Stop the recording and clean tools if necessary.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The carved linoleum block shows raised and recessed areas; no image is present on the paper.2. During Inking: Ink adheres only to the raised surfaces of the block, creating a thin, even layer.3. During Pressing: The paper conforms closely to the block under hand pressure.4. Final Result: When the paper is lifted, a reversed image appears on the paper, corresponding to the raised, inked areas of the block.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLinocut is a relief printmaking process. The carved linoleum block has raised areas that receive ink, while recessed areas remain uninked. When paper is placed on the inked block and pressure is applied by hand, ink transfers from the raised surfaces to the paper. The clarity of the print depends on even inking, correct paper placement, and consistent pressure. Fixing the camera focus ensures visual continuity and accurate time-lapse documentation of the process.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Relief printmaking through linocut, demonstrating ink transfer from raised surfaces via hand pressure. Minimum assumptions: a carved linoleum block, ink applied with a brayer, paper placed on top, and manual pressing causing ink transfer; camera remains fixed.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with carved block and fixed camera; (2) inking phase where brayer coats raised surfaces; (3) paper placement without shifting; (4) hand pressing as the causal action; (5) lifting paper to reveal the printed image. Visibility constraints: the block, brayer, paper, and hands must remain in frame, and the reveal of the print must be clearly observable to verify causal correctness.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Constructing Eye-Level Perspective Using a Horizon LineI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Horizon Line and Vanishing Points in Eye-Level PerspectiveSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Drawing/Perspective)Objective: To understand the horizon line as the observer’s eye level, learn that all vanishing points lie on the horizon line, and construct one-point and two-point perspective using simple boxes and a road.II. MaterialsWhite drawing paper, pencil, ruler, eraser; optional camera or screen recorder for time-lapse capture.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the paper horizontally. Fix the camera above the paper if recording.2. Draw a straight horizontal line across the page and label it ‘Horizon Line’.3. One-Point Perspective: Mark a single point on the horizon line (Vanishing Point 1). Draw a rectangle below the horizon. Use the ruler to draw straight lines from the rectangle’s corners to the vanishing point to form a box or road.4. Two-Point Perspective: Mark two points far apart on the same horizon line (Vanishing Point 1 and 2). Draw a vertical edge of a box between them. Connect its top and bottom ends to both vanishing points to form a two-point box.5. Focus and Recording: Keep the horizon and vanishing points in frame; optionally record as a short time-lapse.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena- The horizon line remains fixed and parallel to the paper edge.- All receding edges converge exactly to the vanishing point(s) on the horizon line.- Objects appear smaller as they extend toward the vanishing point(s).- Adding a second vanishing point changes the orientation of the box while maintaining eye level.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe horizon line represents the observer’s eye level in linear perspective. All vanishing points for horizontal directions lie on this line. Straight edges parallel in reality visually converge to vanishing points, creating the illusion of depth. The height of the horizon determines whether the viewer looks up, down, or straight ahead at objects.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Eye-level linear perspective in drawing. Minimum assumptions: a fixed observer eye level, a straight horizon line, and vanishing points placed on that line.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish the horizon line as eye level; (2) place one vanishing point and show lines converging to form depth; (3) add a second vanishing point on the same horizon to change object orientation; (4) observe consistent size reduction and convergence. Visibility constraints: the horizon line and vanishing points must remain visible and stable; convergence must be clearly observable, even in accelerated time-lapse.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Intaglio Printing (Etching)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Intaglio Printing (Etching) DemonstrationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the intaglio printing process by showing how ink retained in recessed etched lines of a copper plate is transferred onto damp paper under pressure, forming delicate printed lines.II. Experimental EquipmentEtched copper plate with recessed lines, intaglio printing ink, ink card or spatula, tarlatan or soft cloth, clean newsprint, dampened printing paper, intaglio press, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the etched copper plate flat on the work surface with recessed lines facing up.2. Inking: Apply ink evenly over the entire plate using a card, pressing ink firmly into the recessed etched grooves.3. Wiping: Use tarlatan and then clean newsprint to wipe the surface of the plate, removing ink from raised areas while leaving ink only in recessed lines.4. Paper Placement: Lay dampened printing paper carefully on top of the inked plate, ensuring full contact.5. Printing: Run the plate and paper together through the intaglio press with steady pressure.6. Revealing the Print: Lift the paper gently from one corner to reveal the printed image.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the copper plate shows dark ink filling fine recessed lines while the surface appears clean. After pressing, the lifted paper displays delicate, slightly embossed lines corresponding exactly to the etched pattern, labeled as an Intaglio Pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIntaglio printing works by holding ink in recessed areas of a plate. When damp paper is pressed onto the plate under high pressure, the paper is forced into the grooves and absorbs the ink. Raised areas, having been wiped clean, do not print, resulting in fine, recessed-line imagery characteristic of etching.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Basic Screen Printing DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Screen Printing Using a Perforated Mesh Screen2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic screen printing technique by observing how ink passes through a permeable mesh screen and stencil to form a printed pattern with characteristic mesh texture.II. Experimental EquipmentScreen frame with permeable mesh, stencil/template (paper or film with cut-out pattern), printing ink, squeegee or scraper, flat paper substrate, tape or clamps, work surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place clean paper flat on the work surface. Secure it to prevent movement. Position the mesh screen directly on top of the paper.2. Template Placement: Place the stencil on the screen so that its cut-out areas define the desired pattern. Ensure alignment and fix it in place.3. Ink Application: Deposit a small amount of printing ink along one edge of the screen.4. Printing Operation: Using a squeegee, apply steady pressure and pull the ink across the screen so that ink passes through the open mesh areas not blocked by the stencil.5. Screen Lifting: After one pass, carefully lift the screen vertically away from the paper.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Paper is clean and blank; ink rests on the screen surface.2. During Printing: Ink spreads across the screen and is pressed through permeable mesh openings.3. Final Result: After lifting the screen, a clear printed pattern appears on the paper, showing slight mesh texture and soft edge marks characteristic of screen printing.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleScreen printing works by forcing ink through a permeable mesh screen. Areas blocked by the stencil prevent ink transfer, while open areas allow ink to pass through under pressure. When the screen is lifted, the ink deposited on the paper forms a pattern that reflects both the stencil design and the fine texture of the mesh.VI. NotesFor demonstration purposes, the process can be shown with close-up focus or time-lapse photography to emphasize ink transfer and pattern emergence.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: screen printing as a printmaking technique based on ink transfer through a permeable mesh controlled by a stencil. Minimum assumptions: a mesh screen allows ink to pass only where not blocked; pressure causes ink movement; lifting the screen reveals the print.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – paper, screen, and stencil aligned in a stable top-down view; (2) Action phase – ink applied and pulled across the screen with visible pressure; (3) Causal transition – ink passes through open mesh areas; (4) Reveal phase – screen lifted to expose the printed pattern. Visibility constraints: close or overhead view to verify mesh texture, stencil blocking, and the cause-effect link between ink movement and pattern appearance.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Drawing Structural Lines of a Simple ObjectSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Sketching Fundamentals)Objective: To understand and practice the use of structural lines by drawing the internal skeleton, main axis, and proportions of a simple object, focusing on structure rather than light, shadow, or surface details.II. Experimental Materials1. A simple object (e.g., cup, bottle, box, or fruit)2. Table or flat surface3. Pencil (HB or 2B)4. Drawing paperIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the simple object steadily on a table. Sit or stand at a fixed viewpoint and place the paper in front of you.2. Observation: Observe the overall shape of the object, identifying its main axis, symmetry, and basic geometric volume.3. Drawing the Main Axis: Lightly draw a straight structural line indicating the main axis of the object, allowing the line to pass through the object.4. Establishing Proportions: Add additional light structural lines to mark height, width, and major turning points, keeping lines simple and straight.5. Building the Internal Skeleton: Draw internal structural lines that suggest the object’s inner framework and spatial orientation. Do not add shading or surface details.6. Completion: Stop once the structural framework is clear. Keep all lines light and visible, emphasizing structure only.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The paper is blank, and the object is stationary on the table.2. During Drawing: Light pencil lines gradually appear, crossing through the object to indicate axes and proportional guides.3. Final State: The drawing consists only of internal structural lines and a clear skeleton; no shading, texture, or light-shadow effects are present.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesStructural lines are internal guide lines used in sketching to represent the underlying skeleton and proportions of an object. These lines do not change with light or shadow and help the artist understand and construct accurate form. By focusing only on axes, proportions, and internal structure, the artist builds a solid foundation for further detailed drawing.VI. Precautions1. Use light pencil pressure so lines remain adjustable.2. Avoid shading, contour refinement, or decorative details.3. Maintain a fixed viewpoint to ensure proportional accuracy.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Structural Line drawing in sketching, emphasizing internal skeleton, main axis, and proportional relationships, independent of light and shadow. Minimum assumptions include a simple object, a stable table surface, a pencil, and a fixed viewpoint.Expected Phenomena and Phased Storyline: Phase 1 – Setup: A simple object is placed on a table, paper and pencil prepared, camera/viewpoint stable. Phase 2 – Axis Establishment: Light pencil movement creates a main axis line passing through the object. Phase 3 – Proportion Mapping: Additional straight guide lines appear, marking height, width, and balance. Phase 4 – Skeleton Completion: Internal structural lines form a clear framework of the object. Visibility Constraints: Lines must remain light, straight, and unshaded; the progression should appear continuous or time-lapse-like to verify causal and structural accuracy.

manual: Two-Point Perspective Drawing Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Two-Point Perspective (Side View Box)2. Subject: Arts – Drawing and Perspective3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate the principle of two-point perspective by drawing a side-view box with parallel edges converging to two vanishing points on a horizon line, and to visually verify perspective rules through a time-lapse drawing process.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite drawing paper (A4 or similar), pencil, ruler or straightedge, eraser, camera or screen-recording device for time-lapse capture.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the paper on a flat surface and fix the camera above the drawing area to ensure the whole page is visible and focused.2. Draw the Horizon Line: Using a ruler, draw a straight horizontal line across the paper to represent the horizon line.3. Mark Vanishing Points: On the horizon line, mark two distinct points—one on the left and one on the right. Clearly label them as Vanishing Point 1 and Vanishing Point 2.4. Sketch the Box: Between the two vanishing points, lightly draw a vertical line to represent the nearest edge of a box viewed from the side.5. Draw Converging Edges: From the top and bottom of the vertical edge, use straight guide lines to draw edges converging toward Vanishing Point 1 on one side and Vanishing Point 2 on the other side.6. Complete the Box: Add the remaining vertical edges where the converging lines intersect, forming a complete three-dimensional box.7. Finalization: Darken the final box edges, keep guide lines light or erase them, and ensure both vanishing points and the horizon line are clearly visible and labeled.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: A blank page with no spatial depth.2. During Drawing: After adding the horizon line and vanishing points, lines drawn toward each vanishing point visually recede into depth.3. Final Result: The completed box appears three-dimensional, with parallel edges correctly converging toward two vanishing points on the horizon line.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleTwo-point perspective is a drawing method where parallel lines are divided into two groups, each converging toward a separate vanishing point on the horizon line. This simulates how objects appear in human vision when viewed from an angle, creating a realistic sense of depth and space on a flat surface.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Two-point perspective drawing, assuming basic Euclidean geometry and visual perspective rules (parallel lines converge toward vanishing points on the horizon).Minimum Assumptions: A fixed horizon line represents eye level; two vanishing points lie on this line; straight edges remain straight and converge consistently.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish a stable horizon line and two vanishing points; (2) introduce a vertical edge as the box’s nearest corner; (3) draw edges converging to each vanishing point, causing perceived depth; (4) complete and clarify the box. Visibility Constraints: The camera must maintain a top-down, stable view so the horizon line, vanishing points, and convergence directions are always visible for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Art Demonstration Experiment: Cross HatchingI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Cross Hatching with Parallel LinesSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Drawing Techniques)Objective: To demonstrate the basic cross hatching technique by drawing two groups of evenly spaced parallel lines crossing at a fixed angle (about 45°), and to understand how this technique creates rough texture representation.II. MaterialsSketch paper (one sheet, light-colored), pencil or fine-line pen, flat drawing surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sketch paper flat on the table. Hold the pencil steadily in a comfortable drawing grip.2. First Line Set: Draw a group of evenly spaced parallel lines in one direction across the paper. Maintain consistent pressure and spacing.3. Second Line Set: Rotate the drawing direction slightly and draw a second group of evenly spaced parallel lines crossing the first set at about a 45° angle.4. Completion: Continue until a clear grid-like cross hatching pattern is formed. Stop drawing once the grid is uniform.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Blank sketch paper with no marks.2. After First Line Set: Paper shows uniform, parallel lines in one direction.3. After Second Line Set: Lines intersect at a fixed angle, forming a regular grid pattern typical of cross hatching.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCross hatching is an artistic shading technique based on the controlled repetition of parallel lines. By overlaying a second set of lines at a fixed angle, visual density increases, creating the perception of rough texture and tonal variation. Consistent spacing, angle, and steady hand motion are the core factors determining the clarity of the texture effect.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pottery Crazing Technique on Glazed Ceramic TileI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pottery Crazing Technique: Irregular Cracks on Glaze Surface2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Ceramic Art)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the formation of glaze crazing by applying glaze to a ceramic tile, firing it in a kiln, and inducing rapid cooling, and to visually observe naturally irregular cracks on the glaze surface for primitive artistic expression.II. Experimental EquipmentUnglazed ceramic tile (bisque-fired), ceramic glaze (contrasting color recommended), glaze brush or dipping container, kiln (capable of glaze firing temperature), kiln shelf and tongs, heat-resistant gloves, cooling surface or ambient air, camera for close-up time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Glazing: Evenly apply a layer of ceramic glaze to the surface of the ceramic tile using a brush or dipping method. Ensure full coverage and a uniform thickness.2. Firing: Place the glazed tile on a kiln shelf and fire it in the kiln to the appropriate glaze maturation temperature according to the glaze specifications.3. Cooling (Core Step): After reaching peak temperature, remove the tile or allow rapid cooling by opening the kiln or transferring the tile to ambient air, creating thermal stress between glaze and clay body.4. Recording: Use close-up, fixed-angle time-lapse photography focused on the glaze surface during cooling to capture crack formation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The fired glaze surface appears smooth and glossy immediately after firing.2. During Cooling: Fine cracks begin to appear on the glaze surface as temperature drops.3. Final State: A network of irregularly distributed cracks (crazing area) forms naturally, without regular pattern, giving a primitive and expressive visual effect.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGlaze crazing occurs due to a mismatch in thermal expansion between the glaze layer and the ceramic body. During rapid cooling, the glaze contracts more than the clay body, creating tensile stress that is released through irregular surface cracks. This phenomenon is intentionally used in ceramic art to achieve expressive, primitive visual textures.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Pottery glaze crazing as an artistic technique caused by thermal expansion mismatch. Minimum assumptions: a glazed ceramic tile, kiln firing to mature the glaze, and rapid cooling to induce stress. Phased storyline: (1) Glaze is applied to a ceramic tile (smooth wet surface); (2) Tile is fired in a kiln (no visible cracks); (3) Rapid cooling begins; (4) Irregular cracks gradually emerge on the glaze surface, captured in close-up time-lapse. Visibility constraints: camera remains focused on the tile surface, emphasizing crack formation rather than kiln mechanics.
