manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Acrylic Gesso on Water Absorption of Raw CanvasI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Applying Acrylic Gesso to Raw Canvas and Comparing Water AbsorptionSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Painting Materials)Objective: To demonstrate how acrylic gesso seals raw cotton canvas fibers and alters water absorption behavior through visual comparison.II. MaterialsRaw cotton canvas (one piece), white acrylic gesso, flat brush or foam roller, palette or container for gesso, clean water, dropper or pipette, flat working surface.III. Procedure1. Preparation: Place the raw cotton canvas flat. Visually divide it into left and right halves.2. Gesso Application: Using a brush or roller, apply an even coat of white acrylic gesso only to the left half. Leave the right half uncoated.3. Drying: Allow the gessoed half to dry completely until matte and non-tacky.4. Water Test: Using a dropper, place equal-sized clear water droplets onto the gessoed left half and the raw right half at similar positions.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial State: Left half appears matte white and sealed; right half shows visible raw fabric texture.After Droplet Placement: On the gessoed half, water droplets bead up and retain a rounded shape. On the raw canvas, droplets spread, darken the fabric, and are absorbed more quickly.V. Experimental Principle SummaryAcrylic gesso forms a polymer-based ground that fills and seals the pores between canvas fibers, creating a less absorbent surface. As a result, water remains on the surface as beads. Raw cotton canvas has open fibers that readily absorb water, causing droplets to spread and soak in. This demonstrates why gesso is applied before painting to control paint absorption and surface behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Acrylic gesso acts as a ground that seals raw canvas fibers, reducing absorbency and altering liquid behavior on the surface. Minimum assumptions: a raw cotton canvas with visible texture, white acrylic gesso forming a matte sealed film when dry, and clear water droplets behaving according to surface absorbency.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish the canvas with a clear left–right division; (2) Apply white acrylic gesso only to the left half; (3) Imply or show drying to a matte state; (4) Place equal water droplets on both halves; (5) Reveal causal contrast—beading on the gessoed side versus spreading/absorption on the raw side. Visibility constraints: maintain a stable overhead or angled view so droplet shape, spreading, and surface texture differences are clearly verifiable.

manual: Instructions for the Art Experiment Blending Shaded Areas with a Paper BrushI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Uniform Blending of Sketch Shadow Areas Using a Paper Brush2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Drawing Techniques)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how to use a paper brush to blend shaded areas of a completed sketch into a uniform soft gray tone, eliminating visible hatching while preserving sharp contrast with adjacent unblended areas.II. Experimental MaterialsCompleted graphite sketch with clearly hatched shadow areas, paper brush (tortillon), clean drawing surface, optional soft cloth for cleaning brush tip.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the completed sketch flat on the drawing surface. Ensure the shaded area contains visible hatching and the adjacent area remains unshaded.2. Tool Positioning: Hold the paper brush lightly at a low angle to the paper, keeping the tip clean and dry.3. Core Operation (Blending): Using light, even pressure, move the paper brush in small circular or short directional motions across the shaded area only. Maintain consistent pressure to avoid streaks.4. Boundary Control: As the brush approaches the edge of the shaded area, slow down and stop before touching the adjacent unblended area to preserve a sharp boundary.5. Lift-Off: Cleanly and crisply lift the paper brush straight off the paper to end the blending action.6. Completion: Observe the blended area and set the brush aside.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The shaded area shows visible graphite hatching lines with a rough texture.2. During Blending: Hatching lines gradually soften and merge as the brush moves, and the tone becomes more even.3. Final State: The blended area appears as a uniform soft gray tone labeled Blended Area, with no obvious hatching traces and a sharp contrast against the unblended area.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBlending redistributes graphite particles on the paper surface through gentle friction. Even pressure spreads graphite uniformly, reducing line contrast and creating a smooth tonal field. Controlled stopping and clean lifting prevent graphite transfer to unblended areas, preserving clear tonal boundaries.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Artistic blending technique using a paper brush to achieve uniform tone. Minimum assumptions: a completed graphite sketch, a paper brush, and intentional control of pressure and boundaries. Phased storyline: (1) show completed sketch with hatched shadows; (2) brush contacts shaded area and moves evenly, causing hatching to soften; (3) brush stops before unshaded area, preserving boundary; (4) brush lifts cleanly; (5) final view shows uniform soft gray blended area with sharp contrast. Visibility constraints: close-up view of brush-paper contact and clear before-after tonal comparison.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Single-Side Light Gradually Illuminating a Human FaceSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Visual Arts / Photography)Objective: To demonstrate how a single light source placed on one side gradually reveals facial form, volume, and emotional tone through controlled illumination, and to observe changes using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Camera (DSLR or mirrorless) mounted on a tripod2. Fixed focal length or zoom lens with manual focus3. Single adjustable lamp (continuous light source)4. Dark room or enclosed space with controllable ambient light5. Chair or standing mark for the subject6. Black or neutral background (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Environment Setup: Darken the room completely, ensuring no ambient or stray light sources are present.2. Subject Positioning: The person sits or stands facing directly toward the camera, keeping head and body still.3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod, frame the face centrally, set manual focus on the subject’s eyes, and lock focus and exposure settings.4. Light Placement: Place a single lamp on the left side of the subject at approximately 45 degrees to the face, initially set to minimum brightness or turned off.5. Core Operation (Time-Lapse Capture): Start recording or time-lapse shooting. Slowly and continuously increase the lamp brightness over time without moving its position.6. Completion: Stop recording once the left side of the face is clearly illuminated while the right side remains relatively dark.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The frame appears almost completely dark, with facial features barely visible.2. Gradual Change: As the lamp brightens, the left side of the face slowly emerges; facial contours, texture, and expressions become visible.3. Contrast Formation: The illuminated side shows increasing detail, while the opposite side remains in shadow, creating strong light–dark contrast.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on artistic lighting principles in visual arts. A single-side (side-key) light creates contrast and depth by exploiting the directional nature of light. Gradual increase in light intensity reveals form progressively, emphasizing three-dimensional facial structure. Fixing camera focus and position ensures that observed changes are solely caused by lighting variation, allowing clear analysis of light–form relationships.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the camera remains completely still throughout the experiment.2. Do not adjust focus or framing once recording begins.3. Avoid any additional light sources or reflections.4. The subject should minimize movement to maintain visual consistency.

Visibility Constraint: The camera must maintain a frontal view of the face to verify lighting direction and contrast evolution.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Demonstrating Size Perspective (Near Big, Far Small)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Size Perspective (Near Big, Far Small) in Painting2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Fine Arts / Painting)3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate size perspective in painting, where objects closer to the viewer are drawn larger and objects farther away are drawn smaller, in accordance with perspective rules. Through hands-on drawing, learners observe how artists use relative size on the canvas to create a sense of depth and spatial distance.II. Experimental MaterialsDrawing paper or sketchbook (A4 or similar size), pencil (HB or 2B), eraser, ruler (optional), colored pencils or markers (optional), reference image of a simple landscape or street scene (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the drawing paper flat on a desk. Decide on a simple scene that includes both near and distant objects, such as a road with trees, people, or houses. Lightly mark a horizon line across the paper to indicate eye level.2. Foreground Drawing: In the lower part of the paper (foreground), draw one or two objects that are meant to be close to the viewer, such as a person, tree, or building. Draw these objects relatively large, with clear outlines and more visible details.3. Background Drawing: Above or beyond the foreground objects (toward the horizon line), draw the same type of objects again, but make them noticeably smaller. Reduce the height, width, and detail level of these objects to indicate greater distance.4. Size Adjustment and Comparison: Compare the foreground and background objects. Adjust sizes so that the objects farther away are consistently smaller than those in the foreground, following the rule that object size is inversely proportional to distance.5. Optional Enhancement: Lightly add color or shading. Use stronger colors and clearer contrasts for near objects, and lighter or less detailed treatment for distant objects to reinforce depth.6. Completion: Review the entire drawing to ensure a clear size relationship between near and far objects. Erase unnecessary construction lines and finalize the work.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At the start, the paper is blank or contains only a horizon line, with no sense of depth.2. During Drawing: As large foreground objects are added, they visually dominate the scene. When smaller background objects are added near the horizon line, a clear contrast in size appears.3. Final Result: The completed drawing shows a convincing sense of space: objects in the foreground appear large and prominent, while similar objects in the background appear smaller and farther away, creating visual depth on a flat surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe principle demonstrated in this experiment is size perspective, also known as relative size perspective. In visual art, when two objects are known or assumed to be similar in actual size, the one depicted larger is perceived as being closer to the viewer, while the one depicted smaller is perceived as farther away. This follows human visual experience and perspective rules: as distance increases, the image of an object on the retina becomes smaller. Artists apply this principle on the canvas to create the illusion of three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure that foreground and background objects are comparable in type so that size differences clearly indicate distance.2. Avoid making distant objects too detailed or too large, as this weakens the depth effect.3. Keep the horizon line consistent to maintain a stable spatial reference.4. Focus on relative size relationships rather than exact measurements; visual clarity is the key goal.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Size perspective in painting, defined by the rule that objects closer to the viewer are depicted larger and objects farther away are depicted smaller. Minimum assumptions: a flat canvas, a fixed viewer position, and comparable objects placed at different implied distances.Phased Storyline: (1) An empty or lightly marked canvas establishes spatial reference (horizon line). (2) Large foreground objects are drawn first, occupying lower or nearer areas of the canvas. (3) Similar objects are added farther back, closer to the horizon, with visibly reduced size. (4) The final composition shows a stable size gradient from foreground to background, creating clear depth. Visibility requirement: the entire canvas and the relative size comparison between near and far objects must remain in view for verification.

Equipment and ConditionsStandard badminton court with clear boundary lines, badminton racket, shuttlecock, two players (attacker and opponent), appropriate sportswear and non-slip badminton shoes.III. Demonstration Procedure1. Preparation: The attacker stands near the midcourt while the opponent stands on the opposite court in a ready position.2. Backcourt Retreat: The attacker moves quickly backward to the backcourt area, positioning the body sideways with the non-racket shoulder facing the net.3. Jump and Smash: As the shuttle descends, the attacker jumps upward, raises the racket arm overhead, and strikes the shuttle at the highest point with a full-arm swing, snapping the wrist to apply maximum force downward.4. Shuttle Landing and Scoring: The shuttle travels rapidly in a steep downward trajectory, crosses the net, and lands inside the opponent’s front service line. The opponent reacts but fails to make contact.5. Completion: The rally ends immediately, and the smash is counted as a winning point.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. The attacker’s movement shows a clear retreat followed by an explosive vertical jump.2. The smash produces a sharp sound and a visibly fast, steep shuttle trajectory.3. The shuttle lands clearly inside the opponent’s front service line.4. The opponent is unable to return the shuttle before it touches the ground.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe backcourt smash is based on sports biomechanics and physics. Retreating allows proper positioning; jumping increases the contact height, enabling a steeper downward angle. The coordinated rotation of the shoulder, elbow extension, and wrist snap transfers kinetic energy efficiently to the shuttlecock. This results in high speed and a sharp downward trajectory, reducing the opponent’s reaction time and leading to a successful score.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Badminton backcourt smash as a scoring technique. Minimum assumptions: a standard badminton court, gravity acting on the shuttlecock, and human biomechanics allowing jumping and overhead striking.Phased Storyline: (1) Player retreats to backcourt and sets stance; (2) Player jumps and contacts shuttle at highest point with an overhead smash; (3) Shuttle accelerates downward in a steep trajectory; (4) Shuttle lands inside opponent’s front service line; (5) Opponent fails to return. Visibility requirements: clear side or diagonal view showing court lines, player jump, shuttle flight path, and landing location for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Athletics 100m Crouching Start DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Athletics 100m Crouching Start DemonstrationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – SportExperiment Objective: To demonstrate and understand the correct technique of the 100m crouching start, where the athlete prepares in a crouching position and pushes off the ground to start sprinting after hearing the starting gun.II. Experimental EquipmentStandard 400m track straight lane, starting blocks, starting line markings, starting gun or electronic start signal, sportswear and sprint spikes (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the starting blocks firmly on the track behind the starting line. The athlete wears appropriate sportswear and sprint shoes.2. Crouching Position Setup: The athlete positions both feet against the starting blocks, places hands shoulder-width apart behind the starting line, fingers spread, arms straight, head lowered, and hips raised slightly above shoulder level.3. Ready Phase: The athlete stabilizes the body, distributes weight between hands and feet, and remains motionless while focusing on the upcoming start signal.4. Core Operation (Start): Upon hearing the starting gun or signal, the athlete reacts immediately, forcefully pushes off the starting blocks with both legs, drives arms explosively, and leans the body forward.5. Completion: The athlete transitions smoothly from the crouching start into acceleration running.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Athlete remains stationary in a stable crouching position with tense but controlled posture.2. At the Gun Signal: An immediate reaction occurs; legs extend powerfully, arms swing forward and backward, and the body moves forward.3. After Push-off: The athlete leaves the blocks and enters the acceleration phase with a forward-leaning sprint posture.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe crouching start is based on sprint biomechanics and reaction principles. The starting gun acts as an auditory stimulus triggering a rapid neuromuscular response. By pushing forcefully against the starting blocks, the athlete applies ground reaction force backward and downward, producing forward propulsion. Proper body angles and coordinated limb movement maximize acceleration efficiency in the initial phase of the 100m sprint.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Athletics 100m crouching start technique. Minimum assumptions: a standard track environment, a single athlete, starting blocks, and an audible start signal. The scenario must clearly show the athlete responding to the gun. Phased storyline: (1) Static crouching preparation at the blocks; (2) Audible gun signal as the causal trigger; (3) Immediate explosive push-off with leg extension and arm drive; (4) Transition into forward acceleration. Key causal transition is from sound cue to motion onset. Visibility requirements: clear side or front-angle view showing posture, block push-off, and timing between gun sound and movement for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Tennis Ace Scoring DemonstrationI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Tennis Ace Scoring DemonstrationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – SportObjective: To demonstrate the definition and scoring logic of an ace in tennis through a complete serve-and-score scenario.II. Experimental Setup and EquipmentStandard tennis court with clearly marked service boxes; tennis racket; tennis ball; two players (server and receiver); referee (or umpire); electronic or manual scoreboard.III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation: The server stands behind the baseline on the deuce or ad court; the receiver stands in the correct receiving position; referee and scoreboard are ready.2. Serve Execution: The server tosses the ball and performs a legal serve, striking the ball diagonally toward the opponent’s service box.3. Ball Landing: The tennis ball lands in the extreme inner corner of the opponent’s service area, clearly within the boundary lines.4. Receiver Reaction: The receiver does not touch the ball; no racket or body contact occurs.5. Referee Decision: The referee immediately announces ‘Ace’ based on the untouched valid serve.6. Score Update: The scoreboard increases the server’s score by one point.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both players are stationary; scoreboard shows the previous score.During Serve: Ball travels in a clear arc and lands sharply in the inner corner of the service box.After Landing: Receiver makes no contact; referee’s announcement is heard; scoreboard visibly updates.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn ace in tennis is defined as a legal serve that lands within the correct service box and is not touched by the receiver. According to tennis scoring rules, such a serve immediately awards one point to the server. The experiment demonstrates the rule-based causal relationship between serve validity, opponent response, referee judgment, and score change.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Understanding and visually verifying the rule-based definition of an ace in tennis. Minimum assumptions: standard tennis court, legal serve mechanics, clear service box boundaries, and an authority (referee/scoreboard) to confirm scoring.Phased storyline: (1) Pre-serve setup with visible court and players; (2) Serve action and ball flight; (3) Ball lands precisely in extreme inner corner of service box; (4) Receiver makes no contact; (5) Referee announces ace; (6) Scoreboard updates. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show landing location, lack of contact, and score change to verify causality.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Camera Circling an Eames Lounge ChairI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Camera Circling Demonstration of the Eames Lounge ChairSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Industrial DesignExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how a continuous circular camera movement can be used to present and analyze the form, materials, and iconic design features of the Eames Lounge Chair designed by Charles Eames and Ray Eames.II. Experimental EquipmentEames Lounge Chair with ottoman (classic configuration); controlled indoor environment (studio or living-room-like setting); virtual or physical camera with orbit capability; stable lighting setup emphasizing wood veneer and leather texture.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the Eames Lounge Chair and ottoman at the center of the scene. Ensure the chair is stationary and well-lit from multiple angles.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera at seated-eye height, approximately 2–3 meters from the chair, aimed at the chair’s front.3. Core Operation: Initiate a smooth, continuous circular camera movement around the chair, maintaining a constant radius and height. The camera should complete one full 360-degree orbit within a short, accelerated timeframe suitable for a 10-second demonstration.4. Framing Control: Keep the chair fully within frame throughout the motion, allowing clear visibility of the molded plywood shell, leather cushions, and ottoman alignment.5. Completion: End the camera movement at the original front-facing position, briefly holding the final frame.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The Eames Lounge Chair is static, clearly visible from the front, with recognizable proportions and materials.During Camera Movement: As the camera circles, different design aspects become visible in sequence—side profile, rear plywood shell, and opposite side—while the chair itself remains unchanged.Final State: The camera returns to the front view, reinforcing the overall form and symmetry of the design.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on principles of industrial design presentation and visual communication. A circular camera movement provides a comprehensive, continuous perspective of a product, allowing viewers to understand form, structure, ergonomics, and material relationships without altering the object itself. The causal logic is simple: controlled camera motion causes systematic changes in viewpoint, which reveal different design features while maintaining object integrity.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure camera motion is smooth and uninterrupted; avoid changes in lighting during the orbit; keep the chair stationary to preserve spatiotemporal consistency.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is an industrial design demonstration in which a stationary Eames Lounge Chair is revealed through a continuous circular camera movement. Visibility Constraints: The chair must remain fully visible, centered, and undistorted throughout, with no abrupt changes in scale, position, or lighting, enabling clear verification of camera-driven perspective change.

manual: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip Turn DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Swimming Freestyle Forward Flip Turn DemonstrationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – SportExperiment Objective: To demonstrate and understand the standard technique of a freestyle forward flip turn, including approach, rotation, wall push-off, posture adjustment, and continuation of swimming.II. Experimental Equipment and ConditionsStandard swimming pool with clear lane markings; pool wall with visible T-mark; swimmer wearing standard swimwear, goggles, and swim cap; safe water depth suitable for flip turns.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Preparation: The athlete starts several meters from the pool wall and adopts a standard freestyle swimming posture.2. Freestyle Approach: The athlete swims freestyle toward the wall at a steady speed, maintaining a horizontal body position and rhythmic arm strokes.3. Head Lowering and Leg Tuck: About one arm’s length from the wall, the athlete lowers the head, engages the core, and quickly tucks the knees toward the chest to initiate a forward rotation.4. Forward Flip: Using forward momentum and the tucked position, the athlete completes a forward somersault underwater, rotating so the feet face the wall.5. Wall Push-Off: The soles of both feet contact the pool wall simultaneously; the athlete extends the legs forcefully to push off, changing direction.6. Posture Adjustment: After push-off, the athlete forms a streamlined position (arms extended, head between arms, body straight) and glides briefly.7. Continuation: The athlete rotates to a prone position, resumes freestyle kicking and arm strokes, and continues swimming away from the wall.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before Turn: The swimmer approaches the wall smoothly with continuous freestyle motion.2. During Turn: The swimmer’s head lowers, legs tuck, and a compact forward flip occurs underwater; feet make clear contact with the wall.3. After Turn: A strong push-off results in a streamlined glide, followed by a smooth transition back into freestyle swimming.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe freestyle forward flip turn is based on principles of biomechanics and hydrodynamics. Forward swimming speed provides momentum for rotation; tucking the legs reduces rotational radius and increases angular velocity. A strong wall push-off converts stored muscular force into forward propulsion in the opposite direction. Streamlining reduces water resistance, allowing efficient continuation of swimming.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure sufficient distance from the wall before initiating the flip; avoid shallow water; maintain controlled speed to prevent collision; practice under supervision if inexperienced.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: a standard freestyle forward flip turn in competitive swimming. Minimum assumptions include a real swimming pool, a human swimmer capable of freestyle, normal gravity, and realistic water resistance. Expected phenomena follow a phased storyline: (1) approach phase with visible freestyle strokes toward the wall; (2) transition phase where head lowers and knees tuck, causing forward rotation; (3) contact phase where feet touch the wall and legs extend to push off; (4) exit phase with streamlined glide and rotation back to prone; (5) continuation phase resuming freestyle. Key causal transitions include momentum enabling rotation and wall force enabling direction change. The camera should clearly show the swimmer’s body relative to the wall, with underwater visibility sufficient to verify tuck, flip, foot contact, and streamline.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Fosbury Flop Bar Clearance ObservationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Fosbury Flop Bar Clearance ObservationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – SportObjective: To observe and understand the Fosbury flop technique, focusing on arc approach, backward clearance posture, and the lowest point of the athlete’s center of gravity relative to the bar using image focusing and time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentHigh jump bar and uprights; standard high jump landing mat; marked curved approach track; athletic footwear; high-speed or time-lapse camera; tripod; labeling software or overlay tools.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set the bar at a moderate height; mark an arc-shaped approach path; position the camera perpendicular to the bar with full-body view.2. Approach Run: Athlete runs along the marked arc toward the bar, maintaining increasing speed and inward lean.3. Take-off: Athlete plants the take-off foot, allowing body rotation to initiate.4. Clearance: Athlete jumps backward over the bar, forming a supine arch; back contacts the bar first while head and limbs droop.5. Recording: Capture the motion using focused framing and time-lapse or sequential frames; label the back-bar contact and center of gravity path.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The approach path is visibly curved.2. Take-off foot causes body rotation toward the bar.3. During clearance, the athlete’s back is the first contact point with the bar.4. The body forms a clear supine arch, with limbs hanging downward.5. The labeled center of gravity reaches its lowest relative position below the bar during clearance.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Fosbury flop uses an arc approach to generate angular momentum. During take-off, this rotation allows the athlete to clear the bar backward in a supine arch. By arching the body, the athlete’s center of gravity passes below the bar while the body clears it, enabling higher jumps without raising the center of gravity above the bar.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure safe bar height and proper landing mat placement; maintain consistent camera position; simplify motion capture for short time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Fosbury flop bar clearance mechanics. Minimum assumptions: an athlete, a horizontal bar, arc approach, single-foot take-off, backward supine clearance.Phased Storyline: (1) Curved approach generating inward lean; (2) take-off foot plant causing rotation; (3) backward leap into supine arch; (4) back-first bar contact with limbs drooping; (5) visual emphasis on center of gravity passing below the bar. Visibility requirements: side-on camera view, stable framing, and clear labeling of bar, body posture, and center of gravity path.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Variance Contraction in an Economic Time SeriesI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Variance Contraction in an Economic Time Series2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visualize and understand the variance contraction feature of an economic indicator by plotting a time-series line graph whose fluctuation amplitude decreases over time, and to interpret this phenomenon as economic stabilization.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsComputer or tablet, spreadsheet or statistical software (e.g., Excel, Python, or similar), sample economic time-series data (e.g., inflation rate, exchange rate, or stock index returns), graphing function, screen recording or time-lapse capture tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Data Preparation: Open the software and load a time-series dataset of an economic indicator arranged chronologically. Ensure early-period data show larger fluctuations than later-period data.2. Graph Setup: Insert a line chart. Set the horizontal axis as time and the vertical axis as the economic indicator value. Label both axes clearly.3. Core Operation (Time-Lapse Plotting): Gradually reveal or animate the data points from the earliest to the latest time period, using a time-lapse effect so the line extends from left to right.4. Focused Observation: Keep the chart centered and stable while the line grows over time, ensuring no changes to scale or axis limits.5. Completion: Stop the animation once the full time range is displayed and save the final chart.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Stage: At the beginning of the time axis, the line fluctuates sharply with large peaks and troughs.2. Intermediate Stage: As time progresses, the amplitude of fluctuations becomes smaller and more moderate.3. Final Stage: In the later time period, the line appears smoother and more stable, with only minor variations around a central value.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesVariance contraction refers to the economic phenomenon in which the volatility of an indicator decreases over time. This often occurs due to market maturation, policy stabilization, learning effects, or reduced uncertainty. In a line chart, variance contraction is visually represented by a progressive reduction in fluctuation amplitude along the time axis, reflecting increased stability of the economic system.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is variance contraction in economics, defined as a time-dependent decrease in the volatility of an economic indicator. Minimum assumptions include a correctly labeled time axis, a single continuous economic indicator, and a fixed chart scale.Phased Storyline for Verification: Phase 1 shows early high volatility with large visual fluctuations; Phase 2 shows a transition period where fluctuations visibly shrink; Phase 3 shows late-stage stabilization with small, consistent deviations. The camera/view must remain fixed on the chart, with a clear time-lapse progression from left to right, enabling direct visual verification of causal time-to-stability transition.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment No Correlation Feature Demonstration Using a Scatter PlotI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstrating No Correlation Between Two Economic Variables Using a Scatter Plot2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Economics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the feature of no correlation by inputting paired data from two independent economic variables into a spreadsheet and generating a scatter plot with randomly distributed points and no obvious trend.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsComputer or laptop, spreadsheet software (e.g., Excel, Google Sheets), sample paired data of two independent economic variables (e.g., daily coffee sales in one city and stock prices of an unrelated company), screen recording or time-lapse capture tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the spreadsheet software and create a new blank worksheet. Ensure the screen is clearly visible and recording is ready.2. Data Input: In column A, enter numerical values for Economic Variable X. In column B, enter paired numerical values for Economic Variable Y, ensuring the two variables are chosen to be independent.3. Selection: Highlight both columns of paired data, including headers.4. Chart Generation: Use the Insert Chart function to select a scatter plot (XY scatter) without connecting lines.5. Display Adjustment: Label the horizontal axis as Variable X and the vertical axis as Variable Y. Adjust scaling if necessary so points are clearly visible.6. Observation Stage: Observe the distribution of points on the scatter plot. Use time-lapse to show the process from data entry to final chart.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The spreadsheet initially shows only numerical data arranged in two columns.2. During Chart Generation: After inserting the scatter plot, data points appear simultaneously on the chart area.3. Final State: The scatter plot displays points distributed randomly across the graph, with no clear upward or downward trend and no visible pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn economics, correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. When two variables are independent, changes in one do not systematically affect the other. As a result, plotting paired values of such variables on a scatter plot produces a random distribution of points with no obvious trend. This visual pattern represents the no correlation feature and indicates that the correlation coefficient is close to zero.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the selected variables are truly independent to avoid accidental correlation.2. Use sufficient data points to clearly display randomness.3. Choose the correct scatter plot type, not a line or bar chart.4. Keep the recording focused on the spreadsheet to clearly show each operation step.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: No correlation between two economic variables, defined as the absence of a systematic linear relationship, visually represented by a scatter plot with randomly distributed points. Minimum assumptions: two independent numerical variables, correct spreadsheet operations, and use of an XY scatter plot. Phased storyline: (1) clear spreadsheet interface appears; (2) paired economic data are entered into two columns over time (time-lapse); (3) data are selected and a scatter plot is generated; (4) points appear randomly with no discernible trend. Visibility constraints: axes labels and point distribution must be clearly visible; camera remains fixed on the screen with smooth time progression to verify causal transitions from data input to uncorrelated outcome.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plotting the Demand Curve (Downward-Sloping)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plotting the Demand Curve with Price and Quantity2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the law of demand by plotting price–quantity combinations on a coordinate graph and forming a downward-sloping demand curve, understanding the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.II. Experimental MaterialsGraph paper or digital plotting software, ruler or straightedge, pen or stylus, predefined table of price–quantity data, optional camera or screen recorder for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Prepare a set of price–quantity data where higher prices correspond to lower quantities demanded. Fix the camera or screen recorder to capture the full graph area.2. Plot Axes: Draw the coordinate axes. Label the vertical axis as Price and the horizontal axis as Quantity. Mark clear and even scales on both axes.3. Plot Points: According to the data table, plot multiple price–quantity points one by one in sequence, from high price–low quantity to low price–high quantity.4. Curve Connection: Use a smooth line to connect the plotted points, forming a continuous curve.5. Time-lapse Focus: Use time-lapse photography or accelerated screen recording to show the sequential appearance of points and the gradual formation of the curve.6. Completion: Ensure labels are clear and the final curve slopes downward from top-left to bottom-right.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only labeled coordinate axes are visible.2. During Plotting: Individual points appear sequentially, each new point lying lower and further to the right than the previous one.3. Final State: A smooth curve connects all points, clearly sloping downward from top-left to bottom-right.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the law of demand in economics. Under the assumption that other factors remain constant, an increase in price leads to a decrease in quantity demanded, while a decrease in price leads to an increase in quantity demanded. Plotting price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis results in a demand curve that slopes downward from left to right, visually representing this inverse relationship.VI. Precautions1. Ensure axes are correctly labeled and scaled before plotting points.2. Plot points accurately according to the data to avoid distortion of the curve.3. Keep the camera or recording frame stable to maintain clear time-lapse continuity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: The demand curve illustrates the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded under ceteris paribus conditions. Minimum assumptions include rational consumers, stable preferences, and no change in non-price factors.Phased Storyline: (1) A blank graph with clearly labeled axes establishes spatial reference; (2) price–quantity points appear sequentially, each reflecting a higher price with lower quantity or vice versa; (3) points are smoothly connected into a continuous curve; (4) the final image shows a clear downward-sloping demand curve. Visibility constraints require the full axes, labels, and curve to remain in frame throughout, with time-lapse acceleration emphasizing sequence without altering order.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment Stagflation: Inflation and Unemployment Rising SimultaneouslyI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Stagflation Demonstration Using Time-Series GraphsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EconomicsObjective: To visually demonstrate the economic phenomenon of stagflation by plotting inflation and unemployment rates that rise simultaneously over time, and to understand its core characteristics through graphical analysis.II. Experimental MaterialsBlank coordinate grid or digital graphing interface; horizontal axis labeled Time; vertical axis labeled Inflation Rate and Unemployment Rate; two distinct colored plotting lines (e.g., red for inflation, blue for unemployment); time-lapse or accelerated plotting tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up the coordinate axes with time on the horizontal axis and rate levels on the vertical axis; ensure labels are clear and legible.2. Initial State: Begin with both inflation and unemployment at relatively low and stable levels at the starting time point.3. Step-by-Step Plotting: As time progresses, plot the inflation rate upward in small increments; simultaneously plot the unemployment rate upward at corresponding time points, using a step-by-step method.4. Time-Lapse Focus: Use accelerated or time-lapse visualization to show the gradual but continuous upward movement of both curves.5. Completion: End the plotting when both curves clearly show a sustained upward trend over the same time period.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, both curves start at low values; as time advances, the inflation curve rises steadily; at the same time, the unemployment curve also rises; the final graph shows two upward-sloping curves occurring simultaneously over the same time axis.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleStagflation is an economic condition characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of high inflation and high unemployment during a period of stagnant economic growth. Contrary to traditional economic theory suggesting a trade-off between inflation and unemployment, stagflation demonstrates that adverse supply shocks or structural problems can cause both indicators to rise together. The experiment uses synchronized upward curves to visually represent this principle.VI. NotesThe experiment focuses on conceptual visualization rather than numerical accuracy; the key requirement is the simultaneity and direction of the trends.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Stagflation, defined as the simultaneous rise of inflation and unemployment over time. Minimum assumptions: a time axis, two economic indicators, and the ability to plot their changes sequentially. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) establish labeled axes; (2) show initial low levels for both indicators; (3) progressively and simultaneously plot rising inflation and unemployment using step-by-step increments; (4) accelerate the process with time-lapse to fit within a short video; (5) end with a clear visual of two upward-sloping curves, confirming stagflation. Visibility constraints: curves must be distinct in color and remain within the same coordinate system for direct comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Demonstration: Plotting the Marginal Cost CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plotting the Marginal Cost Curve (U-shaped)2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the U-shaped feature of the marginal cost curve, understand why marginal cost first decreases and then increases with output, and learn how to correctly plot and interpret a marginal cost point on a cost-output graph.II. Experimental MaterialsCoordinate axis template or blank graph paper, marker or digital drawing tool, ruler (optional), time-lapse recording device or software (for demonstration).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up a clear coordinate axis. Label the horizontal axis as Output (Q) and the vertical axis as Cost (MC). Ensure the origin and scale are visible.2. Initial Plotting: Starting from a low level of output, draw the marginal cost curve with a downward slope, representing decreasing marginal cost due to specialization and improved efficiency.3. Turning Point: Gradually reduce the downward slope until reaching the lowest point of the curve, indicating minimum marginal cost.4. Rising Section: Continue plotting the curve upward as output increases further, showing rising marginal cost caused by diminishing marginal returns.5. Marking Point A: Select a specific output level on the curve and mark it clearly as marginal cost point A, using a dot and label.6. Demonstration Method: Use time-lapse photography or accelerated drawing so the entire plotting process is visible within a short time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The coordinate axis remains fixed, with output on the horizontal axis and cost on the vertical axis.2. The marginal cost curve initially slopes downward, then reaches a minimum, and finally slopes upward, forming a clear U-shape.3. Point A appears on the curve at a specific output level, clearly indicating a marginal cost value.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe marginal cost curve reflects the change in total cost resulting from producing one additional unit of output. In the short run, marginal cost initially decreases due to improved efficiency, division of labor, and better utilization of fixed factors. As output continues to expand, diminishing marginal returns set in, causing marginal cost to rise. This combination leads to the characteristic U-shaped marginal cost curve. Point A represents the marginal cost at a specific output level, helping analyze production decisions.VI. PrecautionsEnsure axes are correctly labeled; avoid drawing a purely upward-sloping curve; maintain clear visibility of the curve and point A throughout the demonstration.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The demonstration focuses on the marginal cost curve in microeconomics, assuming a short-run production context with fixed factors and diminishing marginal returns. The minimum assumption is that output changes affect marginal cost through efficiency gains first and capacity constraints later.Expected Phenomena and Phased Storyline: Phase 1 shows a stable coordinate axis with correct labels. Phase 2 displays the marginal cost curve falling as output increases, indicating efficiency gains. Phase 3 shows a turning point where marginal cost is minimized. Phase 4 shows the curve rising as output expands further, reflecting diminishing returns. Phase 5 highlights and labels point A on the curve. The camera or viewpoint remains fixed, and time-lapse acceleration ensures all phases are visible and verifiable within a short duration.

manual: Experiment Title: Using a Pie Chart to Represent a Perfectly Competitive IndustrySubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EconomicsExperiment Objective: To visually illustrate the characteristics of a perfectly competitive industry by using a pie chart to represent the market shares of multiple firms.Experimental Materials: Paper or digital drawing tool, pen or chart software, hypothetical market share data for five companies (A, B, C, D, E).Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Assume an industry composed of five companies (A–E) operating under perfect competition, where no single firm dominates the market.2. Data Setting: Assign each company a similar market share (for example, each holding about 20 percent of the total market).3. Chart Construction: Draw a circle to represent the total industry market size. Divide the circle into five equal or nearly equal sectors.4. Labeling: Mark each sector clearly as Company A, B, C, D, and E, and use different colors or patterns to distinguish them.5. Display and Observation: Present the completed pie chart for observation and discussion.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. Initial State: A blank circle representing the total market.2. During Construction: The circle is divided into several similar-sized sectors.3. Final State: The completed pie chart shows five companies with nearly equal market shares, and no single sector is significantly larger than the others.Summary of Experimental Principle:In a perfectly competitive industry, there are many firms, each with a small and similar share of the total market. A pie chart visually represents this structure by showing the total market as a whole and each firm as a proportion of that whole. When the slices are nearly equal in size, the chart intuitively demonstrates the absence of market power and the competitive nature of the industry.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Perfect competition, defined by many firms with small and roughly equal market shares and no dominant firm. Minimum assumptions include a fixed total market size and five representative firms.Phased Storyline: (1) Introduce the total market as a circle; (2) divide it into five similar slices; (3) label slices A–E; (4) present the final chart. The key causal transition is that equal slice sizes visually imply equal market power. Visibility requires a clear, front-facing view of the chart with legible labels and stable proportions for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Average Cost Curve Feature (U-shaped Curve)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Visual Demonstration of the Average Cost CurveSubject: Economics – MicroeconomicsObjective: To visually demonstrate how average cost changes with output, forming a U-shaped curve, and to understand its relationship with marginal cost.II. Equipment and MaterialsDigital screen or computer display, graphing software or simulation interface, coordinate axis template (output on horizontal axis, cost on vertical axis), data point markers, focused imaging and time-lapse display function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a blank coordinate axis on the screen with output labeled on the horizontal axis and cost on the vertical axis.2. Data Input: Gradually input cost data corresponding to increasing levels of output.3. Point Marking: Mark each cost-output pair as a visible data point on the axis.4. Time-lapse Connection: Using time-lapse visualization, connect the data points sequentially to form the average cost curve.5. Focused Imaging: Zoom or highlight the curve as it forms to emphasize its shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low output levels, average cost decreases as output increases.2. After reaching a minimum point, average cost begins to increase with further output.3. The connected data points form a smooth U-shaped curve on the coordinate axis.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe average cost curve is U-shaped due to economies of scale at low output levels, which reduce average cost, and diseconomies of scale at high output levels, which increase average cost. The marginal cost curve intersects the average cost curve at its minimum point, reflecting the underlying cost structure of production.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The U-shaped average cost curve in microeconomics, assuming a standard production process with economies and diseconomies of scale and a consistent cost-output relationship.Expected phenomena storyline: (1) A clear coordinate axis appears with output and cost labeled; (2) data points emerge sequentially as output increases; (3) early points show declining average cost, followed by rising costs; (4) points connect smoothly over time to form a U-shaped curve. Visibility requirements: stable front-facing view of the graph, clear labels, and smooth time-lapse transitions to verify causal and temporal consistency.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Diminishing Marginal Utility CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Diminishing Marginal Utility Using a Utility Curve2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the law of diminishing marginal utility by plotting utility against quantity consumed and observing the downward-sloping utility curve.II. Experimental MaterialsCoordinate grid (digital or drawn), horizontal axis labeled Quantity, vertical axis labeled Utility, data point markers (dots), animation or time-lapse recording tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up a clear coordinate axis with Quantity on the horizontal axis and Utility on the vertical axis; ensure the frame is stable and focused.2. Initial State: Begin with zero or low quantity consumption and mark the first utility point high on the utility axis.3. Core Operation: Gradually increase quantity consumed. For each increase, add a new data point showing total utility, ensuring that each additional unit adds less utility than the previous one.4. Time-lapse Display: Use time-lapse photography or animation so data points appear sequentially and smoothly over time.5. Curve Formation: Connect or visually align the points to reveal a curve that becomes flatter as quantity increases.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At low quantities, added points show large increases in utility.2. As quantity increases, added points show smaller incremental increases in utility.3. The resulting curve slopes downward in marginal terms, appearing concave and flattening as quantity grows.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe law of diminishing marginal utility states that as a person consumes more units of the same good, the additional satisfaction (marginal utility) gained from each extra unit decreases. Graphically, this is represented by a utility curve where increases in quantity correspond to progressively smaller increases in utility.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Diminishing marginal utility, assuming rational consumers and measurable utility for identical goods. Minimum assumptions include a single good, consistent preferences, and sequential consumption.Phased storyline: (1) Display stable coordinate axes with clear labels; (2) Introduce initial high-utility data point; (3) Add subsequent points at increasing quantities with visibly smaller vertical gaps; (4) Reveal a smooth, flattening curve via time-lapse. The camera remains fixed and focused on the graph to ensure visibility of causal transitions from increased quantity to reduced marginal utility.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Demonstration of Heteroscedasticity Using a Scatter PlotI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visual Demonstration of Heteroscedasticity (Trumpet-Shaped Scatter Plot)Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EconomicsObjective: To visually demonstrate heteroscedasticity by gradually constructing a 2D scatter plot in which the variance of the dependent variable increases as the independent variable increases.II. Experimental ToolsComputer with plotting software (e.g., Python/Excel), blank 2D coordinate system, dataset generator or manual point input.III. Experimental Procedure1. Plot Setup: Create a 2D coordinate system with the x-axis labeled as the independent variable and the y-axis labeled as the dependent variable. Ensure the x-axis increases from left to right. No data points are shown initially.2. Initial Data Addition: Add a small number of data points at low x-values. Ensure these points are tightly clustered around a central trend, showing low variance.3. Progressive Data Addition: Gradually add more data points as x-values increase. With each step, allow the vertical spread of points to increase slightly.4. Final Stage: Continue adding points at higher x-values, clearly increasing the spread of the dependent variable, forming a visible trumpet or fan shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The plot is empty, showing only axes.2. Early Stage: Points at low x-values are closely grouped with small variance.3. Middle Stage: As x increases, points begin to spread vertically.4. Final Stage: At high x-values, points show large variance, creating a trumpet-shaped distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHeteroscedasticity refers to a situation in which the variance of the dependent variable is not constant across levels of the independent variable. In this experiment, as the independent variable increases, external influences or scaling effects cause the variability of the dependent variable to grow. This violates the homoscedasticity assumption of classical linear regression and is visually represented by a widening scatter plot.VI. Experimental NotesThe focus is on visual pattern recognition rather than precise numerical values. The chronological order of adding points is essential to understanding the causal relationship.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Heteroscedasticity in economics, defined as increasing variance of the dependent variable with respect to the independent variable. Minimum assumptions include a correctly oriented 2D plot, labeled axes, and a monotonic increase in x-values.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 shows an empty coordinate system; Phase 2 adds low-variance points at small x-values; Phase 3 progressively adds points with increasing vertical dispersion; Phase 4 culminates in a clear trumpet-shaped scatter. Visibility requires a stable camera/viewpoint, cumulative point addition, and no resetting of the plot, enabling verification of causal transitions from low to high variance.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Price Ceiling Below Equilibrium in a Supply–Demand GraphI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Demonstration of a Price Ceiling Below Market Equilibrium2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate, using a coordinate graph, how a government-imposed price ceiling set below the market equilibrium price affects the market. Students will understand the relationship between demand, supply, equilibrium price, and a binding price ceiling through step-by-step graphical construction.II. Experimental Materials and EnvironmentCoordinate axis displayed on screen (digital whiteboard, tablet, or computer drawing software), drawing tool (pen/line tool), labels for axes (Demand/Quantity on horizontal axis, Price on vertical axis). Image-focused screen recording or time-lapse capture is required; no physical materials are needed.III. Experimental Operation Process1. Axis Setup: Display a blank coordinate system on the screen. Clearly label the horizontal axis as Demand (Quantity) and the vertical axis as Price.2. Drawing the Demand Curve: From the upper-left to the lower-right, draw a downward-sloping line and label it Demand, indicating the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.3. Drawing the Supply Curve: From the lower-left to the upper-right, draw an upward-sloping line and label it Supply, indicating the direct relationship between price and quantity supplied.4. Marking Equilibrium: Identify and mark the intersection point of the demand and supply curves. Label this point as Equilibrium and draw a horizontal guide (optional) to indicate the equilibrium price level.5. Adding the Price Ceiling: Draw a horizontal line across the graph at a price level below the equilibrium price. Label this line Price Ceiling to indicate a policy-imposed maximum price.6. Time-Lapse Presentation: Present the drawing process in a smooth, accelerated time-lapse, ensuring each step appears in logical order and remains visually clear.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only the coordinate axes are visible, with clear labels for price and demand.2. Mid-Process: The demand and supply curves appear sequentially, crossing at a single equilibrium point.3. Final State: A horizontal price ceiling line is clearly visible below the equilibrium price, visually separating the regulated price from the market equilibrium.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the core economic principle of price controls. In a free market, the equilibrium price is determined by the intersection of supply and demand. When a price ceiling is imposed below this equilibrium, it becomes binding, preventing prices from rising to the equilibrium level. Graphically, this is shown as a horizontal line below the equilibrium point, illustrating potential market effects such as excess demand (shortage). The visual relationship between curves and lines is the key focus of this demonstration.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Ensure axes labels and curve directions are correct according to economic theory.2. The price ceiling must be clearly below, not at or above, the equilibrium price.3. Keep the background simple to avoid distracting from the graph relationships.

Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the inverse relationship between interest rates and money demand using a coordinate graph, and to understand why higher interest rates reduce money demand.II. Experiment Title: Plotting a Bar Chart under a Fiscal Surplus Situation2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To understand the concept of fiscal surplus by visually representing government income and expenditure using a bar chart, and to master the basic method of plotting and interpreting economic data graphs.II. Experimental MaterialsCoordinate grid or charting software (or whiteboard), data set showing government income and expenditure, ruler or digital plotting tool, colored pens or chart colors (two distinct colors for income and expenditure).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Draw a set of perpendicular axes on the screen or canvas. Label the horizontal axis as Funds (categories such as Income and Expenditure) and the vertical axis as Currency (monetary units).2. Data Setup: Confirm that the income value is greater than the expenditure value to reflect a fiscal surplus condition.3. Plotting Bars: On the horizontal axis, mark Income and Expenditure categories. Draw vertical bars upward from the baseline, using the vertical axis scale to represent currency values.4. Differentiation: Use different colors or shading to distinguish income bars from expenditure bars, and add simple labels or a legend.5. Completion: Review the chart to ensure income is visibly higher than expenditure, then finalize the display.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Final State: The income bar is taller than the expenditure bar, clearly indicating a fiscal surplus.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the economic principle of fiscal balance. A fiscal surplus occurs when government income exceeds government expenditure within a given period. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Drawing a Monopoly Demand CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Drawing a Monopoly Demand Curve2. Subject: Economics – Microeconomics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate that a monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve identical to the market (industry) demand curve, and to help learners understand the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded through graphical representation.II. Experimental EquipmentWhiteboard or paper, ruler (optional), black or blue marker/pen, graph template (optional), camera or screen-recording device capable of time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Fix the camera above the drawing surface to ensure a clear, centered view of the graph area; enable time-lapse recording to compress the drawing process.2. Drawing Axes: Draw two perpendicular axes. Label the vertical axis as Price (P) and the horizontal axis as Quantity (Q). Ensure labels are clear and remain fixed throughout.3. Scaling and Orientation: Add arrowheads to both axes to indicate increasing values of price and quantity.4. Core Operation – Drawing the Demand Curve: Starting from a higher point on the price axis, draw a smooth curve sloping downward to the right toward a higher quantity, representing the monopoly (market) demand curve.5. Emphasis and Labeling: Label the curve as Demand (D) or Monopoly Demand Curve to distinguish it clearly.6. Completion: Stop the recording after the full curve and labels are visible; keep the final image on screen briefly for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: A blank surface with no markings.2. During the Drawing Process: Axes appear first, followed by labels; the curve gradually emerges from top-left to bottom-right.3. Final State: A complete graph showing price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis, and a clearly downward-sloping monopoly demand curve.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn monopoly theory, the firm is the sole producer in the market and therefore faces the entire market demand curve. Market demand reflects consumers’ inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: as price increases, quantity demanded decreases. Graphically, this relationship is represented by a downward-sloping curve with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. Unlike perfect competition, the monopolist’s demand curve is not horizontal but slopes downward, consistent with industry demand.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure axes are correctly oriented before drawing the curve.2. Keep the camera fixed to avoid spatial inconsistency.3. Use time-lapse to shorten the process while preserving the correct sequence of steps.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Monopoly demand curve as the market demand curve, downward sloping due to inverse price–quantity relationship. Minimum assumptions: single seller, consumers respond to price changes, price on vertical axis and quantity on horizontal axis. Expected Phenomena Storyline: (1) A blank drawing space appears; (2) axes are drawn with clear orientation and labels; (3) a smooth downward-sloping curve is drawn from high price–low quantity to low price–high quantity; (4) the curve is labeled and remains stable in view. Visibility Constraints: camera remains fixed and centered; all elements stay in frame for verification of order, shape, and causal meaning.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Thermal Camera Showing Handprint Cooling on a TabletopI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Thermal Camera Showing Handprint Cooling on a Tabletop2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe heat transfer between the human body and an indoor surface using a handheld thermal infrared camera, and to understand surface temperature change and cooling over time.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld thermal infrared camera (with time-lapse or recording function), smooth tabletop surface (wood, plastic, or stone), bare hand of the participant, stable indoor environment (no strong airflow).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the thermal camera and select a suitable temperature color palette; ensure the tabletop surface is clean and dry.2. Initial Observation: Aim the thermal camera at the tabletop to confirm a uniform background temperature.3. Core Operation: Press the bare hand flat onto the smooth tabletop surface for about 3–5 seconds.4. Hand Removal: Lift the hand vertically away from the surface.5. Recording: Keep the thermal camera focused on the contact area and record continuously or via time-lapse to capture temperature changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. During Contact: The contact area under the hand appears warmer (brighter or red/yellow colors) than the surrounding surface.2. Immediately After Lifting: A clear handprint-shaped warm region remains visible on the tabletop.3. Over Time: The handprint gradually cools, with colors shifting toward cooler tones until it blends into the background temperature.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates heat transfer by conduction from the human hand to the tabletop. When the hand contacts the surface, thermal energy flows from the warmer hand to the cooler table. After the hand is removed, the warmed area loses heat to the surrounding material and air through conduction, convection, and radiation, causing the visible thermal handprint to fade over time.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid touching the surface with objects before recording; minimize airflow to reduce uneven cooling; hold the camera steady to ensure clear time-lapse observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visualizing heat transfer and cooling using thermal infrared imaging. Minimum assumptions: a handheld thermal camera accurately maps surface temperature; the hand is warmer than the tabletop; the tabletop is smooth and stationary. Phased storyline: (1) Baseline uniform tabletop temperature in thermal view; (2) Hand presses flat for a few seconds, causing localized warming; (3) Hand lifts, revealing a warm handprint; (4) Time-lapse shows gradual cooling and fading of the handprint. Key causal transitions: contact causes heat conduction; removal initiates cooling. Visibility constraints: thermal color palette must clearly distinguish warm vs cool regions; camera perspective remains fixed on the tabletop throughout.

Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the trays, ensuring both trays are fully visible. Fix the focus and keep the camera stationary for time-lapse photography.4. Rainfall Simulation: Start the camera recording. Apply steady and uniform artificial rain simultaneously over both trays from the same height and intensity.5. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Chemical Weathering of Limestone by VinegarI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Vinegar Reacting with Limestone Causing Surface Erosion2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography (Physical Geography)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the process of chemical weathering by showing how weak acid (vinegar) reacts with limestone, leading to surface erosion; to help learners visually understand chemical weathering of carbonate rocks in natural environments through time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment- Pale limestone rock (1 piece, clean and dry, surface clearly visible)- Clear glass dish (shallow, transparent)- Clear vinegar (approximately 100–150 mL, household vinegar)- Measuring cup or beaker (for pouring vinegar)- Camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-position time-lapse photography)- Absorbent paper or tray (to protect the surface under the dish)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place absorbent paper on a stable table. Put the clear glass dish on top. Ensure sufficient lighting so that surface details of the limestone are clearly visible.2. Placement of Rock: Place the pale limestone rock flat in the center of the clear glass dish, with its upper surface fully exposed.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera or smartphone on a tripod directly above or at a slight angle to the dish. Fix the focus and frame so the entire limestone surface is visible. Do not adjust the camera during the experiment.4. Adding Vinegar: Slowly pour clear vinegar over the surface of the limestone until the upper surface is fully covered and in continuous contact with the liquid.5. Reaction and Recording: Allow the vinegar to remain in contact with the limestone. Start time-lapse recording or continuous video. Do not disturb the setup during recording.6. Completion: After sufficient observation time (or accelerated time-lapse), stop recording. Carefully pour off the vinegar and remove the limestone for inspection.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The limestone surface appears pale, solid, and relatively smooth; the vinegar is colorless and transparent.2. Early Reaction: Small bubbles appear on the limestone surface shortly after vinegar contact, especially at cracks or rough areas.3. Continued Reaction: Bubbling continues; the limestone surface gradually becomes rougher and duller, with tiny pits or etched marks becoming visible.4. Final State: Compared with the initial state, the limestone shows visible surface erosion, while the vinegar may appear slightly cloudy due to dissolved material.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates chemical weathering of limestone. Limestone is mainly composed of calcium carbonate (CaCO3). Vinegar contains acetic acid, a weak acid. When vinegar comes into contact with limestone, a chemical reaction occurs in which calcium carbonate reacts with the acid, producing soluble calcium salts, carbon dioxide gas (observed as bubbles), and water. This reaction gradually removes material from the rock surface, causing erosion. In nature, similar reactions occur when acidic rainwater or soil water weathers limestone landscapes, forming features such as karst terrain.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a clear glass dish to ensure phenomena are visible from the side and above.2. Pour vinegar slowly to avoid splashing and disturbing the rock position.3. Fix the camera firmly; do not refocus or move it during recording.4. Dispose of used vinegar safely and clean the equipment after the experiment.

(2) Action phase – clear vinegar poured over the limestone surface, fully covering it. (3) Reaction phase – bubbles gradually appear on the rock surface, indicating CO2 release. (4) Erosion phase – surface becomes rougher and slightly etched over time, visible via time-lapse. Visibility constraints: transparent dish, clear liquid, close and fixed camera perspective to verify surface changes and bubbling clearly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ball Rolled Across a Rotating Turntable (Overhead View)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ball Rolled Across a Rotating Turntable Viewed from Above2. Subject: Geography – Earth Rotation and Apparent Motion3. Experiment Objective: To observe the apparent deflection of a moving object on a rotating surface, understand motion in a rotating reference frame, and relate the phenomenon to the Coriolis effect.II. Experimental EquipmentCircular turntable with a clearly marked center, small smooth ball (contrasting color), stable overhead camera or tripod mount, uniform lighting, marker tape for edge reference (optional).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the turntable on a stable horizontal surface. Mark the center and ensure the surface is clean and level. Mount the camera directly above the center, ensuring a fixed overhead view. Lock focus and exposure for time-lapse or continuous recording.Rotation Setup: Set the turntable to rotate clockwise at a steady, moderate speed. Allow it to reach constant rotation before releasing the ball.Core Operation: Gently place the ball at the exact center of the rotating turntable. Release the ball smoothly so it rolls straight outward toward the edge without an initial sideways push.Recording: Record the entire process from release until the ball reaches the edge, maintaining a fixed camera position and focus.Completion: Stop the rotation after the ball reaches the edge and end the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The turntable rotates clockwise; the ball is stationary at the center.2. During Motion: As the ball rolls outward, its path appears curved relative to the rotating turntable surface.3. Final State: The ball reaches the edge at a position that is deflected relative to a straight radial line on the turntable.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn an inertial (non-rotating) reference frame, the ball moves approximately in a straight line. However, when observed from the rotating turntable, the surface rotates beneath the ball. This causes the ball’s path to appear curved relative to the turntable. This apparent deflection is analogous to the Coriolis effect in geography, where moving objects on the rotating Earth appear to deflect due to Earth’s rotation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the camera remains fixed and overhead. Release the ball gently without sideways force. Keep rotation speed constant throughout the experiment.

Phase 2 – Release: The ball is released and begins moving outward. Phase 3 – Apparent Deflection: As the turntable rotates beneath it, the ball’s trajectory appears curved relative to the surface.
