manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Burning a Candle and Bubbling Exhaust Gas Through Limewater to Show CO₂ ReleaseI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Burning a Candle and Bubbling Exhaust Gas Through Limewater to Show CO₂ Release2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography (Human–Environment Interaction)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that carbon dioxide is released during candle combustion by guiding the exhaust gas into clear limewater and observing the resulting change, and to strengthen understanding of gas composition changes caused by human-related combustion activities.II. Experimental EquipmentCandle (1), lighter or matches, glass funnel (inverted), rubber or glass delivery tube, clear limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), two identical transparent glasses, stand or support for funnel and tube, heat-resistant surface, camera or mobile phone with tripod (for fixed-position time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent glasses side by side in the camera frame. Pour an equal amount of clear limewater into one glass (experimental glass); leave the other glass empty or filled with unchanged clear limewater as a control.2. Apparatus Setup: Place a candle on a heat-resistant surface. Light the candle. Invert the funnel over the flame, ensuring the candle burns steadily beneath it. Connect the narrow end of the funnel to a delivery tube, and insert the other end of the tube into the limewater in the experimental glass, with the tube end submerged.3. Recording Setup: Fix the camera focus and position so that the candle, funnel, tube, experimental glass, and control glass are all continuously visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Core Operation: Allow the candle to burn naturally. Combustion exhaust gas is collected by the funnel and guided through the tube, bubbling into the limewater.5. Completion: After sufficient observation, extinguish the candle safely and stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The limewater in the experimental glass is clear and colorless; the control glass shows no change.2. During Combustion: As the candle burns, bubbles are observed passing through the limewater. The limewater gradually becomes cloudy or milky.3. Comparison: The control glass remains unchanged, highlighting that the turbidity in the experimental glass is caused by the combustion exhaust.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCandle combustion produces carbon dioxide gas. When carbon dioxide is guided into clear limewater containing calcium hydroxide, a chemical reaction occurs forming insoluble calcium carbonate, which causes the solution to become turbid. This demonstrates that combustion releases carbon dioxide, an important concept in understanding human energy use and its environmental impact.Core reaction: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃↓ + H₂OVI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the funnel does not extinguish the flame due to lack of oxygen; keep the tube securely connected; avoid touching hot equipment; maintain a fixed camera position for clear comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Combustion of a candle produces carbon dioxide, which can be identified by its reaction with limewater. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: candle combustion occurs steadily; exhaust gas is effectively collected by an inverted funnel; carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide to form visible turbidity.Phased storyline for verification: (1) Static setup phase – candle, inverted funnel, tube, experimental limewater glass, and identical control glass are clearly visible in a fixed camera frame; (2) Combustion phase – candle burns under the funnel, exhaust gas is guided through the tube, and bubbles appear in the experimental glass; (3) Reaction phase – limewater gradually changes from clear to milky while the control glass remains unchanged; (4) End state – candle extinguished or burning reduced, with a clear visual contrast between experimental and control glasses. Visibility constraints: all key objects must remain in view throughout, and the camera perspective must remain fixed to support time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Formation of Barchan Dune vs Longitudinal DuneI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wind-driven Formation of Barchan and Longitudinal Dunes2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the formation processes of barchan dunes and longitudinal dunes under different wind directions, and to understand the relationship between wind regime and dune morphology.II. Experimental EquipmentFlat sand table or tray, dry fine sand (uniform grain size, light color preferred), electric fan with adjustable direction and speed, tripod-mounted camera or mobile phone, marker or tape (to mark wind direction), power supply.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the sand table on a stable surface. Spread a thin, even layer of dry sand to create a flat initial surface. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the sand table; ensure the field of view remains unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Formation of Barchan Dune: Position the fan at one side of the sand table and blow a steady wind from a single fixed direction at moderate speed. Continue blowing until sand begins to migrate and accumulate, gradually forming a crescent-shaped dune. Ensure the two horns of the dune point downwind.3. Adjustment of Wind Direction: Without moving the camera or sand table, rotate the fan to change the wind direction (for example, to be more parallel to the dune ridge). Maintain steady blowing.4. Formation of Longitudinal Dune: Continue blowing as sand redistributes and elongates, gradually forming a dune ridge oriented roughly parallel to the new wind direction.5. Recording: Keep the camera fixed and record the entire process. Use time-lapse or accelerated recording to capture the gradual formation within a short video.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sand surface is flat and uniform, with no distinct relief.2. Under Single-direction Wind: Sand grains move by rolling and hopping; sand accumulates to form a crescent-shaped barchan dune with the convex side facing upwind and horns extending downwind.3. After Wind Direction Change: The original dune shape is modified; sand is redistributed along the wind direction, and an elongated ridge forms, characteristic of a longitudinal dune.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBarchan dunes form under conditions of limited sand supply and a single prevailing wind direction, with sand transported up the gentle windward slope and deposited on the steep leeward slope. Longitudinal dunes develop when wind directions vary or become bidirectional, causing sand to align parallel to the resultant wind direction. The experiment demonstrates how wind regime controls dune shape and orientation through wind-driven sand transport.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Wind regime controls dune morphology. Minimum assumptions: dry loose sand, a visible steady wind source, and a fixed observation perspective. Phased storyline: (1) flat sand under no wind; (2) steady unidirectional wind causes sand migration and accumulation into a crescent-shaped barchan dune with horns pointing downwind; (3) wind direction is adjusted; (4) sand redistributes and elongates into a longitudinal dune. Verification requires a fixed camera, visible wind source orientation, and continuous time-lapse showing causal transitions without scene changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Demonstration of the Transverse Mercator ProjectionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Transverse Mercator Map Projection2. Subject: Geography – Map Projection3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how the transverse Mercator projection transforms a spherical Earth with latitude and longitude into a rectangular planar map by selecting a central meridian and unfolding the globe, and to understand distortion characteristics through observation.II. Experimental EquipmentSpherical globe model with clearly marked latitude and longitude grid; adjustable stand or virtual 3D globe software; projection demonstration apparatus or animation software; camera or screen-recording device with time-lapse function; dark background for contrast.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the spherical globe model on the stand, ensuring latitude and longitude lines are clearly visible. Set up the camera or screen recorder facing the globe.2. Central Meridian Selection: Rotate the globe and visually highlight one longitude line as the central meridian (e.g., by color or brightness).3. Focusing Stage: Use time-lapse recording to capture the camera focusing on the central meridian, emphasizing its vertical orientation.4. Projection Operation: Gradually unfold or mathematically project points from the globe surface onto a plane using the transverse Mercator method, keeping the central meridian straight and vertical.5. Map Formation: Continue unfolding until all visible points form a complete rectangular planar map.6. Completion: Stop recording and display the final rectangular map with grid lines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: A spherical globe with evenly spaced latitude and longitude lines.2. During Projection: The central meridian remains straight; areas near it retain shape, while regions farther away stretch horizontally.3. Final State: A rectangular planar map where meridians and parallels form a grid, with noticeable distortion increasing away from the central meridian.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe transverse Mercator projection is a cylindrical map projection where the cylinder is tangent to the Earth along a chosen central meridian. This results in minimal distortion along that meridian and increasing distortion farther east and west. By unfolding the globe onto a plane, spherical coordinates are transformed into planar coordinates while preserving local angles, making the projection suitable for large-scale mapping of north–south regions.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the central meridian is clearly identified; maintain smooth unfolding to preserve causal continuity; simplify or accelerate the projection process for time-lapse recording while keeping the correct sequence.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Transverse Mercator map projection. Minimum assumptions: Earth approximated as a sphere; latitude–longitude grid is visible; one longitude is chosen as the central meridian; projection preserves angles locally and produces a rectangular map.Phased storyline: (1) Present a spherical globe with clear grid; (2) rotate and highlight the central meridian; (3) focus camera on the meridian; (4) unfold/project surface points outward from the meridian in time-lapse; (5) reveal a final rectangular map with increasing distortion away from the center. Visibility constraints: central meridian must remain vertical and straight; deformation from sphere to plane must be continuous and observable.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Projection Distortion Map DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Projection Distortion Using Mercator and Transverse Mercator ProjectionsSubject: Geography – CartographyObjective: To visualize and compare spatial distortion patterns under different map projections by displaying a projection distortion map with a red–blue color scale and error labels, and to understand how projection choice affects distortion distribution.II. Experimental ToolsDigital globe or GIS/map visualization software with projection switching; distortion analysis layer (Tissot indicatrix or areal/linear error layer); adjustable color scale legend; screen recording or time-lapse capture tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open a global map dataset and enable the projection distortion map layer. Set the color scale to blue (low distortion) through red (high distortion), and turn on numeric or symbolic error labels.2. Mercator Projection: Select the Mercator projection. Center the map on the global view and adjust the legend so color differences are clear.3. Observation: Pause briefly to observe distortion distribution and error labels, especially toward high latitudes.4. Projection Switching: Smoothly switch from Mercator to Transverse Mercator projection using animated transition.5. Transverse Mercator Observation: Focus the view along the central meridian, observe changes in distortion distribution and error labels.6. Time-lapse Capture: Record the entire process with a short time-lapse, ensuring smooth transitions and a stable focus.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Under Mercator projection, low distortion appears near the equator (blue), while distortion increases toward the poles (red), with error labels increasing in magnitude.2. During switching, distortion patterns redistribute smoothly rather than abruptly.3. Under Transverse Mercator projection, low distortion concentrates along the chosen central meridian, while distortion increases away from it laterally.V. Experimental Principle SummaryMap projections transform the Earth’s curved surface onto a plane, inevitably causing distortion. The Mercator projection preserves angles but greatly enlarges areas at high latitudes, leading to strong polar distortion. The Transverse Mercator projection rotates the projection surface, minimizing distortion along a central meridian. The distortion map and color scale visually encode these errors, allowing direct comparison of projection effects.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the same dataset and scale are used for both projections; keep the color legend consistent; avoid abrupt camera movements that obscure distortion changes.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Map projection distortion and its visual comparison using Mercator and Transverse Mercator projections. Minimum assumptions: the Earth is spherical/ellipsoidal; projecting to a plane introduces distortion measurable by color and labels. Phased storyline: (1) Global Mercator view with polar distortion highlighted in red; (2) smooth animated transition to Transverse Mercator; (3) redistribution of low-distortion zones toward the central meridian; (4) stable focused view with time-lapse compression. Verification requires clear visibility of color scale, error labels, and continuous spatial alignment during transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Chemical Weathering of Karst Landforms (Guilin vs Croatian)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Chemical Weathering of Karst Landforms: Guilin Peak Forest vs Croatian Stone ForestSubject: Geography – Physical GeographyObjective: To observe and compare the morphological differences caused by limestone chemical dissolution in different karst environments, focusing on conical peak forests in Guilin and columnar stone forests in Croatia.II. Materials and MediaInstructional video or animation, world map (optional), labeled images of limestone karst, pointer or captions for key features.III. Demonstration Procedure1. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Robinson Map ProjectionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Robinson Map Projection2. Subject: Geography – Map Projections3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how the Robinson projection transforms the Earth from a spherical globe into a flat rectangular world map, helping learners understand the compromise nature of this projection and its basic geometric characteristics.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. A 3D spherical globe model with clearly marked continents2. Digital mapping or animation software capable of morphing shapes (or physical globe with projection animation)3. Reference grid showing latitude (parallels) and longitude (meridians)4. Screen or canvas for displaying the flat map resultIII. Experimental Operation Process1. Initial Display: Present a spherical globe centered in the frame, with continents clearly visible and a latitude–longitude grid wrapped around the sphere.2. Grid Emphasis: Highlight evenly spaced meridians and parallels on the globe to prepare for projection.3. Projection Start: Begin flattening the globe surface horizontally, keeping meridians evenly spaced while parallels begin to curve.4. Gradual Transformation: Continue the deformation step by step in a time-lapse manner, showing the sphere stretching into a rectangular outline while continents gradually change shape.5. Final State: Complete the transformation into a flat rectangular Robinson world map with curved parallels and balanced continental distortion.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At the start, Earth appears as a true sphere with accurate relative shapes.2. During transformation, polar regions compress vertically, equatorial regions remain wider, and parallels become curved.3. At the end, the map is rectangular with evenly spaced meridians, curved parallels, and visually balanced continents typical of the Robinson projection.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Robinson projection is a compromise map projection that does not preserve area, shape, distance, or direction perfectly. Instead, it minimizes overall distortion by mathematically adjusting the spacing of parallels while keeping meridians evenly spaced. This experiment demonstrates how spherical coordinates are systematically transformed into a flat plane, resulting in a visually pleasing and widely used world map.VI. Notes and Precautions1. The demonstration focuses on visual understanding rather than mathematical calculation.2. Time-lapse acceleration is used to condense the full projection process into a short, clear sequence.3. The final map should be clearly identifiable as a Robinson projection, not Mercator or other projections.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Robinson map projection as a compromise projection transforming a spherical Earth into a flat rectangular world map. Minimum assumptions: Earth is spherical; projection converts curved surface to plane using systematic distortion; meridians are evenly spaced and parallels are curved.Phased storyline: (1) Clear spherical globe with continents and grid; (2) initiation of flattening with grid deformation; (3) gradual, continuous projection showing increasing distortion toward poles; (4) completion as a rectangular Robinson world map. Visibility requirements: fixed camera, centered framing, clear grid lines, time-lapse smoothness to verify causal and spatial continuity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Sunlight Angle on Surface HeatingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sunlight Angle Heating: Melting of Ice at the Equator and Poles2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography (Earth–Sun Relationship)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that the angle of sunlight affects heating intensity by comparing the melting rates of identical ice blocks placed at the equator and polar regions of a tilted globe.II. Experimental EquipmentLarge globe with axis tilt, fixed heat lamp (simulating the Sun), two identical ice blocks, insulating gloves or tongs, stable stand for lamp, camera (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the globe on a table with its axis tilted and ensure it remains motionless. Mark the equator and a polar region clearly.2. Placement: Press one ice block firmly onto the equatorial region and the other onto the polar cap area, ensuring equal contact conditions.3. Lamp Setup: Fix the heat lamp at a constant height and position so that it shines equally on the globe without moving.4. Operation: Turn on the heat lamp and start the camera, focusing on both ice blocks.5. Observation Period: Allow heating to continue while recording, using accelerated or time-lapse capture to show melting differences clearly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice blocks are the same size and shape, with no melting.2. During Heating: The ice at the equator begins to melt faster, forming water earlier and shrinking more quickly than the polar ice.3. Later Stage: The equatorial ice shows significant melting, while the polar ice melts more slowly and retains its shape longer.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBecause the globe is spherical and tilted, light from the heat lamp strikes the equatorial region at a larger (more direct) angle, concentrating energy on a smaller area. At the poles, light arrives at a smaller (more oblique) angle, spreading energy over a larger area and reducing heating intensity. Therefore, the equatorial ice melts faster than the polar ice, demonstrating how sunlight angle influences surface heating on Earth.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Cooling Effect When Water Evaporates from SkinI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cooling Effect of Water Evaporation on Human Skin2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography (Human–Environment Interaction)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that evaporation of water from human skin absorbs heat and lowers skin temperature, and to visually compare the cooling effect on wet and dry skin using a thermal camera under airflow.II. Experimental EquipmentThermal imaging camera (with fixed focus and time-lapse function), electric fan with gentle airflow, spray bottle filled with clean water, chair or standing space for participant, towel or tissue (for cleanup).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The participant sits or stands in a stable position and extends both forearms horizontally at the same height. Ensure both forearms are initially dry and exposed to the same ambient conditions.2. Camera Setup: Position the thermal camera facing both forearms simultaneously. Fix the focus and field of view, and start continuous or time-lapse recording.3. Water Application: Lightly spray one forearm evenly with water, ensuring visible wetness. Leave the other forearm dry as a control.4. Airflow Application: Turn on the fan and allow a gentle, steady airflow to blow across both forearms at the same time.5. Observation Period: Maintain the posture and airflow for several seconds to tens of seconds while the thermal camera records temperature changes.6. Completion: Stop the fan and recording, and allow the participant to relax and dry the wet forearm.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both forearms show similar temperatures on the thermal image.2. During Airflow: The wetted forearm gradually appears cooler (darker or lower-temperature color) than the dry forearm.3. Comparison Result: Over time, the temperature difference becomes more apparent, with the wet forearm consistently cooler than the dry one.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWhen water evaporates from the skin, it requires energy in the form of heat (latent heat of vaporization). This heat is taken from the skin surface, causing the skin temperature to decrease. Airflow accelerates evaporation by removing moist air near the skin, enhancing heat loss. Therefore, skin with water evaporating from it cools more than dry skin under the same conditions.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure airflow is gentle and consistent; avoid excessive spraying; keep the thermal camera fixed throughout the experiment; conduct the experiment in a stable indoor environment to reduce external temperature interference.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Spherical Plane ProjectionI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Map Projection – Spherical Plane ProjectionSubject: Geography – Map ProjectionsObjective: To demonstrate how geographic points and latitude–longitude lines on a spherical Earth are projected onto a plane tangent to the sphere, forming a planar map, and to understand the principle of spherical plane projection.II. Experimental EquipmentGlobe with clearly marked latitude and longitude lines; point light source (lamp or LED); flat white projection plane (cardboard or screen); stand or holder to fix relative positions; darkened room; camera for time-lapse recording (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the globe on a stable stand. Position the flat plane so that it is tangent to the globe at a chosen point (e.g., the equator or a pole). Darken the room.2. Light Focusing: Place the point light source on the opposite side of the tangent point, aligned with the globe’s center, and adjust until the globe is evenly illuminated.3. Projection: Turn on the light source. Observe how points and latitude–longitude lines on the globe are projected onto the tangent plane.4. Mapping: Trace the projected outlines and graticule on the plane to form a planar map.5. Recording: Use time-lapse photography to capture focusing, projection, tracing, and the final map.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial state: The globe shows clear latitude and longitude lines; the plane is blank.2. During projection: Light rays project globe features onto the plane; distortion increases with distance from the tangent point.3. Final result: A planar map outline corresponding to the spherical surface appears on the plane.V. Experimental Principle SummarySpherical plane projection uses straight light rays from a point source to project features of a sphere onto a plane tangent to it. Because a curved surface is mapped onto a flat surface, scale and shape distortions increase away from the point of tangency. This experiment visually demonstrates the geometric and optical basis of map projection.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the plane is truly tangent to the globe; keep the light source fixed; avoid ambient light interference.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Water Infiltration Comparison: Humus-rich Dark Soil vs Sandy SoilI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Water Infiltration in Humus-rich Dark Soil and Sandy SoilSubject: Geography – Soil and Water ConservationExperiment Objective: To compare the water infiltration capacity of humus-rich dark soil and sandy soil through direct observation, and to understand how soil texture and organic matter affect water movement.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear containers, humus-rich dark soil, sandy soil, measuring cup or beaker, clean water, flat tray or table surface.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two identical clear containers side by side on a flat surface. Fill the left container with humus-rich dark soil and the right container with sandy soil. Lightly level the soil surfaces without compacting them.2. Setup Check: Ensure both soil columns have similar height and volume, and the containers are clearly visible from the side.3. Core Operation: Measure an equal volume of water. Pour the water simultaneously and evenly onto the surface of each soil sample.4. Observation: Observe the speed at which water penetrates into each soil and whether water remains on the surface or quickly disappears.5. Completion: Stop pouring once all water is added and continue observing for a short time to compare infiltration results.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both soils are dry, with the humus-rich soil appearing dark and fine, and the sandy soil appearing light-colored and coarse.2. During Water Pouring: In the sandy soil, water quickly infiltrates and disappears into the soil. In the humus-rich soil, water infiltrates more slowly, with some water temporarily remaining on the surface.3. After Pouring: The sandy soil shows rapid downward movement of water, while the humus-rich soil retains more moisture near the surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSoil infiltration rate depends on soil texture and structure. Sandy soil has larger particles and pores, allowing water to pass through quickly. Humus-rich dark soil contains more organic matter and finer particles, which enhance water retention but slow down infiltration. This difference explains variations in soil water-holding capacity and runoff generation in natural environments.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how the Morweg projection transforms a spherical Earth with latitude and longitude into a flat world map, understanding the core projection operations and spatial transformation rules.II. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Demonstration of Cyclone Rotation in the Northern and Southern HemispheresI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Cyclone Rotation in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and compare the rotation directions of cyclones in the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere, understand the influence of Earth’s rotation (Coriolis effect) on large-scale atmospheric motion, and correctly interpret standard cyclone diagrams.II. Experimental Materials and Media1. Two schematic cyclone diagrams displayed side-by-side (digital image or printed poster).2. Labels indicating ‘Northern Hemisphere Cyclone’ (left) and ‘Southern Hemisphere Cyclone’ (right).3. Curved arrows drawn around each cyclone center to indicate airflow rotation direction.4. Optional: globe or rotating Earth model for explanation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the two cyclone diagrams side-by-side in the same field of view. Ensure the left diagram is clearly labeled as the Northern Hemisphere and the right diagram as the Southern Hemisphere. Confirm that cloud bands and central low-pressure areas are visible.2. Identification Stage: Point out the center of each cyclone (low-pressure center) and the surrounding cloud patterns spiraling toward the center.3. Core Demonstration Operation:   (1) For the Northern Hemisphere diagram (left), trace the arrows showing air spiraling inward in a counterclockwise direction toward the cyclone center.   (2) For the Southern Hemisphere diagram (right), trace the arrows showing air spiraling inward in a clockwise direction toward the cyclone center.4. Comparison Operation: Visually compare the opposite rotation directions of the two cyclones while keeping their positions (left: Northern Hemisphere; right: Southern Hemisphere) unchanged.5. Conclusion Operation: Reiterate the rotation direction for each hemisphere and emphasize that the only difference between the two diagrams is the hemisphere, not cyclone type.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Northern Hemisphere Cyclone: Clouds form a spiral pattern rotating counterclockwise and converging toward the low-pressure center.2. Southern Hemisphere Cyclone: Clouds form a spiral pattern rotating clockwise and converging toward the low-pressure center.3. Comparative Phenomenon: The two cyclones show mirrored rotation patterns when placed side-by-side, with opposite spiral directions.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Core Principle: The Coriolis effect caused by Earth’s rotation deflects moving air.2. Principle in the Northern Hemisphere: Air moving toward a low-pressure center is deflected to the right, producing a counterclockwise rotation around cyclones.3. Principle in the Southern Hemisphere: Air moving toward a low-pressure center is deflected to the left, producing a clockwise rotation around cyclones.4. Conclusion: Cyclone rotation direction depends on the hemisphere, not on the cyclone’s strength or size.VI. Precautions and Notes1. This is a schematic demonstration, not a real-time weather simulation.2. Always confirm hemisphere labels before interpreting rotation direction.3. Do not confuse cyclones with anticyclones, which rotate in opposite directions.

manual: Experiment Title: Demonstration of UTM Projection and Zone 32NI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Geography (Humanities and Social Sciences)Objective: To demonstrate the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM) projection by displaying a world map divided into 60 vertical zones, highlighting zone 32N, overlaying a right-angle grid, and showing step-by-step how geographic coordinates are projected into the UTM grid.II. Experimental MaterialsDigital world map (latitude–longitude reference), UTM zone overlay layer, grid overlay tool (right-angle Cartesian grid), coordinate marker, animation or time-lapse visualization software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a global map with latitude and longitude lines. Ensure the Earth is shown in an equirectangular reference view.2. Zone Division: Gradually divide the world map into 60 vertical zones, each 6° of longitude wide, numbered from west to east.3. Zone Selection: Highlight and label zone 32N clearly, emphasizing its longitudinal extent and northern hemisphere designation.4. Central Meridian Identification: Mark the central meridian of zone 32N and visually distinguish it from zone boundaries.5. Grid Overlay: Overlay a right-angle UTM grid aligned with the central meridian, showing eastings and northings as straight, perpendicular lines.6. Coordinate Projection: Select a sample geographic coordinate within zone 32N and animate its transformation from latitude–longitude into UTM easting and northing values.7. Conclusion: Freeze the final frame showing zone 32N, the orthogonal grid, and the projected coordinate for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, the map shows curved latitude–longitude lines.2. After zoning, the Earth is divided into uniform vertical strips.3. Zone 32N becomes visually prominent with clear boundaries and label.4. The overlaid grid appears as perpendicular straight lines within the zone.5. A geographic point shifts into a rectangular grid position, illustrating projection.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe UTM system divides the Earth into 60 longitudinal zones, each using a Transverse Mercator projection centered on its central meridian. Within each zone, geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) are mathematically transformed into planar coordinates (eastings and northings), forming a right-angle grid that minimizes distortion locally. Zone 32N applies this principle to its specific longitudinal range in the northern hemisphere.VI. NotesThis demonstration focuses on conceptual understanding; numerical calculations are simplified and visualized through animation and time-lapse techniques.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Cloud Classification by Form Using Satellite ImageryI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cloud Classification by Form in Satellite Images2. Subject: Geography – Atmospheric Phenomena3. Experiment Objective: To identify and distinguish cirrus, cumulus, and stratus clouds in satellite imagery based on their unique forms and implied altitudes, and to understand the principle of cloud classification by morphology.II. Experimental MaterialsSatellite cloud images or animation sequence (digital); display screen or projector; cloud classification labels (cirrus, cumulus, stratus).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Ensure the satellite image sequence is arranged in a gradual order from high-altitude to low-altitude cloud scenes; prepare labels for each cloud type.2. Step One – Cirrus Observation: Display a satellite image showing thin, filamentary or feathery clouds spread sparsely. Label the clouds as cirrus and indicate their high-altitude position.3. Step Two – Cumulus Observation: Transition to an image showing clustered, cotton-like, lumpy clouds with clear boundaries. Label these as cumulus and note their mid-to-low altitude distribution.4. Step Three – Stratus Observation: Transition to an image showing broad, uniform cloud sheets covering large areas. Label these as stratus and indicate their low-altitude characteristics.5. Comparison and Identification: Briefly compare the three images, emphasizing differences in shape, thickness, and coverage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Cirrus clouds appear as thin, wispy, feather-like streaks with light tone and broken structure.2. Cumulus clouds appear as bright, puffy clusters with rounded tops and distinct edges.3. Stratus clouds appear as continuous, flat, gray or white sheets with little visible structure.4. The visual change from one cloud type to another is gradual and clearly ordered.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleClouds are classified in geography primarily by their visible form and typical altitude. Cirrus clouds form at high altitudes and have filamentary shapes due to ice crystals. Cumulus clouds develop in mid-to-low altitudes with strong vertical motion, giving them a lumpy appearance. Stratus clouds form at low altitudes and spread horizontally, creating uniform cloud layers. Satellite imagery allows clear identification of these forms, making morphology-based classification possible.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Cloud classification by visible form and relative altitude in satellite imagery, assuming a top-down satellite perspective and standard geographic cloud definitions.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 shows high-altitude cirrus clouds as thin, feathery streaks with clear labeling. Phase 2 transitions smoothly to mid–low altitude cumulus clouds, appearing as cotton-like clusters with distinct labels. Phase 3 transitions to low-altitude stratus clouds, shown as broad, uniform sheets covering wide areas. Each phase must maintain a consistent satellite viewpoint, clear labels, and a gradual visual transition to verify correct classification and causal logic.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment Equal-Area Projection Compared with Mercator ProjectionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Comparison of Mercator Projection and Equal-Area Projection2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Geography3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that equal-area projections preserve the proportional area of landmasses while slightly twisting shapes, by visually comparing Greenland and Africa during a gradual transition from a Mercator projection.II. Experimental MaterialsDigital world map in Mercator projection, digital world map in equal-area projection (such as Gall-Peters), animation or GIS software capable of morphing projections, clear text labels for Greenland and Africa, screen recording or time-lapse recording tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Initial Setup: Open a standard Mercator world map centered on the Atlantic Ocean. Ensure Greenland and Africa are clearly visible and labeled.2. Baseline Observation: Pause briefly to allow observation of the Mercator projection, noting the apparently large size of Greenland relative to Africa.3. Projection Transition: Activate the projection transformation function to gradually switch from the Mercator projection to an equal-area projection using a smooth time-lapse animation.4. Focused Observation: Keep the map centered and stable while observing land areas rescale. Ensure no zooming or rotation occurs.5. Completion: End the transition when the equal-area projection is fully displayed, with labels for Greenland and Africa still visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At the start, Greenland appears disproportionately large compared to Africa on the Mercator map.2. During the transition, landmasses gradually change shape and size; coastlines twist slightly.3. As the equal-area projection emerges, Africa becomes much larger than Greenland, reflecting their true proportional areas.4. The total area of continents appears balanced without exaggeration, while shapes are slightly distorted.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Mercator projection preserves angles and directions but greatly distorts area, especially at high latitudes, making regions like Greenland appear much larger than they are. Equal-area projections mathematically adjust the spacing of latitude lines so that all regions maintain correct proportional area. As a result, landmasses rescale accurately, while their shapes and coastlines undergo slight twisting. This demonstration visually confirms the core principle of equal-area projections: no area distortion, with minor shape deformation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is the difference between Mercator and equal-area map projections, focusing on area distortion versus area preservation. The minimum assumption is that the viewer recognizes a standard world map and can visually compare relative land areas, especially Greenland and Africa.Phased Storyline and Expected Phenomena: Phase 1 shows a static Mercator map with Greenland appearing oversized. Phase 2 introduces a smooth, time-lapse projection transition without camera movement, where land areas continuously rescale and coastlines gently twist. Phase 3 ends with a stable equal-area map where Africa is clearly larger than Greenland. The camera remains centered and fixed throughout to ensure clear verification of proportional area change and causal linkage between projection change and observed shape transformation.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Lithosphere Symbol Comparison of Continental and Oceanic CrustI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Color Symbol Comparison of Asian Continental Crust and Pacific Oceanic CrustSubject: Geography – Lithosphere StructureObjective: To visually distinguish continental crust and oceanic crust by comparing granite and basalt layers, and to understand how rock color and composition symbolize different lithospheric types.II. Experimental MaterialsGranite sample or granite simulation layer (flesh red); Basalt sample or basalt simulation layer (black gray); Display board or digital screen divided into two vertical columns; Labels for rock type and crust type.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up a display with two vertical columns side-by-side on the screen or board.2. Left Column Operation: Place or display a layer of granite in the left column, ensuring its flesh-red color is clearly visible.3. Right Column Operation: Place or display a layer of basalt in the right column, ensuring its black-gray color is clearly visible.4. Labeling: Mark the left column as Asian continental crust (granite) and the right column as Pacific oceanic crust (basalt).5. Observation Guidance: Keep the camera or viewer perspective fixed, focusing on the color contrast and left–right arrangement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Two empty columns are visible side-by-side.2. After Placement: The left column appears flesh red, representing granite; the right column appears black gray, representing basalt.3. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Drawing the Atmospheric Vertical Layers Temperature–Altitude MapSubject: Geography – Physical GeographyObjective: To understand the vertical structure of the atmosphere by plotting a temperature–altitude curve, identifying temperature inflection points, and labeling the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, and thermosphere with approximate altitude ranges.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite paper or graph paper, pencil, ruler, colored pens (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the paper vertically. Use a ruler to draw a straight vertical axis on the left side and label it Altitude (km), marking approximate values from 0 to 120 km.2. Drawing the Curve: Starting near the surface (0 km), draw a temperature curve that decreases with altitude (troposphere), then changes direction to increase (stratosphere), then decreases again (mesosphere), and finally increases sharply (thermosphere). Ensure clear bends at each direction change.3. Marking Inflection Points: At each temperature direction change, mark the boundary between layers.4. Labeling Layers: From bottom to top, label the regions as Troposphere (0–10/12 km), Stratosphere (10–50 km), Mesosphere (50–80 km), and Thermosphere (above ~80 km).5. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaThe temperature curve shows alternating decreases and increases with altitude. Distinct inflection points divide the curve into four regions, each corresponding to a specific atmospheric layer with increasing altitude.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe atmosphere is divided into layers based on temperature variation with altitude. Changes in temperature trend (inflection points) reflect differences in heating mechanisms, such as solar radiation absorption and decreasing air density, which define the boundaries of the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, and thermosphere.

manual: Experiment Title: Observation of Flow Pattern Differences Between Cumulus and Cirrus CloudsSubject: Geography – Atmospheric PhenomenaExperiment Objective: To observe and compare the shapes, altitudes, and flow patterns of cumulus and cirrus clouds, and to understand how atmospheric height influences cloud motion.Experimental Materials: Reference image or simulation showing two cloud layers; sky background with altitude cues (brightness, haze); observation record sheet.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Display an image or simulation of the sky divided into left and right sections, ensuring clear visibility of two cloud layers.2. Identification: Observe the left side and identify low-altitude clouds with thick, cotton-like shapes (cumulus). Observe the right side and identify high-altitude clouds with thin, filament-like shapes (cirrus).3. Flow Observation: Focus on the motion of each cloud layer. Note the movement speed, direction, and continuity of the cumulus clouds versus the cirrus clouds.4. Comparison: Compare the flow patterns: cumulus clouds show slower, localized, sometimes vertical development; cirrus clouds show faster, smoother, horizontally stretched flow.5. Recording: Record observations on cloud shape, altitude cues, and flow characteristics.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- Cumulus clouds appear dense, white, and clustered at low altitude, moving slowly with visible shape changes.- Cirrus clouds appear thin, wispy, and stretched at high altitude, moving quickly and smoothly with little shape change.Summary of Experimental Principle:Cloud type and flow pattern are closely related to altitude. Low-altitude cumulus clouds form in denser air with weaker horizontal winds, resulting in slow, localized motion. High-altitude cirrus clouds form in thinner air where wind speeds are higher, producing fast, streamlined flow patterns. This experiment visually demonstrates how atmospheric structure affects cloud behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Differences between cumulus and cirrus clouds in shape, altitude, and flow pattern. Minimum assumptions: cumulus are low-altitude, thick, and slow-moving; cirrus are high-altitude, thin, and fast-moving due to stronger winds.Phased storyline: (1) Establish a clear sky scene with two vertically separated cloud layers arranged left–right; (2) Highlight static shape differences—cumulus as cotton-like clusters, cirrus as filament-like streaks; (3) Show dynamic contrast—cumulus drifting slowly with minor deformation, cirrus gliding rapidly in smooth streams; (4) Maintain consistent perspective and altitude cues to verify causal linkage between height and flow speed.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Comparison of Mechanical Weathering Types (African Desert vs Asian Mountain)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Mechanical Weathering Comparison: Spheroidal vs Angular Rocks2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the external characteristics of rocks formed under different mechanical weathering environments, and understand how climate and geomorphic conditions influence rock shape and surface texture.II. Experimental Materials1. One spheroidally weathered rock (smooth, rounded), labeled African Desert.2. One angularly weathered rock (sharp edges, rough surface), labeled Asian Mountain.3. Flat table or ground surface.4. Camera or mobile phone for photographing.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two rocks on a flat surface with sufficient lighting. Ensure labels African Desert and Asian Mountain are clearly visible.2. Placement: Arrange the spheroidally weathered rock and the angularly weathered rock side by side, with a small gap between them for clear comparison.3. Observation Setup: Adjust the camera angle to directly face the rocks. Move closer if necessary to highlight surface texture and overall shape.4. Core Operation: Take photographs focusing on the contrast between the rounded, smooth surface of the desert rock and the sharp, rough surface of the mountain rock.5. Completion: Review the images to ensure both rocks, labels, shapes, and surface details are clearly captured.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. African Desert Rock: Appears generally rounded or spheroidal, with smooth surfaces and few sharp edges.2. Asian Mountain Rock: Appears angular, with sharp corners, uneven faces, and a rough surface texture.3. Comparative Phenomenon: The side-by-side display clearly shows differences in shape and surface roughness.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMechanical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces without changing their chemical composition. In arid desert environments, wind abrasion and temperature changes gradually smooth rock surfaces, producing spheroidal forms. In high mountain regions, freeze-thaw action and gravity cause rocks to fracture along joints, resulting in angular shapes with rough surfaces.VI. Precautions1. Ensure labels are accurate and readable.2. Avoid shadows or poor lighting that obscure surface details.3. Do not alter the rock surfaces artificially; rely on natural features for observation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Mechanical weathering differences caused by contrasting geographic environments, focusing on spheroidal weathering in deserts and angular weathering in mountains. Minimum assumptions: two naturally weathered rocks with distinct shapes and textures, clear labels, and stable side-by-side placement.Expected phenomena storyline: (1) Initial frame shows both labeled rocks placed side by side on a flat surface; (2) camera framing emphasizes overall shape, revealing one rounded smooth rock and one angular rough rock; (3) closer perspective highlights surface texture differences, reinforcing the causal link between environment and weathering type. Visibility constraints: labels must remain readable, and lighting must clearly reveal surface roughness and edges for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment Seasonal Insolation Variation in JuneI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Seasonal Insolation Variation in June2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography (Earth–Sun Relationship)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the spatial difference in solar radiation intensity between the Northern Hemisphere and Southern Hemisphere during June, understand that the Northern Hemisphere experiences summer with enhanced insolation while the Southern Hemisphere experiences winter with weakened insolation, and correctly interpret color-coded radiation intensity maps labeled Seasonal Insolation [June].II. Experimental Materials1. World map or globe (flat map preferred for visualization)2. Seasonal insolation distribution image for June (Northern Hemisphere in red tones, Southern Hemisphere in blue tones)3. Color legend showing radiation intensity (light red = strong, dark red = extremely strong; light blue = weak, dark blue = extremely weak)4. Pointer or digital annotation toolIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the world map or insolation image in front of the observer. Ensure the image is clearly labeled Seasonal Insolation [June] and that the color legend is visible.2. Northern Hemisphere Observation: Focus first on the Northern Hemisphere. Use the pointer to trace high-latitude regions, especially the Arctic. Observe the color changes from yellow to light red and dark red.3. Southern Hemisphere Observation: Shift focus to the Southern Hemisphere. Use the pointer to trace Antarctica and surrounding high-latitude regions. Observe the color changes from light blue to dark blue.4. Comparison Operation: Compare the two hemispheres simultaneously, noting opposite radiation intensity patterns in June.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Northern Hemisphere Phenomena: During June, the Northern Hemisphere shows enhanced radiation. Mid- to high-latitude regions display red shades, with darker red indicating extremely strong radiation near the Arctic Circle.2. Southern Hemisphere Phenomena: During June, the Southern Hemisphere shows weakened radiation. Antarctic regions display blue shades, with darker blue indicating extremely weak radiation.3. Overall Pattern: The two hemispheres show opposite seasonal radiation conditions at the same time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis demonstration is based on the tilt of Earth’s axis and Earth’s revolution around the Sun. In June, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, receiving higher solar altitude angles and longer daylight duration, resulting in enhanced insolation. The Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, receiving lower solar angles and shorter daylight duration, resulting in weakened insolation. Color gradients (red for strong, blue for weak) visually represent these differences in radiation intensity.VI. Precautions1. Ensure correct interpretation of the color legend before observation.2. Observe hemispheres in sequence to avoid confusion.3. Do not reverse color meanings (red always indicates stronger radiation; blue indicates weaker radiation).
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Seasonal variation of insolation caused by Earth’s axial tilt, focusing on June conditions. Minimum assumptions: Earth is spherical, axis tilted ~23.5°, and June corresponds to Northern Hemisphere summer and Southern Hemisphere winter. Expected phenomena storyline: Phase 1 – present a global view labeled Seasonal Insolation [June]; Phase 2 – highlight Northern Hemisphere with increasing red intensity toward the Arctic, indicating enhanced radiation; Phase 3 – shift focus to Southern Hemisphere with blue tones intensifying toward Antarctica, indicating weakened radiation; Phase 4 – compare hemispheres to emphasize opposite seasonal conditions. Visibility constraints: hemispheric boundaries, color gradients, and labels must remain clear and stable for verification within a short video.

manual: Experiment Title: Simulation Observation of Aeolian Erosion Landforms (Sahara Mushroom Rock vs American Western Hoodoo)Subject: Geography – Physical Geography (Geomorphology)Experiment Objective: To understand how wind erosion shapes different rock landforms by comparing the morphology of Sahara mushroom rocks and American western hoodoos, and to identify the relationship between erosion intensity, height above ground, and rock shape.Experimental Materials: Multimedia images or animation of Sahara mushroom rocks and American western hoodoos; schematic diagram of wind erosion intensity with height; labels or markers for left–right comparison.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Display a comparative image or animation. Place the Sahara mushroom rock on the left and the American western hoodoo on the right, each clearly labeled.2. Observation Step 1 (Overall Shape): Observe the left rock, noting its wide top and narrow base. Observe the right rock, noting its relatively uniform, columnar shape.3. Observation Step 2 (Erosion Focus): Introduce the concept of wind erosion acting more strongly near the ground where sand particles are concentrated.4. Demonstration: Use arrows or animation to show stronger wind abrasion at the base of the Sahara rock, and more even wind action along the height of the hoodoo.5. Comparison Summary: Directly compare the two rocks, emphasizing differences in base width, top shape, and overall profile.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. The Sahara mushroom rock shows a明显 undercut base and a broader, heavier top.2. The American western hoodoo appears more evenly eroded, forming a tall, column-like structure.3. The contrast highlights different wind erosion patterns acting on rocks of varying structure and exposure.Summary of Experimental Principles:Aeolian erosion is caused by wind carrying sand and dust that abrade rock surfaces. Near the ground, wind carries more sand and has stronger erosive power, leading to intense erosion at the base of rocks. In the Sahara, this creates mushroom rocks with narrow bases and wide tops. In the American West, more uniform rock layers and erosion conditions result in columnar hoodoos. The differing morphologies reflect variations in erosion intensity with height and rock resistance.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Comparison of Watershed Drainage Features of the Amazon Basin and Congo BasinI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Satellite Image Comparison of Amazon and Congo Basin Drainage Patterns2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare watershed drainage characteristics using satellite images, and to understand the differences between dendritic drainage (Amazon Basin) and centripetal drainage (Congo Basin).II. Experimental Materials1. High-resolution satellite image of the Amazon Basin drainage network.2. High-resolution satellite image of the Congo Basin drainage network.3. Display device (computer screen, projector, or interactive whiteboard).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure both satellite images are ready and clearly labeled. Adjust the display so that river networks are visible against the background.2. Observation of Amazon Basin: Display the satellite image of the Amazon Basin first. Focus the view on the river system. Guide observation toward the branching, tree-like river pattern spreading outward from main channels.3. Observation of Congo Basin: Switch to the satellite image of the Congo Basin. Focus the view on the river system converging toward the central basin area.4. Comparative Observation: Place emphasis on the overall shape of drainage lines in both images, noting differences in direction, convergence, and network structure.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Amazon Basin: The river network appears widely spread, with numerous tributaries branching irregularly from main rivers, forming a dendritic, interwoven pattern.2. Congo Basin: The river network shows tributaries flowing inward from surrounding areas toward a central lowland, forming a centripetal, inward-converging pattern.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWatershed drainage patterns are controlled by topography and geological structure. The Amazon Basin lies on relatively uniform terrain, allowing rivers to branch freely and form a dendritic drainage system. The Congo Basin is a structural basin with surrounding higher terrain, causing rivers to flow inward toward the center, forming a centripetal drainage system. Satellite imagery makes these large-scale drainage features clearly observable.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Comparison of watershed drainage patterns using satellite imagery, focusing on dendritic versus centripetal systems. Minimum assumptions: viewers recognize satellite images, river lines, and basin-scale geography.Phased storyline: (1) Present Amazon Basin satellite image with a stable, zoomed-out view emphasizing branching river lines; (2) Transition smoothly to Congo Basin satellite image, emphasizing inward-flowing river lines; (3) Implicit comparison through sequential visualization. Visibility constraints: drainage lines must be clearly visible, high contrast, and centrally framed to allow verification within a short video duration.

manual: Instructions for the Geography Demonstration Experiment: River Hydrology – Flood Season vs Dry SeasonI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: River Hydrology Changes in Flood Season and Dry Season2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the differences in river water level and water clarity between the flood season and the dry season, and to explain these changes using basic hydrological principles.II. Experimental Materials and Conditions1. Observation Object: A natural river section with visible riverbanks.2. Recording Equipment: Camera or mobile device with time-lapse function; tripod for fixed position.3. Environmental Requirement: Same observation location and viewing angle for both seasons.III. Experimental Procedure1. Site Fixing: Select a stable riverbank location and fix the camera to ensure the river channel remains centered in the frame.2. Flood Season Recording: During the flood season, use time-lapse photography to record the river over a period of rising water. Ensure the footage captures higher water levels, faster flow, and visibly turbid (muddy) water.3. Dry Season Recording: During the dry season, record the same river section using time-lapse photography. Capture lower water levels, exposed riverbanks, slower flow, and clearer water.4. Sequence Editing: Arrange the footage so that the flood season segment appears first, followed by the dry season segment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Flood Season: The river water level rises, the channel widens, flow speed increases, and the water appears yellow-brown or muddy due to suspended sediments.2. Dry Season: The river water level drops, parts of the riverbed or banks are exposed, flow slows, and the water becomes clearer and more transparent.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. During the flood season, increased precipitation leads to greater surface runoff, higher discharge, and stronger erosion, which carries more sediment into the river, raising water levels and increasing turbidity.2. During the dry season, reduced precipitation results in lower runoff and discharge, weaker erosion, less suspended sediment, lower water levels, and clearer water.3. These seasonal hydrological changes reflect the interaction between climate, runoff, sediment transport, and river dynamics.VI. Notes1. The camera position and framing must remain consistent to ensure comparability.2. Time-lapse photography is used to compress long-term changes into a short, observable sequence.

Transition – precipitation decreases over time. Phase 2 (Dry Season) – water level gradually falls, riverbanks emerge, flow slows, water becomes clear. Visibility Constraints: River channel, water surface height relative to banks, and water color must be clearly visible; time-lapse must show continuous change rather than abrupt cuts.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Seasonal Color Changes in Tropical Savanna ClimateI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Seasonal Color Changes in African and Brazilian Savannas2. Subject: Geography – Climate and Vegetation3. Experiment Objective: To observe and compare the wet–dry seasonal vegetation changes of the African savanna and the Brazilian savanna using satellite time-lapse imagery, and to understand the relationship between rainfall patterns and vegetation color.II. Experimental MaterialsDigital display screen or computer, satellite imagery database (or prepared image set), time-lapse visualization software, world map for regional reference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Open the satellite visualization interface and load two datasets covering one full year for the African savanna and the Brazilian savanna.2. Layout Setup: Arrange the images side by side on the screen, with Africa on the left and Brazil on the right; mark basic geographic labels.3. Time-Lapse Operation: Activate time-lapse playback to accelerate monthly changes into a short continuous sequence.4. Focused Observation: Play the sequence once continuously, then replay key segments highlighting transitions from dry season to rainy season and back.5. Comparison: Pause at peak dry and peak wet periods to compare color differences between the two regions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. African Savanna: During the dry season, vegetation appears yellowish-brown; during the rainy season, it turns green, showing a yellow–green alternation.2. Brazilian Savanna: During the dry season, exposed soil and sparse vegetation appear reddish; during the rainy season, vegetation becomes green, showing a red–green alternation.3. Both regions show clear periodic changes synchronized with wet and dry seasons.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTropical savanna climates are controlled by seasonal shifts in atmospheric circulation, leading to distinct wet and dry seasons. Rainfall increases vegetation growth and chlorophyll content, producing green tones in satellite images. In dry seasons, reduced vegetation and exposed soil dominate. Differences in soil color and vegetation type cause African savannas to show yellow–green alternation, while Brazilian savannas show red–green alternation.VI. NotesEnsure correct regional identification and consistent time scales when comparing the two savannas.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Azimuthal Isometric Projection (North Pole)I. Basic InformationTitle: Demonstration of Azimuthal Isometric Projection Centered on the North PoleSubject: Geography – Map ProjectionsObjective: To understand how an azimuthal isometric projection is formed by projecting Earth’s surface from the North Pole onto a tangent plane, and to observe the geometric characteristics of straight meridians, concentric parallels, and equal distances from the center.II. Experimental MaterialsTransparent globe or clear sphere with latitude and longitude lines; flat circular drawing board or paper; ruler; compass; fine-tip marker or pencil; camera or mobile device with time-lapse function; stable stand for globe.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the transparent globe on a stand. Ensure latitude and longitude lines are visible. Place the camera above the workspace and set time-lapse recording.2. Determining the Center: Identify the North Pole on the globe and mark it clearly as the projection center.3. Setting the Projection Plane: Place a flat circular plane tangent to the globe at the North Pole.4. Projecting Meridians: From the North Pole, project meridians radially onto the plane. Use a ruler to draw straight lines radiating from the center at equal angular intervals.5. Projecting Parallels: Project parallels of latitude onto the plane. Use a compass to draw concentric circles centered at the North Pole, with spacing determined by their distance from the pole.6. Completion: Continue until several major parallels are drawn. Stop recording after the final circular map is complete.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only the blank circular plane and the globe touching at the North Pole are visible.2. During Projection: Straight lines radiate evenly from the center, representing meridians; circular rings gradually appear, representing parallels.3. Final State: The completed map is circular, with straight meridians, concentric latitude circles, and distances along each meridian measured outward from the center.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe azimuthal isometric projection projects points from the Earth’s surface onto a plane tangent at a single point (the North Pole). All meridians become straight lines radiating from the center, and all parallels become concentric circles. Distances measured from the center along any meridian are preserved, which is the defining isometric property of this projection.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the globe is stable; keep drawing tools precise; maintain a fixed camera angle for clear time-lapse continuity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Azimuthal isometric projection centered on the North Pole. Minimum assumptions: a spherical Earth model, a plane tangent at the North Pole, and radial projection of surface points.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase – transparent globe and tangent plane are shown with the North Pole aligned at the center. (2) Projection phase – meridians are drawn as straight radial lines, followed by parallels as concentric circles, with visible cause–effect between projection method and geometry. (3) Result phase – the final circular map clearly shows equal-distance property along meridians. Visibility constraints: overhead or slightly angled top-down view to verify radial symmetry and concentric structure.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Dynamic Comparison of Advection Fog and Radiation FogI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Dynamic Comparison of Advection Fog and Radiation FogSubject: Geography – Physical Geography (Atmospheric Phenomena)Experiment Objective: To visually compare the formation mechanism and flow characteristics of advection fog and radiation fog through side-by-side dynamic demonstrations, and to understand their different spatial forms and causes.II. Experimental MaterialsMultimedia display device (computer or tablet), simulation or animation software capable of displaying atmospheric processes, two synchronized dynamic images or animations.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the display device and open the fog simulation interface. Ensure the screen is divided into left and right sections.2. Left Image Setup (Advection Fog): Set conditions to represent sea surface with cold water. Introduce warm, moist air moving horizontally across the surface.3. Right Image Setup (Radiation Fog): Set conditions to represent land surface at night. Gradually reduce ground temperature under clear and calm conditions.4. Demonstration: Play both dynamic images simultaneously. The left shows fog forming and moving horizontally; the right shows fog forming in place and thickening vertically.5. Observation: Pause at key moments to compare fog shape, movement, and stability between the two images.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Advection Fog (Left): Fog forms as warm moist air moves over cold sea, appearing as a continuous horizontal belt that flows with the wind.2. Radiation Fog (Right): Fog forms near the ground due to radiative cooling, appearing as a relatively stationary, block-like mass over land.3. Comparison: Advection fog shows clear horizontal motion; radiation fog shows little movement and strong vertical accumulation.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAdvection fog forms when warm, moist air is transported horizontally over a colder surface, causing cooling and condensation, resulting in belt-shaped fog. Radiation fog forms when land surfaces lose heat rapidly at night, cooling the near-surface air to saturation, producing stable, block-like fog. The difference in heat exchange and air movement leads to distinct fog shapes and dynamics.VI. PrecautionsEnsure left-right correspondence is clear; avoid mixing surface conditions; focus on core dynamic differences rather than time duration.

manual: Experiment Title: Latitudinal Radiation Distribution from Equator to PolesSubject: Geography (Humanities and Social Sciences)Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how solar radiation varies with latitude, showing that radiation is highest at the equator and decreases toward the poles.Experimental Equipment: Digital globe model or globe animation software; display screen.Experimental Procedure:1. At the equator (0°), the globe surface appears red, indicating the highest radiation levels (>300 W/m²).2. Moving toward mid-latitudes, colors gradually shift from red to yellow and green, showing decreasing radiation.3. At the poles (90°N/S), the surface appears blue, indicating the lowest radiation levels (<100 W/m²).4. Radiation forms clear zonal bands parallel to latitude lines.Summary of Experimental Principle:Solar radiation distribution is primarily controlled by latitude. manual: Instructions for the Geography Demonstration Experiment: Mercator Map ProjectionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Mercator Map Projection2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To understand the basic idea of the Mercator projection by visually demonstrating how the curved surface of the Earth is transformed into a rectangular map with straight, perpendicular latitude and longitude lines, and to recognize the characteristics and limitations of this projection.II. Experimental Materials1. A standard globe clearly marked with lines of latitude and longitude.2. Projection demonstration tool (can be a physical cutting-and-unfolding model, a flexible globe sleeve, or a digital Mercator projection simulation).3. Flat rectangular board or screen for displaying the projected map.4. Camera or mobile device with time-lapse photography function.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the globe on a stable surface with clear visibility of latitude and longitude lines. Adjust the camera to face the globe directly and set it to time-lapse mode.2. Initial Observation: Rotate the globe slowly to show that lines of longitude converge at the poles and latitude lines form parallel circles.3. Projection Operation: Using the Mercator projection method, conceptually or visually ‘unwrap’ the globe’s surface from the equator toward the poles. Ensure that each meridian is transformed into a straight, evenly spaced vertical line and each parallel into a straight horizontal line.4. Map Formation: Gradually display or reveal the rectangular Mercator map on the flat board or screen, forming a complete grid of straight longitude and latitude lines.5. Recording: The entire process, from globe display to final rectangular map, is continuously recorded using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. On the globe, longitude lines curve and meet at the poles, while latitude lines are circular.2. During projection, the curved surface visually stretches outward, especially toward high latitudes.3. In the final rectangular map, all longitude and latitude lines appear straight and perpendicular, forming a regular grid.4. Regions near the poles appear significantly enlarged compared to their size on the globe.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Mercator projection is a cylindrical conformal map projection. It can be understood as projecting the Earth’s surface onto a cylinder tangent at the equator and then unrolling the cylinder into a flat rectangle. This projection preserves local angles and directions, making it useful for navigation, but it distorts area, especially at high latitudes, causing polar regions to appear much larger than they are in reality.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Electromagnetic Spectrum Band Color Map Observation2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To recognize and understand the distribution of electromagnetic spectrum bands by observing a standard band color chart, identify the correspondence between color, wavelength range, and band name, and comprehend the basic principle of electromagnetic spectrum ordering from short to long wavelengths.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Printed or digital electromagnetic spectrum band color map (UV–Visible–IR–Microwave).2. Chart labels including wavelength units in micrometers (μm).3. Pointer or cursor (hand, pen, or digital pointer).4. Display medium (paper poster, screen, or projection).III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the electromagnetic spectrum band color map on a flat surface or display it clearly on a screen. Ensure that all bands and wavelength labels in micrometers are visible from left to right.2. Orientation: Confirm that the left side of the chart represents shorter wavelengths and the right side represents longer wavelengths.3. Step-by-Step Demonstration:   (1) Use a pointer to indicate the leftmost band labeled Ultraviolet (UV), colored purple, with very short wavelength values in micrometers.   (2) Slowly move the pointer to the right across the Visible Light band, identifying colors in order: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet (ROYGBIV), and noting their corresponding μm ranges.   (3) Continue moving right to the Infrared (IR) band, shown in red tones, and point out the increase in wavelength values.   (4) Finally, point to the Microwave band, colored brown, emphasizing its longest wavelength values in micrometers.4. Completion: Re-scan from left to right once more to reinforce the overall sequence and relationship between color and wavelength.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The spectrum is displayed as a continuous horizontal band.2. Colors change gradually from purple (UV) on the left to brown (Microwave) on the right.3. Wavelength labels in micrometers increase progressively from left to right.4. Visible light appears as a narrow central section compared to the wider non-visible bands.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe electromagnetic spectrum is an ordered arrangement of electromagnetic waves according to wavelength and frequency. Shorter wavelengths (such as ultraviolet) have higher energy and are placed on the left, while longer wavelengths (such as microwaves) have lower energy and are placed on the right. Visible light occupies only a small portion of the spectrum and is organized by color according to increasing wavelength. The color map visually represents this scientific principle, allowing learners to intuitively understand the relationship between wavelength, color, and electromagnetic band classification.VI. Experimental Notes1. This is a demonstration-based observation experiment and does not involve radiation emission.2. Ensure accurate color representation and correct wavelength units (μm).3. Focus on left-to-right order rather than memorizing exact numerical values.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: The electromagnetic spectrum is ordered by wavelength, with UV (purple) at short wavelengths, visible light (ROYGBIV) in the middle, IR (red) next, and microwaves (brown) at long wavelengths, labeled in micrometers.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Wavelength increases monotonically from left to right; color is a visual encoding of wavelength range; labels in μm correspond to band positions.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish full view of the spectrum chart; (2) Pointer identifies UV at the left with short μm values; (3) Pointer moves steadily across visible ROYGBIV colors; (4) Transition into IR with longer μm labels; (5) End at microwave band on the right, confirming maximum wavelength. Visibility must allow clear reading of colors, band names, and μm labels from a fixed frontal perspective.
