Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Turn on the display device and open the presentation containing two satellite overhead images. Ensure both images are at the same scale and orientation for fair comparison.2. Step One – Plateau Observation: Display the satellite overhead view of the American Plateau. Keep the image static for observation.3. Step Two – Mountain Observation: Switch the screen to the satellite overhead view of an Asian mountain range.4. Step Three – Comparison: Guide observers to compare the two images, focusing on surface shape (flat vs rugged) and color (light brown vs dark brown).IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. American Plateau Image: The landform appears broad and flat, with gentle elevation changes and a relatively uniform light-brown color.2. Asian Mountain Image: The landform appears as a narrow, rugged strip with sharp elevation changes, complex textures, and darker brown coloration.3. Comparative Result: The plateau shows large-scale flatness and uniformity, while the mountain range shows strong relief and visual complexity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPlateaus and mountain ranges are formed by different lithospheric processes. The American Plateau is shaped mainly by long-term stability and erosion, resulting in flat terrain and lighter satellite tones. Asian mountain ranges are formed by active plate collision and uplift, producing rugged relief, strong shadows, and darker tones in satellite images. Satellite imagery highlights these differences through color and texture contrasts.VI. Experimental NotesEnsure images are true satellite views and not artistic renderings. manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Winkel Triple Map Projection2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Knowledge Point: Map Projection – Winkel Triple Projection4. Experiment Objective: To understand how the spherical Earth surface is transformed into a planar world map using the Winkel triple projection method; to visually recognize the process of projection from a globe with latitude and longitude grids to a world map with relatively uniform distortion; to enhance spatial cognition through image focusing and time-lapse demonstration.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Physical or digital globe (spherical Earth model) with clearly marked latitude and longitude gridlines.2. Computer or multimedia display system (projection screen or monitor).3. Geographic visualization software or animation tool capable of showing map projection transformations (supporting Winkel triple projection).4. Camera or screen-recording tool with image focusing and time-lapse functions (or pre-made time-lapse animation).5. Pointer or cursor (optional, for explanation).III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Place the globe at the center of the demonstration area or open a digital 3D globe on the screen.   (2) Ensure latitude lines (parallels) and longitude lines (meridians) are clearly visible and evenly spaced.   (3) Adjust lighting or screen brightness so gridlines and continental outlines are easy to observe.2. Spherical Earth Display:   (1) Slowly rotate the globe (or rotate the digital sphere) to show the global distribution of continents and oceans.   (2) Emphasize that the Earth is approximately spherical and that latitude and longitude form a grid on its surface.   (3) Use image focusing to center the globe and highlight the grid structure.3. Projection Transformation (Core Operation):   (1) Start the projection animation or software function.   (2) Gradually transform the spherical Earth into a flat surface using time-lapse photography or accelerated animation.   (3) During the transformation, observe how meridians change from curved lines on the sphere to specific curved and straight forms on the plane.   (4) Clearly indicate that the transformation method applied is the Winkel triple projection.4. Final Planar Map Display:   (1) Stop the animation when the final planar world map is fully formed.   (2) Display the complete world map with continents, oceans, and latitude–longitude gridlines.   (3) Adjust focus to show the overall shape of the map, emphasizing balanced distortion.5. Ending and Review:   (1) Briefly compare the spherical globe and the planar map side by side (or before–after comparison).   (2) Turn off or pause the animation and conclude the demonstration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Phenomenon: The Earth appears as a sphere with evenly distributed latitude and longitude gridlines; continents retain their true relative positions on the curved surface.2. Transformation Phenomenon: As the projection proceeds, the spherical surface gradually flattens; gridlines bend and adjust smoothly, with no abrupt breaks, showing continuous deformation.3. Final Phenomenon: The resulting planar world map shows all continents and oceans; overall distortion of area, shape, and distance appears relatively uniform compared with other projections, and polar regions are not excessively stretched.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: A map projection is a systematic method of transforming the Earth’s spherical surface onto a plane.2. Winkel Triple Projection Principle: The Winkel triple projection is a compromise projection that mathematically combines the Aitoff projection and the equirectangular (equidistant cylindrical) projection. It aims to minimize and balance three types of distortion: area, shape, and distance.3. Geographic Significance: Because it provides relatively uniform overall distortion and a visually natural appearance of the world, the Winkel triple projection is widely used for general-purpose world maps and atlases.VI. Experimental Notes1. This is a demonstration experiment; accuracy depends on the clarity of the animation or model.2. Time-lapse or accelerated animation is recommended to fit within a short video while preserving the correct transformation order.3. The focus should remain on the transformation process and final projection characteristics, not on complex mathematical derivations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The core concept is the Winkel triple map projection as a compromise method transforming a spherical Earth into a planar world map with relatively uniform distortion. Minimum assumptions: Earth is spherical; latitude and longitude form a global grid; projection is a continuous mathematical transformation.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – A clearly visible spherical Earth with latitude–longitude gridlines is shown and centered. Phase 2 – Through focused view and accelerated time-lapse, the sphere gradually deforms and flattens, with gridlines bending smoothly, indicating projection rather than cutting. Phase 3 – The final planar world map appears, showing continents with balanced distortion and no extreme polar stretching. Visibility constraints: the entire globe and final map must remain within frame, with smooth transitions to verify causal and temporal continuity.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Simulation of Evaporation and Condensation in the Hydrological CycleI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Evaporation and Condensation in the Hydrological Cycle2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography (Hydrological Cycle)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate evaporation (water surface vapor, white fog) and condensation (air water droplets, white cloud) using a simple model, and to help students understand the transformation of water between liquid and gaseous states in the hydrological cycle.II. Experimental Equipment1. Transparent heat-resistant container (1)2. Warm water (about one-third of the container volume)3. Transparent lid or glass plate (1)4. Cooling source for lid (ice pack or chilled water, optional)5. Heating source (hot plate or alcohol lamp, low heat)6. Camera or recording device with time-lapse functionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Pour a suitable amount of warm water into the transparent container and place it on a stable surface. Cool the transparent lid in advance using an ice pack or cold water.2. Setup: Place the cooled transparent lid horizontally over the top of the container, ensuring it seals the opening but remains visible.3. Heating Operation: Slowly heat the bottom of the container using a low and steady heat source.4. Core Process: As heating continues, observe water vapor rising from the water surface. Allow the vapor to contact the cooled inner surface of the lid.5. Recording: Use time-lapse photography to record the entire process, focusing on vapor rise and droplet formation on the lid.6. Ending: After clear condensation appears, stop heating and end the recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water is liquid and relatively still; the lid is clear with no droplets.2. During Heating: White fog-like water vapor forms above the water surface and rises upward.3. Condensation Stage: When vapor contacts the cooled lid, small transparent water droplets appear, gradually merging into larger droplets, resembling cloud formation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHeating increases the kinetic energy of water molecules, causing some liquid water to change into water vapor (evaporation). The warm water vapor rises and encounters the cooled lid, where it loses heat and changes back into liquid water droplets (condensation). This process simulates evaporation and condensation in the hydrological cycle, corresponding to surface evaporation and cloud formation in the atmosphere.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use gentle heating to avoid boiling or splashing.2. Ensure the container and lid are transparent for clear observation.3. Handle heating equipment carefully to ensure safety.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Evaporation and condensation as core processes in the hydrological cycle, requiring only basic assumptions that heating increases evaporation and cooling causes condensation.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with transparent container, warm water, and cooled lid; (2) bottom heating causes visible white water vapor to rise from the water surface; (3) vapor contacts the cooled lid and condenses into visible droplets; (4) droplets grow and stabilize, clearly linking cause (heating and cooling) to effect (state change). Visibility constraints require a fixed camera angle, clear transparency of materials, and time-lapse acceleration to ensure all phases are observable within a short video.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Constructing a Simple Parliamentary Public Administration StructureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Constructing a Parliamentary Public Administration Organizational Chart2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Public Policy and Administration3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate a simple parliamentary public administration structure, highlighting Parliament as the oversight body, the Prime Minister as the core executive coordinator, and multiple departments reporting in parallel, through a sequential, time-lapse style organizational chart construction.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Digital canvas or white background2. Graphic elements: rectangles or boxes for Parliament, Prime Minister, and departments3. Straight line tool for reporting relationships4. Text labels for each organizational unit5. Screen recording or animation tool supporting time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Open a blank digital canvas with a fixed viewpoint; ensure all graphic tools are ready.2. Core Placement: Place a clearly labeled box for Parliament at the top or left as a reference column. Place the Prime Minister box at the center of the canvas to establish it as the core.3. Relationship Setup: Draw a clear line indicating the constitutional or oversight relationship between Parliament and the Prime Minister.4. Sequential Addition of Departments: One by one, add department boxes (e.g., Finance, Health, Education) around or below the Prime Minister. After adding each department, draw a clear line connecting it to the Prime Minister.5. Time-lapse Recording: Record the entire process in a sped-up or time-lapse format, ensuring the sequence of additions is visible and ordered.6. Final Check: Pause on the completed chart, showing Parliament, the Prime Minister, and all departments with clear, parallel reporting lines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The canvas is empty, then shows only Parliament and the Prime Minister.2. Intermediate State: Departments appear sequentially; each new department is immediately connected to the Prime Minister.3. Final State: A complete organizational chart is visible, with Parliament as the oversight body, the Prime Minister at the core, and multiple departments reporting in parallel.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the core principle of parliamentary public administration: executive authority is centralized in the Prime Minister, who operates under parliamentary oversight. Government departments do not report independently to Parliament but are coordinated through the Prime Minister. The sequential, time-lapse visualization reinforces the hierarchical and parallel reporting logic inherent in parliamentary systems.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Maintain a stable canvas to avoid spatial confusion.2. Use consistent shapes and colors for clarity.3. Ensure lines are straight and unambiguous to represent reporting relationships clearly.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: The scenario represents a parliamentary public administration structure where Parliament provides oversight, the Prime Minister acts as the central executive node, and departments report in parallel. Minimum assumptions include a fixed canvas, labeled organizational units, and visible reporting lines.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 shows an empty canvas transitioning to Parliament and the Prime Minister. Phase 2 shows sequential, time-lapse addition of departments connected to the Prime Minister. Phase 3 stabilizes on the completed chart. Visibility must remain centered on the canvas with no camera movement, ensuring clear verification of hierarchy and causal structure.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Constructing a Presidential System Public Administration Organizational ChartI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Constructing a Presidential System Public Administration Organizational Chart2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Public Policy and Administration3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the basic structure of a Presidential Public Administration System by placing the President at the top of an organizational chart and sequentially adding administrative departments as vertical branches, helping learners understand hierarchy, authority flow, and organizational order.II. Experimental Materials and Tools1. Digital canvas or white background (physical board or drawing software)2. Labeling tools (text boxes, markers, or digital text tools)3. Simple shapes (rectangles or boxes for roles and departments)4. Screen or camera capable of recording time-lapse videoIII. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Prepare a blank canvas with a neutral background. Ensure the recording device is fixed and focused on the entire canvas area.2. Step 1 – Placing the President: At the top center of the canvas, draw or place a box labeled President. This box represents the highest executive authority.3. Step 2 – Adding Vertical Structure: Below the President, draw a vertical guiding line or visual alignment to indicate hierarchical flow.4. Step 3 – Sequential Addition of Departments: One by one, add boxes beneath the President, each connected vertically, labeled as major administrative departments (for example: Department of State, Department of Defense, Department of Finance). Each department is added in sequence, not simultaneously.5. Step 4 – Label Refinement: Ensure each box has clear, readable labels and consistent size and spacing to emphasize order and clarity.6. Recording Method: Use time-lapse photography to capture the entire process, compressing the drawing sequence into a short, continuous visual demonstration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The canvas is blank with no organizational elements.2. During the Process: The President appears first at the top. Subsequently, department boxes appear one after another below, forming a clear vertical hierarchy.3. Final State: A complete, simple organizational chart is visible, with the President at the top and administrative departments arranged as orderly vertical branches beneath.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis demonstration is based on the core principle of a Presidential Public Administration Structure, where executive authority is centralized in the President and implemented through specialized administrative departments. The visual hierarchy reflects the flow of authority and responsibility. Sequential construction reinforces the logical order of governance, and time-lapse presentation enhances clarity and learning efficiency by emphasizing process over static outcome.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Keep labels concise and standardized.2. Avoid overcrowding the canvas; clarity is more important than completeness.3. Maintain a fixed camera angle to ensure spatial consistency during time-lapse recording.

Minimum assumptions include hierarchical governance, vertical authority flow, and clear role differentiation.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 – Blank canvas establishes initial condition. Phase 4 – Completed chart shows a stable, ordered hierarchy. Visibility requires a fixed, centered perspective and uninterrupted view to verify sequence, spatial order, and causal progression.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Aspirated vs Unaspirated Stop Consonants Using Candle Flame AirflowI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Candle Flame Test for AspirationSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)Objective: To visually demonstrate the difference between aspirated and unaspirated voiceless stop consonants by observing airflow effects on a candle flame when saying pie and spy.II. EquipmentLit candle (1), lighter or matches, stable candle holder, quiet indoor environment with minimal airflow, optional ruler for distance reference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the candle upright on a stable surface and light it. Ensure the flame is steady and the room has no drafts.2. Positioning: The demonstrator stands or sits upright and holds their mouth approximately 3–5 cm from the candle flame, without touching it.3. Core Operation: Clearly say the word pie toward the flame once, using normal speech volume.4. Observation: Watch the candle flame immediately after saying pie.5. Comparison Operation: Return to the same mouth position and clearly say the word spy toward the flame.6. Observation: Watch and compare the candle flame movement after saying spy.7. Repetition (optional): Alternate pie and spy once more to confirm the contrast.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The candle flame burns upright and steady.2. When saying pie: The flame bends away from the mouth or flickers strongly due to a burst of air.3. When saying spy: The flame shows little or no movement, remaining mostly steady.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn English phonetics, the voiceless stop consonant p in pie is aspirated, meaning it is produced with a strong burst of airflow after the lips open. In contrast, the p in spy is unaspirated because it follows s, resulting in much weaker airflow. The candle flame responds visibly to differences in airflow, making aspiration observable.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Aspirated versus unaspirated voiceless stop consonants in English phonetics. Minimum assumptions: a lit candle flame visibly reacts to airflow; the speaker can articulate pie and spy clearly; aspiration produces stronger airflow than non-aspiration.Phased storyline: (1) Establish a steady candle flame close to the speaker’s mouth; (2) Utter pie, causing a clear burst of air that pushes or flickers the flame; (3) Utter spy from the same position, producing minimal airflow and little flame movement; (4) Visual comparison confirms the aspiration contrast. The camera should maintain a side or three-quarter view showing both mouth and flame clearly for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Thermal Performance Comparison Using Ice Melting on Concrete vs. Wood SlabsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Ice Melting Comparison on Concrete and Wood SlabsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban PlanningExperiment Objective: To visually compare the thermal performance of concrete and wood materials by observing differences in ice melting rates, and to understand how material thermal conductivity affects heat transfer in built environments.II. Experimental Equipment1 gray concrete slab (flat, dry, room temperature)1 light-colored wooden slab (same size as concrete slab)2 identical ice blocks (same mass and shape)Flat supporting surface (indoor, stable temperature)Camera with time-lapse recording functionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the concrete slab on the left and the wooden slab on the right on a flat surface, ensuring both are exposed to the same ambient conditions.2. Placement: Position one identical ice block at the center of each slab simultaneously.3. Recording: Fix the camera directly above or in front of the slabs to capture both ice blocks in the same frame.4. Core Operation: Start time-lapse recording immediately after placing the ice blocks.5. Observation Period: Allow the ice to melt naturally while recording, until a clear difference in melting extent is visible.6. Completion: Stop recording once the comparative melting trend is obvious.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice blocks are solid, transparent-white, and similar in size.2. During Melting: The ice on the concrete slab begins to melt faster, forming a larger water puddle earlier than the ice on the wooden slab.3. Later Stage: The concrete-side ice becomes significantly smaller or nearly melted, while the wood-side ice remains larger.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleConcrete has a higher thermal conductivity than wood, allowing it to transfer heat from the surrounding environment to the ice more efficiently. As a result, the ice on the concrete slab absorbs heat faster and melts more quickly. Wood, with lower thermal conductivity, slows heat transfer, causing the ice to melt more slowly. This experiment demonstrates how material choice in architecture affects thermal performance and surface heat behavior.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: comparison of thermal performance of building materials through heat transfer and ice melting. Minimum assumptions: identical ice blocks, same environment, concrete has higher thermal conductivity than wood. Expected phased storyline: (1) static setup with two slabs and ice blocks; (2) onset of melting on both sides; (3) faster, visibly greater melting on concrete side; (4) clear divergence in ice size and meltwater. Camera must maintain a fixed viewpoint with time-lapse acceleration to verify causal and temporal differences.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Ultraviolet Light Causing Fluorescent Paint to GlowI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Ultraviolet Light Causing Fluorescent Paint to GlowSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Communication & Media StudiesExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how ultraviolet (UV) light reveals hidden visual information by causing fluorescent paint to emit visible light, illustrating selective visibility and mediated perception.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical objects (same shape and size); fluorescent paint (applied evenly to one object); handheld ultraviolet lamp; darkened indoor environment (recommended for clear observation).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the two identical objects side by side on a flat surface; ensure one object is fluorescent-painted and the other is unpainted. Dim ambient lighting if possible.Core Operation: Hold the handheld ultraviolet lamp above both objects at the same distance. First keep the lamp switched off and allow viewers to observe both objects.Switching Operation: Turn the ultraviolet lamp on and illuminate both objects simultaneously for several seconds, then switch it off again.Completion: Repeat the on–off switching once if needed to reinforce observation, then end the demonstration.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State (UV off): Both objects appear similar in color and brightness; the fluorescent-painted object does not visibly glow.UV On: The fluorescent-painted object emits a bright, visible glow, while the unpainted object shows little or no change.UV Off Again: The glow of the fluorescent-painted object disappears immediately, returning to a non-glowing state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFluorescent paint contains substances that absorb ultraviolet light and re-emit it as visible light. When the UV lamp is on, these substances undergo electronic excitation and emit visible photons, causing the glowing effect. When the UV source is removed, excitation stops and the glow disappears. This demonstrates how specific media technologies (UV light) can reveal otherwise invisible information.

Minimum assumptions: presence of UV light, fluorescent material responsive to UV, and a visible contrast with a non-fluorescent object.Phased storyline: Phase 1 – Baseline visibility with UV off, both objects appear similar. Phase 2 – UV on, causal transition where fluorescent-painted object glows while the unpainted object remains unchanged. Phase 3 – UV off, glow ceases immediately. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Visual Features of Stone Core PlatformsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Demonstration of Flat Stone Core Platforms with Radial Flake ScarsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – ArchaeologyExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate controlled striking on stone cores, showing how a flat flaking reference surface produces radial flake scars during flake removal, using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentStone core (flint or similar knappable stone), hammerstone or soft hammer, stable working surface (anvil stone or pad), protective gloves and goggles, camera capable of time-lapse photography, fixed tripod, adequate lighting.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the stone core on a stable surface; ensure one face is prepared as a flat flaking platform. Set the camera on a tripod above or at an oblique angle, focused on the platform surface.Platform Preparation: Lightly grind or trim the platform edge to ensure a flat reference surface suitable for controlled striking.Core Operation: Using the hammerstone, apply controlled, directional strikes to the edge of the flat platform. Each strike should be deliberate and aimed to detach a flake from the core surface.Recording: Capture the process using time-lapse photography, ensuring each flake removal is recorded and the platform surface remains centered in the frame.Completion: Stop striking once multiple flakes have been removed and radial flake scars are clearly visible. Safely set tools aside.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The stone core shows a relatively smooth, flat platform with minimal scars.During Striking: With each controlled strike, flakes detach from the platform edge; the exposed surface develops scars radiating outward from the platform.Final State: The platform surface displays multiple, clearly defined radial flake scars indicating sequential flake removal.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the archaeological principle of controlled stone knapping. A flat flaking reference surface allows force from a strike to propagate predictably through the stone, producing conchoidal fractures and radial flake scars. The orientation and pattern of these scars record the direction, control, and sequence of human strikes, providing evidence of intentional tool production.

manual: Experiment Title: Visualization of Facade Feature Comparison between Romanesque and Gothic ChurchesSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban PlanningI. Experiment ObjectiveTo visually compare key facade features of Romanesque and Gothic churches by observing simplified models, focusing on vaulted ceiling shapes and column thickness, and to understand how structural principles influence architectural form.II. Experimental MaterialsSimplified 3D or schematic facade models (or images) of one Romanesque church and one Gothic church; display interface or screen; color markers: red (Romanesque) and blue (Gothic).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two simplified facade models side by side on the display. Ensure equal scale and neutral background.2. Identification: Mark the left model in red as Romanesque and the right model in blue as Gothic.3. Observation of Vaults: Focus the view on the upper facade and interior cutaway to observe vault shapes. Note rounded barrel/groin vaults on the Romanesque side and pointed ribbed vaults on the Gothic side.4. Observation of Columns: Shift focus to the vertical supports. Compare the thickness and massiveness of Romanesque columns with the slimmer Gothic columns.5. Comparative Summary: Maintain a fixed left–right perspective while verbally or textually summarizing differences.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Romanesque (left, red): Rounded vault forms; heavy, thick columns; overall solid and massive appearance.2. Gothic (right, blue): Pointed vaults; thinner, taller columns; lighter and more vertical appearance.3. Direct Contrast: The visual contrast is strongest when both vaults and columns are viewed simultaneously.V. Experimental Principle SummaryRomanesque architecture relies on rounded vaults that generate strong lateral thrust, requiring thick walls and columns for stability. Gothic architecture introduces pointed arches and ribbed vaults that channel forces more efficiently downward, allowing for thinner columns and a lighter facade. The visualization demonstrates how structural mechanics directly shape architectural form.VI. NotesKeep the models simplified and the comparison simultaneous to emphasize structural–formal causality within a short viewing time.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration: Comparative Observation of Skull Dentition and Tool MorphologyI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Comparative Observation of Carnivore and Herbivore Dentition with Tool AnalogySubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (with Biological Anthropology support)Objective: To visually compare carnivore canines and herbivore molars, and to understand functional morphology by analogy with Egyptian bronze knives from the Nile Valley, which are characterized by straight single-edged cutting features.II. MaterialsCarnivore skull model (with prominent canines), herbivore skull model (with broad molars), pointer or stylus, camera capable of close-up and time-lapse shooting, neutral background, stable table.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place both skull models on a table, side by side, facing the same direction; ensure clear lighting and neutral background.2. Initial Framing: Record a wide shot showing both skulls simultaneously.3. Carnivore Observation: Use the pointer to indicate the canines on the carnivore skull; pause briefly and move the pointer closer to gradually reveal a close-up image.4. Herbivore Observation: Shift the pointer to the herbivore skull and mark the molars; repeat gradual close-up reveal.5. Imaging Technique: Use focus control and time-lapse photography to emphasize tooth shape and edges while keeping camera position fixed.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. Carnivore canines appear long, sharp, and pointed, suitable for piercing and cutting.2. Herbivore molars appear broad, flat, and ridged, suitable for grinding.3. Experimental Principle SummaryFunctional morphology explains that form follows function: carnivore canines resemble straight, sharp cutting edges, comparable to the straight single-edged bronze knives used in ancient Egypt for cutting tasks, while herbivore molars emphasize grinding surfaces. NotesEnsure pointer movement is slow and deliberate; maintain consistent lighting and orientation to support clear comparison.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Comparing Spectral Graphic Features of Fricatives and NasalsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Spectral Comparison of Fricatives (/θ/) and Nasals (/n/)Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)Objective: To record continuous fricative and nasal sounds using a microphone and computer, observe their spectrograms in speech analysis software, and compare their spectral graphic features.II. Experimental EquipmentMicrophone (external or built-in), computer, speech analysis software (e.g., Praat), quiet recording environment, headphones (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Connect the microphone to the computer and open the speech analysis software. Set sampling rate and input level to avoid clipping.2. Fricative Recording: The speaker produces a continuous voiceless fricative /θ/ for about 2–3 seconds. Record and save the audio.3. Nasal Recording: The speaker produces a continuous nasal /n/ for about 2–3 seconds. Record and save the audio.4. Spectrogram Display: Load both recordings into the software. Display spectrograms with identical settings.5. Comparison: Arrange the fricative spectrogram on the left and the nasal spectrogram on the right for direct visual comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Fricative (/θ/): The spectrogram shows aperiodic noise, with strong energy in higher frequency regions and no clear formant structure.2. Nasal (/n/): The spectrogram shows clear voicing with low-frequency energy, visible formant bands, and reduced energy in higher frequencies, often with anti-formants.3. Comparison Result: The fricative appears noisier and less structured, while the nasal appears more regular and voiced.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesFricatives are produced by forcing air through a narrow constriction, creating turbulent airflow and aperiodic acoustic energy, which appears as diffuse noise in spectrograms. Nasals are produced with a lowered velum, allowing airflow through the nasal cavity, resulting in voiced sounds with characteristic low-frequency formants and anti-formants. Spectrograms visually reflect these articulatory and acoustic differences.VI. Experimental NotesMaintain identical spectrogram settings for fair comparison. Ensure a quiet environment to avoid background noise interference.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual and acoustic comparison of fricative and nasal sounds using spectrograms, assuming basic phonetic knowledge and standard speech analysis software.Minimum assumptions: A functional microphone-computer setup, continuous production of /θ/ and /n/, and a spectrogram display with time-frequency axes.Phased storyline: (1) Equipment setup and software ready; (2) recording continuous /θ/ leading to a noisy, high-frequency spectrogram; (3) recording continuous /n/ leading to a voiced, low-frequency spectrogram; (4) side-by-side comparison highlighting structural differences. Visibility constraints: spectrogram axes, energy distribution, and left-right layout must be clearly visible for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tabletop Formation of an Andean Pottery Jar Handle2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the traditional hand-forming process of an Andean pottery jar handle, observe surface marks such as delicate and regular spiral or smoothing lines, and understand how repeated hand motion and rotation shape ceramic features.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsPlastic clay (earthenware), small bowl of water or slip, wooden or bone shaping tool, flat tabletop, partially formed pottery jar body, hands only (no wheel visible), camera fixed above or at an oblique tabletop angle.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the jar body on the tabletop. Wedge a small amount of clay to remove air and roll it into a short coil suitable for a handle.2. Handle Shaping: Using fingers and light pressure, elongate and curve the coil. Rotate it slightly while smoothing, producing subtle, regular surface lines from repeated motion.3. Surface Preparation: Score the attachment points on both the jar and handle; apply a thin layer of slip.4. Attachment: Press the handle ends onto the jar body, adjusting curvature and thickness with fingers and a tool.5. Refinement: Smooth transitions with gentle rotation and strokes, maintaining symmetry and visible fine surface marks.6. Recording: Capture the process with time-lapse photography, keeping the camera focused on the evolving handle shape.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Clay coil is uniform and matte, without cracks.2. During Shaping: Repeated hand motion creates delicate, regular smoothing or spiral-like lines on the surface.3. Attachment Phase: Handle adheres firmly after scoring and slip; shape remains stable.4. Final State: Finished jar handle shows coherent curvature, even thickness, and subtle surface marks indicative of traditional forming techniques.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment reflects archaeological pottery-making principles: plastic clay deforms under controlled hand pressure; repeated rotation and smoothing create regular surface lines. Scoring and slip increase mechanical bonding, allowing separate clay elements to join securely. These visual features help archaeologists identify hand-formed or rotational techniques in ceramic artifacts.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visualization of Vanishing Point Positioning in a One-Point Architectural Perspective SketchI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visualization of Vanishing Point Positioning in Architectural Perspective Sketch2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To understand the role of the horizon line and vanishing point in one-point perspective by visually constructing an architectural sketch, mastering the basic drawing sequence and perspective rules.II. Experimental ToolsWhite drawing paper, pencil or digital drawing tablet, ruler, eraser; optional digital drawing software with line and text tools.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the paper horizontally (or open a blank digital canvas). Keep tools ready and ensure a clear drawing area.2. Drawing Axes: Draw a horizontal line across the paper to establish reference orientation, then draw a vertical line intersecting it near the center to form horizontal and vertical axes.3. Horizon Line Identification: Designate the horizontal axis as the horizon line and label it clearly as Horizon Line.4. Vanishing Point Positioning: Mark a point on the horizon line at the center of the paper and label it Vanishing Point.5. Architectural Outline: In front of the picture plane, draw the front face of a simple building using vertical and horizontal lines.6. Perspective Construction: From the corners of the building’s front face, draw depth lines converging toward the vanishing point.7. Completion: Add the back edges of the building where depth lines visually meet, erase unnecessary guide lines, and reinforce the main structure.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only horizontal and vertical axes are visible, with no sense of depth.2. After Labeling: The horizon line and vanishing point clearly define eye level and depth direction.3. During Perspective Drawing: Lines extending toward the vanishing point visually create depth, and the building appears three-dimensional.4. Final State: A complete one-point perspective architectural sketch is formed, with all depth lines converging consistently at the vanishing point.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOne-point perspective is based on visual projection principles. When an object’s faces are parallel to the picture plane, horizontal depth edges visually converge to a single vanishing point located on the horizon line, which represents the viewer’s eye level. This convergence creates the illusion of three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.VI. Experimental Notes1. Keep vertical lines strictly vertical and horizontal lines parallel to the horizon line.2. Ensure all depth lines converge to the same vanishing point.3. Simplify forms to focus on understanding perspective rather than decorative detail.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: One-point architectural perspective centered on a single vanishing point on the horizon line. Minimum assumptions: a fixed viewer eye level, a flat picture plane, and architectural forms with faces parallel to the picture plane.Phased storyline: (1) Establish orientation by drawing horizontal and vertical axes; (2) Identify and label the horizon line; (3) Place and label a central vanishing point on the horizon line; (4) Draw the front face of a building; (5) Extend depth lines toward the vanishing point to create spatial depth. Key causal transition: marking the vanishing point directly determines the direction of all depth lines. Visibility constraint: labels and convergence must be clearly visible from a single, stable viewpoint for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Visual Features of the Pottery Coiling MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Pottery Jar Formation Using the Coil-Building Method2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To understand the coil-building pottery technique through visual observation of the creation process, and to identify its characteristic feature—irregular raised spiral lines on the inner vessel walls.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsPlastic clay (moderately moist), working table, water bowl, simple turntable (optional), hands as primary tools, camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clay on the working table. Adjust moisture so the clay is flexible but not sticky. Set up the camera to record the entire process using time-lapse mode.2. Coil Making: The ceramic artist rolls the clay between hands and the table to form long, even clay strips (coils) of consistent thickness.3. Base Formation: Form a flat circular base using clay and place it on the table or turntable.4. Wall Construction: Stack the clay coils layer by layer on the edge of the base, pressing gently to join each coil to the one below while maintaining the jar shape.5. Surface Treatment: Lightly smooth the outer wall with fingers or hands, while leaving the inner wall less smoothed.6. Completion: Continue stacking until the jar reaches the intended height. Stop recording once the inner and outer walls are clearly visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. During construction, the jar gradually increases in height as coils are added.2. The outer wall appears relatively smooth due to intentional smoothing.3. The inner wall shows irregular raised spiral lines corresponding to the stacked coils.4. In time-lapse playback, the sequential growth of the vessel and spiral patterns are clearly visible.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe coil-building method forms pottery by stacking rolled clay coils. Each coil contributes to the vessel wall. When inner walls are not fully smoothed, the junctions between coils remain visible as irregular raised spiral lines. These features are key visual evidence used in archaeology to identify coil-built pottery and infer ancient ceramic techniques.VI. Experimental NotesTime-lapse recording accelerates the process for clear observation. Excessive smoothing of inner walls may obscure the characteristic spiral features.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: The pottery coiling method and its diagnostic visual feature—irregular raised spiral lines on inner vessel walls. Minimum assumptions: clay behaves plastically; coils are stacked sequentially; partial smoothing affects wall texture. Phased storyline: (1) clay rolled into long coils; (2) coils stacked on a base forming rising walls; (3) outer wall smoothed while inner wall remains textured; (4) completed jar reveals spiral lines inside. Visibility constraints: camera must show both inner and outer walls, with time-lapse emphasizing sequential growth and causal transitions from action to form.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment One-Point Perspective Street DrawingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: One-Point Perspective Street Drawing with Ruler and Horizon Line2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate the basic principle of one-point perspective by drawing a street scene in which buildings and road edges converge toward a single vanishing point on a horizon line, and to record the process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentWhite drawing paper (A4 or similar), pencil, ruler, eraser, flat drawing surface, camera or smartphone with tripod (for time-lapse), adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place white paper flat on the table. Fix the camera above or in front of the paper, ensure the frame covers the entire drawing area, and lock focus and exposure.2. Horizon Line: Use the ruler and pencil to lightly draw a horizontal line across the paper to represent the horizon line.3. Vanishing Point: Mark a single point at the center (or slightly off-center) of the horizon line as the vanishing point.4. Road Edges: From the vanishing point, use the ruler to draw two straight lines extending downward to the bottom edge of the paper, forming the road.5. Buildings: Along both sides of the road, draw vertical lines for building edges. Use the ruler to connect the tops and bottoms of these verticals back to the vanishing point.6. Detailing: Add windows, doors, and roof lines, ensuring all horizontal depth lines converge toward the same vanishing point.7. Completion: Darken final lines, erase construction marks if needed, and stop the time-lapse recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Blank white paper with no marks.2. During Drawing: Straight lines increasingly converge toward the vanishing point; the street appears to recede into depth.3. Final State: A clear street scene is formed, with buildings and road edges visually shrinking toward the horizon, creating a strong sense of depth.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOne-point perspective is a drawing method based on geometric projection. Objects facing the viewer have horizontal and vertical edges, while depth edges recede toward a single vanishing point on the horizon line. Using a ruler ensures straight projection lines, and consistent convergence creates the illusion of three-dimensional space on a two-dimensional surface.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the ruler steady to avoid skewed lines.2. Ensure all depth lines converge to the same vanishing point.3. Do not move the camera or change focus during time-lapse recording.4. Draw lightly at first to allow corrections.

manual: Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Revealing Starch Residue on Stone Tools Using Iodine Solution2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Residue Analysis)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how iodine solution can be used to visually detect starch residues on a worked stone tool by comparison with an unworked stone control, and to understand the archaeological principle of micro-residue identification.II. Experimental EquipmentStone tool (archaeological replica or cleaned specimen), unworked stone (control), iodine solution (Lugol’s iodine, dilute), dropper or pipette, disposable gloves, absorbent lab paper, lab bench, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the lab bench and place absorbent paper on the surface. Put on disposable gloves to avoid contamination.2. Sample Placement: Place the stone tool and the unworked stone control side by side on the lab bench, with working edges of the tool facing upward and clearly visible.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly above or at a slight angle to the stones. Fix the focus and framing to include both stones in the same field of view. Start time-lapse recording.4. Iodine Application: Using a dropper, apply one to two drops of iodine solution evenly onto the surface of the stone tool, especially along the worked edge. Then apply the same amount of iodine to the surface of the unworked stone control.5. Observation Period: Allow the iodine to remain on the surfaces for a short period while recording continues, without touching or moving the stones.6. Completion: Stop recording after the color changes stabilize. Dispose of gloves and clean the bench according to lab protocols.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both stones appear dry and retain their natural gray or brown coloration before iodine application.2. After Iodine Application: The iodine appears yellow-brown upon contact with both surfaces.3. Result Comparison: On the stone tool, areas containing starch residue gradually turn dark blue to blue-black. The unworked stone shows little to no color change, remaining yellow-brown or fading.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine reacts with starch to form a blue-black complex. In archaeology, worked stone tools used for processing plants may retain microscopic starch residues in surface crevices. When iodine solution is applied, these residues are revealed through a characteristic color change. manual: Experiment Title: Wind Transport of Sand versus Dust in a Fan-Driven SetupSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology (Environmental and Geoarchaeology)Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how particle size influences wind transport, illustrating why fine dust can be carried farther than coarse sand in archaeological and natural settings.Experimental Equipment: Tabletop; two shallow trays of equal size; coarse sand (yellow or brown grains, visibly large); fine dust or silt (light-colored, powdery); household electric fan with steady speed setting; camera or smartphone on tripod with fixed focus (time-lapse mode optional).Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Place the two empty trays side by side on a flat tabletop. Fill one tray evenly with coarse sand and the other evenly with fine dust, keeping surface thickness similar.2. Setup: Position the household fan at the same height as the trays, directly facing the long edge of both trays at a distance of about 30–50 cm. Fix the camera on a tripod, framing both trays and the fan-facing edge; lock focus and exposure.3. Operation: Turn on the fan at a steady, moderate speed and let it blow continuously across both trays for several seconds (or accelerate via time-lapse).4. Observation and Recording: Keep the camera fixed while the fan runs. Do not disturb the trays during airflow.5. Conclusion: Turn off the fan and stop recording. Compare the final surface conditions of sand and dust.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- Initial State: Both materials lie flat and still in their trays.- During Blowing: Fine dust is lifted into the air, forming a faint cloud and moving downwind; some dust leaves the tray. Coarse sand shows little lifting, with only minor rolling or creeping near the surface.- Final State: The dust tray shows noticeable material loss or redistribution, while the sand tray largely retains its original position and shape.Summary of Experimental Principle:Wind transport depends strongly on particle size and mass. Fine dust particles have low weight and cohesion, allowing airflow to lift them into suspension and carry them over long distances. Coarse sand grains are heavier and require stronger wind to move; they typically roll or hop short distances (saltation) rather than becoming airborne. This principle helps archaeologists interpret sediment layers and past environmental conditions.Experimental Precautions:- Avoid very strong fan settings that may scatter materials uncontrollably.- Keep camera focus fixed to ensure valid visual comparison.- Wear a mask if dust is very fine to avoid inhalation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Aeolian (wind-driven) transport differences between coarse sand and fine dust, assuming steady airflow, gravity, and size-dependent particle response.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Airflow from a household fan is continuous and unidirectional; particle size controls lift and transport distance; camera viewpoint remains fixed.Phased Storyline for Verification: (1) Static initial trays with visibly different grain sizes; (2) Fan activation causing immediate airflow across both trays; (3) Fine dust visibly lifts and drifts downwind while coarse sand remains mostly grounded with minor rolling; (4) End state shows greater displacement or loss of dust than sand. Visibility Constraints: Both trays must stay in frame throughout, with no camera movement, to allow direct temporal comparison.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Real-Time AI Style Transfer Applied to a Live Camera Scene2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Communication & Media Studies3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how real-time AI style transfer technology transforms a live camera feed into a painterly visual style, and to observe the continuity, responsiveness, and media effects as a person walks, gestures, turns, approaches, and recedes in a well-lit room with fixed camera focus suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment1. Digital camera or webcam capable of continuous video capture2. Computer with GPU support (or equivalent acceleration hardware)3. Real-time AI style transfer software (preloaded with a painterly style model)4. Stable tripod to fix camera position and focus5. Well-lit indoor room with uniform lighting6. One human participant7. Screen or monitor for observing the processed live feedIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Set up the camera on a tripod, ensuring the frame covers the full walking area of the room.   (2) Adjust lighting so the room is evenly and brightly lit, avoiding strong shadows.   (3) Fix the camera focus and disable autofocus to maintain consistent focal length for time-lapse suitability.   (4) Launch the AI style transfer software and select a painterly style model.2. System Initialization:   (1) Connect the camera feed to the AI style transfer system.   (2) Verify that the live feed is displayed on the monitor with the painterly style applied in real time.   (3) Ensure minimal processing delay and stable frame rate.3. Core Operation:   (1) The participant stands within the camera frame.   (2) The participant begins walking naturally across the room while making simple hand and arm gestures.   (3) The participant turns their body, then walks toward the camera, pauses briefly, and then walks away from the camera.   (4) Throughout the process, the camera remains fixed and the AI style transfer continues uninterrupted.4. Observation and Recording:   (1) Observe the real-time transformation of the live video into a painterly style.   (2) Pay attention to how body movement, gestures, and changes in distance affect the stylized output.   (3) Optionally record a short time-lapse or accelerated clip for later review.5. Experiment Completion:   (1) Stop the participant’s movement.   (2) Terminate the AI style transfer processing.   (3) Save any recorded video and shut down equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The live camera feed shows the participant in a well-lit room with a consistent painterly visual style applied.2. During Movement: As the participant walks and gestures, their outlines, colors, and textures are continuously transformed into painterly brushstroke-like patterns while maintaining recognizable human form and motion.3. Turning and Distance Change: When the participant turns, approaches, or recedes, the stylized representation updates smoothly, preserving spatial depth and motion continuity.4. Temporal Continuity: With fixed camera focus, the stylized video remains stable over time without focus shifts, enabling clear time-lapse observation.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Core Principle: Real-time AI style transfer uses deep neural networks, typically convolutional neural networks, to separate and recombine content features (human movement and spatial structure) with style features (painterly textures and colors) on a frame-by-frame basis.2. Media Communication Logic: The experiment demonstrates how algorithmic mediation reshapes visual communication while preserving semantic content, illustrating the interaction between human action, machine perception, and aesthetic representation.3. Temporal Processing Principle: Fixed focus and continuous processing ensure spatiotemporal coherence, allowing the audience to perceive stable causal relationships between human movement and stylized visual output.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Real-time AI style transfer as a media technology that algorithmically transforms a live camera feed into a painterly aesthetic while preserving human action and spatial structure. Minimum assumptions include a fixed camera, sufficient lighting, a working style transfer model, and a visible human subject.Phased Storyline: (1) Establish a stable, well-lit room with a fixed camera view and immediate painterly style applied; (2) The person begins walking and gesturing, causing continuous stylized transformations; (3) Turning, approaching, and receding introduce depth and perspective changes that are reflected smoothly in the painterly output; (4) The sequence ends with sustained visual coherence, confirming spatiotemporal and causal consistency. Visibility must maintain the full body within frame, and perspective must remain constant for verification.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Automatic Sensor Faucet Shutting Off When Hands Are RemovedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Automatic Sensor Faucet Shutting Off When Hands Are Removed2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how automatic sensor faucets function in public restroom design, compare them with manual handle faucets, and understand their role in water-saving and hygienic urban infrastructure.II. Experimental Environment and Equipment1. Location: Public restroom.2. Equipment: Two identical side-by-side sinks; left sink equipped with an automatic sensor faucet; right sink equipped with a manual handle faucet; stable water supply.3. Participant: One person performing hand placement and removal.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure both sinks are clean and functional. Confirm that the automatic faucet is powered and the manual faucet handle can be turned on.2. Initial State: The automatic faucet is off with no hands detected; the manual faucet is turned on so water is flowing steadily.3. Core Operation:   (1) The person places both hands under the water stream of the left automatic sensor faucet. The sensor detects the hands and water flows automatically.   (2) Simultaneously or sequentially, the person places hands under the water stream of the right manual faucet, where water continues to flow due to the open handle.   (3) The person removes both hands from under the streams while remaining nearby and not touching the faucets.4. Observation Stage: Observe the change in water flow from both faucets after hands are removed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. When hands are placed under the automatic faucet, water flows automatically; when hands are removed, the water flow stops after a short delay.2. The manual faucet continues to release water even after hands are removed, as long as the handle position is unchanged.3. The person does not need to touch the automatic faucet at any stage for it to turn on or off.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAutomatic sensor faucets use infrared or proximity sensors to detect the presence of hands. When reflected infrared signals indicate an object within range, a control unit opens an internal solenoid valve, allowing water to flow. Once the hands are removed and no reflected signal is detected, the control unit closes the valve, stopping the water flow. Manual faucets rely solely on mechanical handle position, so water flow continues until the handle is manually turned off. This design principle supports hygiene and water conservation in public restroom architecture.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate the architectural and engineering principle of automatic sensor faucets versus manual faucets in a public restroom. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: automatic faucet uses a sensor-controlled valve that responds to hand presence; manual faucet flow depends only on handle position.Phased storyline: (1) Establish scene with two identical side-by-side sinks in a public restroom, left automatic and right manual. (2) Hands placed under both streams, causing automatic faucet to activate while manual faucet already flows. (3) Hands removed while person remains nearby. (4) Automatic faucet shuts off after a brief delay, manual faucet continues running. Visibility constraints: faucet types, hand positions, and water flow must be clearly visible in the same frame or continuous sequence for causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Character-Age Contrast Flashback via Match CutI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Character-Age Contrast Flashback via Match Cut2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Literature & Comparative Literature3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the narrative technique of character-age contrast flashback by visually replacing an adult character with their child self using a match cut while maintaining identical framing.II. Experimental Materials and ConditionsFixed camera or tripod; school hallway location; adult actor and child actor (or the same actor styled differently); similar clothing styles for adult and child; consistent lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Setup: Position the camera at eye level facing a school hallway. Lock framing and focus. Ensure consistent lighting.2. Adult Pose: Have the adult character stand still at the center of the frame, facing forward, wearing school-associated clothing.3. Match Cut Preparation: Without moving the camera, replace the adult with the child actor in a nearly identical position and posture, wearing similar clothing.4. Core Operation (Match Cut): Cut directly between the two shots, preserving framing, scale, and background alignment.5. Playback Observation: Play the cut to observe the immediate visual replacement from adult to child.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: An adult stands motionless in a school hallway.2. Transition Phenomenon: Through a match cut, the adult instantly becomes their child self while the environment remains unchanged.3. Resulting Effect: A strong visual impression of temporal regression and memory flashback is created.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment applies a literary and cinematic principle where age contrast within identical spatial framing produces a flashback effect. The unchanged setting anchors spatial continuity, while the sudden age change signals temporal shift, allowing viewers to intuitively perceive memory and past identity without explicit exposition.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: character-age contrast flashback achieved through match cut. Minimum assumptions: fixed camera, identical hallway setting, still adult body enabling seamless replacement, and visible age difference with similar clothing. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Blocked vs Open Mesh Areas Revealed by Single-Pass Screen PrintingI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Single-Pass Screen Print Revealing Blocked vs Open MeshSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Printmaking)Objective: To demonstrate how a stencil blocks ink while open mesh transfers ink to fabric during one hand-pulled squeegee pass; to document the process with fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Materials and EquipmentScreen with mesh coated by stencil (blocked and open areas), water-based screen-printing ink (dark color), hand squeegee, light-colored fabric, flat printing surface, hinge clamps or tape, camera on tripod with fixed focus.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the light-colored fabric flat on the printing surface. Position the stencil-coated mesh screen directly on the fabric, ensuring full contact.2. Ink Loading: Deposit a bead of ink along the near edge of the screen above the image area.3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera on a tripod; frame the screen and fabric; fix focus and exposure for time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Hold the squeegee at approximately 45 degrees. Apply even downward pressure and pull the squeegee once, smoothly, across the screen from near to far edge in a single continuous pass.5. Lift-Off: After completing the pass, lift the screen vertically to reveal the print.6. Cleanup: Stop recording; clean ink and tools appropriately.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Fabric is clean and unprinted; ink rests on the mesh surface.During Pass: Ink is pushed by the squeegee; it passes through open mesh areas while blocked stencil areas prevent transfer.Final Result: The fabric shows a clear printed image where the mesh was open; areas under the stencil remain unprinted.V. Experimental Principle SummaryScreen printing relies on selective permeability of the mesh. Open mesh allows ink to be forced through by squeegee pressure, transferring the image to fabric. Stencil-coated (blocked) areas prevent ink passage, creating negative space. A single, even pass ensures consistent ink deposition and clearly reveals the contrast between blocked and open mesh areas.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Single-pass screen printing demonstrates selective ink transfer through open mesh versus blocked stencil areas.Minimum assumptions: A stencil-coated mesh screen is pressed onto light fabric; ink is applied; a hand squeegee makes one continuous pass; camera focus remains fixed.Phased storyline: (1) Setup—screen contacts fabric, ink bead visible; (2) Action—single smooth squeegee pull applies pressure; (3) Causal transition—ink passes only through open mesh; (4) Outcome—screen lifts to reveal printed vs unprinted areas. Visibility constraints: top-down or slight angle view showing contact, motion direction, and final reveal.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pointillism Technique DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pointillism Technique Demonstration2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the core method and visual principle of pointillism by applying independent small color dots on a canvas and understanding how colors visually blend at a distance.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite canvas (flat, clean), marker or tape for labeling, small round brush or cotton swab, blue paint, yellow paint, red paint, palette or paint containers, camera capable of close-up and time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white canvas flat and clearly label an area as Pointillism Area. Set the camera above or in front of the canvas, focusing only on the labeled area.2. Blue and Yellow Dot Application: Dip the brush or cotton swab into blue paint and place small, round dots within the Pointillism Area. Clean the tool, then apply yellow dots side by side with the blue dots. Do not mix colors; keep each dot separate.3. Red Dot Addition: Using a clean brush or swab, add small red dots near the existing blue and yellow dots, maintaining clear separation between all dots.4. Recording: Capture the entire dot placement process using focused, close-up, time-lapse photography, showing only the sequence of dot placement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The canvas is white and blank except for the Pointillism Area label.2. During Operation: Small blue and yellow dots appear first, followed by red dots placed nearby. All dots remain distinct and unmixed.3. Visual Effect: When viewed from a distance, the separate dots visually suggest blended or new tones without physical mixing.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePointillism is based on optical color mixing. Instead of blending pigments on the palette, artists place small, independent dots of pure color close together. When viewed from a distance, the human eye visually blends these colors into new tones, creating richness and luminosity while preserving color purity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Constructing a High-Rise Building Using Three-Point PerspectiveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Three-Point Perspective Drawing of a Tall Building2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Painting and Drawing)3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate three-point perspective by observing how parallel lines are divided into three groups and converge toward three vanishing points when depicting a high-rise building.II. Experimental MaterialsFlat drawing surface (paper or tablet), pencil or stylus, ruler (optional), eraser.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the drawing surface flat and fix the camera above it for a clear top-down view.2. Horizon Construction: Draw a straight horizontal line across the page to represent the horizon line.3. Vanishing Points Setup: Mark two points far apart on the horizon line and label them Vanishing Point 1 and Vanishing Point 2. Mark a third point above the horizon line and label it Vanishing Point 3.4. Initial Building Edge: Draw a short vertical line below the horizon to represent the nearest vertical edge of a tall building.5. Line Convergence: From the top and bottom of the vertical edge, draw lines converging toward Vanishing Point 1 and Vanishing Point 2 to form the building’s horizontal edges.6. Vertical Convergence: Draw vertical edges of the building converging toward Vanishing Point 3 to indicate height.7. Completion: Add remaining edges by extending lines toward the corresponding vanishing points, forming a complete high-rise building.8. Presentation: Record the drawing process in accelerated time-lapse, clearly showing each step.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The horizon line remains fixed and horizontal.2. Three distinct groups of parallel lines are observed, each converging toward its own vanishing point.3. The building appears tall and dynamic, with vertical lines tilting toward the third vanishing point.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThree-point perspective is used to represent objects viewed from a high or low angle. In this system, parallel lines are divided into three groups, each converging toward a different vanishing point. Two vanishing points lie on the horizon for width and depth, while the third lies above or below the horizon to represent height, enabling realistic depiction of tall structures.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mixing Gray Paint into Bright Red PaintI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Mixing Gray Paint into Bright Red PaintSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Color Theory)Objective: To observe how adding neutral gray to a vibrant red reduces saturation and alters visual intensity through controlled mixing.II. MaterialsWhite palette, vibrant red paint, neutral gray paint, paintbrush, camera or phone for time-lapse (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white palette on a flat, well-lit surface. Ensure the palette is clean and dry.2. Paint Placement: Squeeze a small pool of vibrant red paint onto the palette. Place an equal-sized pool of neutral gray paint beside it, keeping the two pools separate.3. Mixing Operation: Dip the brush into the gray paint and pick up an amount approximately equal to the red paint volume to be mixed.4. Core Action: Transfer the gray paint into the red paint pool. Use the brush to swirl gently in circular motions, keeping the brush tip within the red area.5. Observation and Recording: Continue swirling while focusing visually on the changing color. Optionally record the process for a short time-lapse sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Red paint appears vivid and highly saturated; gray paint appears neutral and low in saturation.During Mixing: As gray is incorporated, the red gradually becomes less vivid, shifting toward a muted, duller red.Final State: The mixed paint shows reduced saturation and intensity compared to the original red.V. Experimental Principle SummaryIn color theory, gray is a neutral color that reduces saturation when mixed with a pure hue. Adding gray to red does not change the hue family but lowers chroma, making the color appear softer and less intense. The visual change results from the balanced combination of pigmented color and neutral tone.VI. PrecautionsUse equal amounts for clear comparison; mix slowly to observe gradual change; keep lighting consistent for accurate color perception.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Constructing Linear Perspective in a Renaissance StudioI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Linear Perspective Construction of a City Street2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Renaissance Painting)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the method of linear perspective used in Renaissance painting by setting a single vanishing point on the horizon line and drawing orthogonal lines to construct the illusion of depth in a city street scene.II. Experimental EquipmentDrawing paper or panel, pencil and ruler, eraser, reference image of a city street (optional), studio lighting, camera mounted on a tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the drawing surface on an easel or table in a studio setting. Fix the camera on a tripod facing the drawing surface and lock the focus and framing.2. Establish Horizon: Draw a straight horizontal line across the paper at eye level to represent the horizon.3. Set Vanishing Point: Mark a single point at the center of the horizon line; this will serve as the vanishing point.4. Draw Orthogonals: From the vanishing point, use a ruler to draw multiple straight lines radiating downward toward the foreground, defining the edges of the street and buildings.5. Construct Forms: Add vertical and horizontal lines between orthogonals to suggest buildings, windows, and street elements.6. Recording: Allow the camera to capture the drawing process in time-lapse, without changing focus or position.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Blank paper with only the horizon line and a single marked point.2. During Drawing: As orthogonals are added, the flat surface begins to suggest depth, with lines visually converging toward the vanishing point.3. Final State: The completed sketch clearly resembles a city street receding into space, creating a convincing illusion of depth.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLinear perspective is based on geometric optics and human visual perception. Parallel lines in the real world appear to converge at a single vanishing point on the horizon when represented on a flat surface. By fixing the viewer’s eye level (horizon) and consistently aligning orthogonals to one vanishing point, Renaissance artists created realistic spatial depth in two-dimensional paintings.

Minimum assumptions: a fixed viewer eye level (horizon), one vanishing point, and straight orthogonal lines governed by simple geometry. Visibility constraints: camera remains fixed and focused so convergence and spatial consistency can be visually verified in the time-lapse.
