manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Palette Knife Technique DemonstrationI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Palette Knife Scraping Technique in Oil PaintingSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Painting)Objective: To demonstrate how an oil painter uses a palette knife to scrape paint across a canvas in a consistent direction, forming flat or textured surfaces with clear knife marks and natural paint blending, and to understand the artistic principle behind the technique.II. Materials and ToolsCanvas (pre-primed), oil paints (2–3 colors), palette knife (metal, medium size), palette, easel, studio lighting, camera set for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the canvas on an easel. Arrange oil paints on the palette. Set the camera facing the canvas to record a time-lapse focused on the painting surface.2. Tool Loading: The painter faces the canvas and holds the palette knife in one hand. Dip the flat edge of the knife into oil paint, picking up a moderate, even amount.3. Core Operation: Press the palette knife against the canvas and scrape the paint across the surface in the same direction repeatedly. Maintain consistent pressure and angle to avoid brush-like textures.4. Layering and Blending: Reload paint as needed and continue scraping, allowing adjacent colors to blend naturally through knife contact rather than mixing with a brush.5. Completion: Stop scraping once the surface shows uniform knife-shaped lines and the intended flat or textured effect. The camera captures the final finished work.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Canvas surface is blank or lightly underpainted, with no visible texture.During Operation: Paint spreads in flat layers or raised ridges; distinct knife-shaped lines appear, aligned in one direction; colors blend softly at contact edges.Final State: The finished painting shows a Palette Knife Area with no brushstroke traces, clear scraping marks, and cohesive texture.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe palette knife technique relies on direct mechanical transfer of viscous oil paint using a rigid metal edge. Unlike brushes, the knife does not flex into fine strands, so it leaves broad, clean marks. Directional scraping and controlled pressure determine whether the surface is flat or textured, while physical contact between paint layers enables natural blending. The visual result directly reflects the artist’s motion, pressure, and angle of the knife.VI. Notes and PrecautionsUse consistent direction to avoid chaotic textures. Clean the knife between color changes to maintain clarity. Ensure stable camera framing for time-lapse continuity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Palette knife oil painting technique demonstrating directional scraping and texture formation. Minimum assumptions: a painter, a canvas, oil paint with visible thickness, and a rigid palette knife acting as the sole painting tool.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – painter faces canvas, knife and paint visible; (2) Action phase – knife is dipped into paint and scraped across canvas in a single direction, producing immediate texture; (3) Accumulation phase – repeated scraping builds flat or textured layers and blends colors; (4) Result phase – time-lapse reveals a finished work with clear knife-shaped lines and no brush traces. Visibility constraints: camera remains focused on canvas surface, with texture and directional marks clearly observable throughout.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Law of Demand – Movement Along the Demand CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Movement Along the Demand Curve When Price Rises2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the law of demand by showing that when price rises, quantity demanded decreases, resulting in a movement upward and leftward along the same demand curve.II. Experimental Materials1. A display screen or digital whiteboard2. A pre-drawn coordinate axis (horizontal axis: quantity demanded; vertical axis: price)3. A downward-sloping demand curve4. Markers or digital annotation toolsIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a coordinate system with quantity demanded on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. Draw a downward-sloping demand curve.2. Initial State: Mark a point A on the demand curve, indicating an initial price and corresponding quantity demanded.3. Core Operation: Increase the price level by moving vertically upward from the original price, then move leftward along the same demand curve to find the new equilibrium point.4. Marking Result: Label the new position on the curve as point B.5. Completion: Ensure both points A and B are clearly visible and connected by the direction of movement along the curve.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initially, point A lies on the demand curve at a lower price and higher quantity demanded.2. As the price rises, the corresponding quantity demanded decreases.3. Point A moves upward and leftward along the same demand curve to point B.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment illustrates the law of demand, which states that, ceteris paribus, when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls. Graphically, this is represented as a movement upward and leftward along an existing demand curve, rather than a shift of the curve itself.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Tennis Double Fault JudgmentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tennis Double Fault Judgment Demonstration2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Sport (Tennis Rules)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and verify the rule that two consecutive serve faults by the same player constitute a Double Fault, resulting in loss of point to the opponent, and to clearly show the serving sequence and umpire decision.II. Experimental Equipment and Environment1. Standard tennis court with net and service boxes2. Two tennis players (Player A as server, Player B as receiver)3. Tennis racket and tennis balls4. Chair umpire or simulated umpire with microphone5. Camera capable of focused recording and time-lapse photographyIII. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Position the camera to clearly capture the server, net, service box, and umpire. Player A stands at the baseline preparing to serve; Player B stands in the receiving position.2. First Serve Execution: Player A performs the first serve. The serve lands out of the service box or hits the net, constituting a serve fault. No point is awarded; Player A prepares for the second serve.3. Second Serve Execution: Player A performs the second serve. The serve again lands out or into the net, constituting a second consecutive serve fault.4. Umpire Decision: Immediately after the second fault, the umpire clearly announces Double Fault using standard fixed penalty language.5. Result Confirmation: The point is awarded to Player B. The serving sequence ends, and players reset for the next point.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Player A prepares to serve; score unchanged.2. After First Serve: Ball contacts net or lands outside service box; play stops briefly with no point awarded.3. After Second Serve: Ball again fails to land legally; play stops immediately.4. Decision Outcome: Umpire announces Double Fault; visual or verbal confirmation of point awarded to Player B.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment is based on the official tennis rule that a server is allowed two attempts to deliver a legal serve. If both the first and second serves are faults, the situation is defined as a Double Fault. According to tennis scoring rules, a Double Fault results in immediate loss of the point for the server. The causal principle is sequential: serve attempt → fault judgment → second attempt → second fault → Double Fault call → point awarded to receiver.VI. Experimental Notes1. Both serve faults must be clearly observable and consecutive.2. The umpire decision must follow immediately after the second fault.3. Time-lapse may be used to compress time but must preserve correct order of events.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Tennis Double Fault judgment. Minimum assumptions: standard tennis rules apply; two consecutive serve faults by the same player automatically result in loss of point. The scenario must include a recognizable tennis court, a serving player, a receiving player, and an umpire authority.Phased storyline: Phase 1 – Setup: camera establishes court, server, and receiver. Phase 2 – First Serve: server hits an illegal serve (out or net), clearly shown. Phase 3 – Second Serve: server hits another illegal serve, again clearly shown. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Perfect Competition Demand Curve for a Single FirmI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Perfect Competition Demand Curve for a Single Firm2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Economics3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate that in a perfectly competitive market, a single firm faces a perfectly elastic (horizontal) demand curve at the given market price.II. Experimental MaterialsMultimedia display or blackboard, coordinate graph template, marker or digital drawing tool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a blank coordinate graph on the screen. Mark the vertical axis as Price (P) and the horizontal axis as Quantity (Q).2. Market Price Setting: Choose a given market price level and mark it on the price axis.3. Plotting the Demand Curve: Through the marked price point, draw a horizontal straight line extending across the graph, parallel to the quantity axis.4. Labeling: Label the horizontal line as Demand (D) for the single firm.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Only the coordinate axes are visible, with clear labels for price and quantity.2. During Plotting: A straight horizontal line appears at the chosen price level.3. Final State: The demand curve remains horizontal regardless of quantity, indicating the firm can sell any quantity at the given market price.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIn a perfectly competitive market, individual firms are price takers. Therefore, the demand curve faced by an individual firm is perfectly elastic, represented by a horizontal straight line at the market price, parallel to the quantity axis.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Visualization of Autocorrelation in Regression ResidualsSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EconomicsObjective: To visually demonstrate autocorrelation by observing regression residuals that are continuously positive or negative along the time axis, and to understand how residual dependence violates classical regression assumptions.II. Experimental MaterialsCoordinate axis background (digital or printed); plotting software or animation tool; simulated or real time-series residual data; screen or canvas for display.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set up a two-dimensional coordinate axis with time on the horizontal axis and residual indicators on the vertical axis.2. Data Input: Prepare a sequence of residual values ordered by time, designed to exhibit autocorrelation (successive residuals with similar signs).3. Plotting Operation: Plot residual points sequentially along the time axis.4. Time-Lapse Operation: Apply a time-lapse or step-by-step animation so that residual points appear gradually over time while keeping the camera focused on the coordinate axis.5. Completion: Allow the full sequence of residual points to be displayed, then pause on the final distribution for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The coordinate axis is empty, with only labeled axes visible.2. During Plotting: Residual points appear sequentially; points remain above or below the zero line for consecutive time periods.3. Final State: Residuals form continuous positive or continuous negative runs rather than random scatter, showing visible clustering along time.V. Experimental Principle SummaryAutocorrelation refers to the correlation between residuals across different time periods. In time-series regression, if residuals are not independent, they tend to cluster above or below zero over consecutive time intervals. This experiment visualizes autocorrelation by plotting residuals over time, showing that current residuals are influenced by previous ones, thereby violating the classical assumption of error independence in econometric models.VI. NotesThe experiment focuses on visual pattern recognition rather than numerical testing; the time-lapse is used to strengthen perception of temporal dependence.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept Definition: Autocorrelation in econometric residuals, defined as dependence between error terms across time, assuming a fixed coordinate system and ordered time-series data.Minimum Assumptions: Time progresses monotonically from left to right; residuals are precomputed; axes remain fixed; residual points appear sequentially.Phased Storyline: (1) Static coordinate axis with clear labels; (2) Residual points appear one by one along the time axis; (3) Successive points stay on the same side of zero, forming visible runs; (4) Final paused frame highlights continuous positive or negative clustering. Visibility Requirements: Fixed camera, centered axis, clear contrast between points and background to verify residual sign and continuity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rugby Tackling from Behind Foul Judgment DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rugby Tackling from Behind Foul Judgment Demonstration2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Sport3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and understand the rule-based judgment of a foul when a defender pulls an attacker"s jersey from behind during forward dribbling, and to recognize the referee"s correct response.II. Experimental Roles and Equipment1. Roles: One attacker (ball carrier), one defender, one referee.2. Equipment: Standard football, football field or marked training ground, two sets of jerseys with visible numbers, referee whistle.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: The attacker stands on the field with the ball at their feet, facing forward. The defender stands slightly behind the attacker. The referee positions themselves at a clear viewing angle.2. Core Operation: The attacker begins to dribble the ball forward at a steady pace. As the attacker advances, the defender reaches from behind and pulls the attacker"s jersey, visibly restricting forward movement.3. Referee Action: Upon observing the pulling action from behind, the referee immediately blows the whistle to stop play and signals a foul.4. End of Demonstration: All players stop moving, and the referee indicates the direction of the free kick.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The attacker controls the ball and moves forward freely; the defender follows from behind without contact.2. During the Action: The defender pulls the attacker"s jersey from behind, causing visible tension in the jersey and a disturbance in the attacker"s balance or speed.3. Resulting Phenomenon: The referee blows the whistle promptly after the pull, and play stops.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on football rules regarding fouls. Pulling an opponent"s jersey from behind while they are dribbling forward is an illegal action because it unfairly impedes movement. The referee must judge the action based on position, direction, and impact of contact, and stop play with a whistle to maintain fairness and safety in the game.VI. Experimental Notes1. The pulling action must be clearly from behind.2. The referee should have an unobstructed view.3. The demonstration should emphasize sequence: dribble, pull, whistle.

Visibility requirements: the camera must clearly show the direction of the pull, the jersey deformation, and the referee"s whistle action for verification.

manual: Experiment Title: Atmospheric Scattering and Sky Color ChangesSubject: Geography – Physical GeographyExperiment Objective: To observe and understand how atmospheric scattering causes sky color changes from sunrise to daytime and sunset under clear weather conditions using time-lapse observation.Experimental Materials and Conditions:1. Clear-weather day with minimal cloud cover.2. Fixed camera or smartphone with time-lapse function.3. Stable tripod or fixed mounting position.4. Open view of the sky (no tall buildings or trees blocking the horizon).Experimental Procedure:1. Site Setup: Choose an outdoor location with an unobstructed view of the sky. Fix the camera on a tripod, ensuring the frame is focused only on the sky and remains unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Sunrise Recording: Start time-lapse recording before sunrise. Capture the gradual change of the sky from dark to red-orange and yellow hues near the horizon.3. Daytime Recording: Continue recording as the sun rises higher. Observe the sky transitioning to a uniform blue color during midday under clear conditions.4. Sunset Recording: Maintain recording until sunset. Capture the sky changing from blue to orange-red and finally to darker tones as the sun sets.5. Completion: Stop recording after sunset. Compile the time-lapse video showing the full sequence.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:1. Sunrise: The sky near the horizon appears red or orange while the upper sky remains darker.2. Daytime: The entire sky appears bright blue under clear conditions.3. Sunset: The sky again turns orange-red near the horizon, with decreasing brightness overall.Summary of Experimental Principle:Atmospheric scattering explains sky color changes. Shortwave blue light is scattered more strongly by air molecules, making the sky appear blue during the day when sunlight passes through a shorter atmospheric path. At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels a longer path through the atmosphere; shortwave light is scattered away, leaving longer-wavelength red and orange light to dominate the sky’s color.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Atmospheric scattering as the mechanism causing systematic sky color changes across the day.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Sunlight consists of multiple wavelengths; air molecules scatter shortwave (blue) light more effectively than longwave (red) light; the optical path length through the atmosphere changes with solar angle.Expected Phenomenon Storyline: Phase 1 (Sunrise): Long atmospheric path leads to red-orange sky near the horizon. Phase 2 (Midday): Short atmospheric path causes dominant blue sky due to strong blue light scattering. Phase 3 (Sunset): Increasing path length again removes blue light, producing orange-red hues. The camera perspective must remain fixed on the sky, and transitions must be continuous and time-lapse accelerated for verification within a short video.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Simulating Volcano Landforms with ClayI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Simulation of Stratovolcano and Shield Volcano Using Clay2. Subject: Geography – Volcanic Landforms3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate and compare the morphological differences between a Japanese stratovolcano (Mt. Fuji-type, steep cone) and an Icelandic shield volcano (broad, gentle slopes) by using different types of clay.II. Experimental Materials1. Thick, firm clay (dark color recommended)2. Soft, malleable clay (light color recommended)3. Flat baseboard or tray4. Plastic knife or spatula (optional)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the baseboard on a flat surface. Separate the thick clay and soft clay for later use.2. Step One – Stratovolcano Simulation: Take the thick clay and stack it upward at the center of the baseboard. Gently press and shape it into a tall, steep, symmetrical cone, simulating the conical shape of Mt. Fuji.3. Observation Pause: Observe and note the steep sides and compact structure of the cone.4. Step Two – Shield Volcano Simulation: Take the soft clay and place it on another area of the baseboard. Press it outward from the center, allowing it to spread horizontally into a wide, low mound with gentle slopes.5. Final Comparison: Place the two models side by side and visually compare their shapes and slopes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The thick clay forms a steep, high cone that maintains its shape and does not easily spread.2. The soft clay spreads easily, forming a broad, low profile with gentle slopes.3. The two models show a clear contrast in height, slope steepness, and overall morphology.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment simulates volcanic landforms based on magma viscosity. Stratovolcanoes like Mt. Fuji are formed by viscous magma that piles up near the vent, creating steep conical shapes. Shield volcanoes in Iceland are formed by low-viscosity magma that flows easily and spreads over large areas, producing wide and gentle slopes. Different clay properties are used to analogically represent these magma behaviors.VI. Notes and Precautions1. This is a simulation model and does not represent actual volcanic activity.2. Ensure clear visual contrast between the two clay types for effective comparison.3. Handle clay gently to maintain stable shapes for observation.

Camera should maintain a stable, frontal or slightly elevated view to clearly verify shapes and causal transitions within a short, accelerated sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pressure Belt Distribution on a Rotating GlobeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pressure Belt Distribution on a Rotating Globe2. Subject: Geography - Physical Geography (Atmospheric Circulation)3. Experiment Objective: To understand the zonal distribution of global pressure belts by marking key latitudes and superimposing corresponding pressure zones, and to relate latitude to atmospheric pressure patterns.II. Experimental EquipmentSimplified globe model (rotatable), marker or digital annotation tool, color indicators (red, blue, dark), latitude reference lines.III. Experimental ProcedureStep 1: Place the globe in an upright position and rotate it slowly to observe latitude lines.Step 2: Clearly mark the equator at 0° latitude.Step 3: Mark the subtropical latitudes at 30°N and 30°S.Step 4: Mark the polar latitudes at 90°N and 90°S.Step 5: Superimpose pressure belts in latitudinal order: mark the equatorial low-pressure belt at 0° using red (<1000 hPa); mark the subtropical high-pressure belts at 30°N/S using blue (>1020 hPa); mark the polar high-pressure belts at 90°N/S using dark color.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. The equatorial region appears as a continuous red belt around the globe.2. Blue belts appear symmetrically at 30°N and 30°S.3. Dark-colored belts appear at both poles (90°N and 90°S).4. All belts show clear zonal (east-west) distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDue to uneven solar heating, air rises at the equator forming a low-pressure belt, descends around 30° forming subtropical high-pressure belts, and remains cold and dense at the poles forming polar high-pressure belts. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Fluvial Deposition – Comparison of Yellow River Delta and Mississippi River DeltaI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluvial Deposition and Delta Formation: Yellow River vs Mississippi River2. Subject: Geography – Physical Geography (Fluvial Geomorphology)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate and compare the formation processes of the Yellow River Delta and the Mississippi River Delta, focusing on differences in delta shape and sediment characteristics using time-lapse imagery.II. Experimental Materials and MediaTime-lapse satellite imagery or simulation footage of the Yellow River Delta and Mississippi River Delta; map base showing river, coastline, and sea; annotation tools (labels, arrows, color overlays).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Display a map locating the Yellow River and Mississippi River, indicating river flow direction and the sea.2. Stage One – Yellow River Delta Formation: Play time-lapse footage showing the Yellow River entering the Bohai Sea. Emphasize rapid sediment accumulation at the river mouth and outward expansion into a fan-shaped delta.3. Observation Pause: Highlight sediment color and texture, showing thick, muddy, yellow-brown deposits spreading laterally.4. Stage Two – Mississippi River Delta Formation: Switch to time-lapse footage of the Mississippi River entering the Gulf of Mexico. Show sediment extending forward along stable river channels, forming a bird-foot-shaped delta.5. Comparison: Use split-screen or sequential labels to contrast delta shape, sediment distribution, and extension patterns.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Yellow River Delta: Delta grows rapidly outward; sediment accumulates near the mouth; shape is broad and fan-like; sediment appears fine and yellowish.2. Mississippi River Delta: Delta grows by narrow protruding lobes; sediment extends far into the sea along channels; shape resembles a bird’s foot; sediment is more localized along distributaries.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDelta formation is controlled by river sediment supply and marine reworking. The Yellow River carries an extremely high sediment load, leading to rapid accumulation and a fan-shaped delta dominated by deposition. The Mississippi River has relatively stable channels and weaker wave and tidal reworking, allowing sediments to extend seaward along distributaries, forming a bird-foot delta. Differences in sediment quantity, transport, and coastal dynamics result in distinct delta morphologies.VI. NotesFor time-lapse demonstrations, the formation process is accelerated, but the chronological order and causal relationships must remain correct.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Fluvial deposition and delta morphology differences between the Yellow River and Mississippi River. Minimum assumptions: rivers transport sediment to the sea; sediment accumulates over time; marine processes modify delta shape.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 shows the Yellow River delivering heavy sediment and rapidly building a fan-shaped delta through accumulation near the mouth. Phase 2 transitions to the Mississippi River, where sediment extends seaward along distributary channels, forming a bird-foot pattern. Key causal transition: difference in sediment load and marine reworking leads to different delta shapes. Visibility requirements: stable overhead or oblique view, clear coastline reference, accelerated time-lapse growth, and visible sediment color and distribution for comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Plotting a Bar Chart Comparing Expenditures under a Fiscal Deficit SituationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plotting a Bar Chart Comparing Income and Expenditure under a Fiscal Deficit2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Economics3. Experiment Objective: To understand the concept of fiscal deficit by visually comparing government income and expenditure using a bar chart, and to master the basic method of representing economic data graphically.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Supply Curve Plotting DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Plotting an Upward-Sloping Supply Curve2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences - Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the supply curve feature by plotting price and quantity on a coordinate graph, showing that quantity supplied increases as price rises, and forming an upward-sloping supply curve.II. Experimental EquipmentGraph paper or digital graphing software, ruler or straightedge, pen or stylus, coordinate axes template, camera or screen-recording device capable of time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Prepare a blank coordinate graph with a vertical axis labeled Price and a horizontal axis labeled Quantity. Ensure the graph is clean and clearly visible in the camera frame.Plotting Points: Select several price levels from low to high. For each higher price, determine a larger corresponding quantity supplied. Plot each price-quantity pair as a point, starting from the bottom-left area of the graph and moving toward the top-right.Progressive Demonstration: Plot points one by one in ascending price order, keeping the camera fixed and focused on the graph. Use time-lapse or accelerated recording to capture the gradual addition of points.Connecting the Curve: After all points are plotted, use a ruler or smooth hand motion to connect the points into a continuous, smooth curve.Completion: Hold the final image steady for a short time to clearly show the completed upward-sloping supply curve.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The graph shows empty axes with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis.2. During Plotting: As price levels increase, newly added points appear progressively further to the right, forming an upward trend.3. Final State: The connected points form a smooth curve sloping upward from bottom-left to top-right.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates the law of supply in economics. Under the assumption that other factors remain constant, higher prices provide producers with greater incentives to supply more goods. As a result, quantity supplied increases with price, which is represented graphically by an upward-sloping supply curve.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure axes labels are correct and clear. Plot points in correct order to avoid misinterpretation. Keep the camera stable to maintain visual consistency during time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: the law of supply, assuming ceteris paribus and rational producer behavior. Minimum assumptions include correctly defined axes and monotonic increase in quantity supplied with price. Expected phenomena unfold in phases: (1) static display of labeled axes; (2) sequential appearance of plotted points as price increases; (3) visual emergence of an upward trend; (4) connection of points into a smooth upward-sloping curve. Visibility requirements include a fixed viewpoint, clear labels, and uninterrupted time-lapse progression to verify causal and temporal consistency.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Adding Core Shadow and Cast Shadow to a Cube DrawingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Adding Core Shadow and Cast Shadow to a Cube Drawing2. Subject: Arts – Drawing Fundamentals3. Experiment Objective: To understand how a single fixed side light source affects form perception by adding correct core shadow and cast shadow to a cube drawing, and to observe tonal changes through time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentWhite drawing paper (A4), graphite pencil (HB–2B), eraser, ruler (optional), single desk lamp with fixed side lighting, drawing table, camera or smartphone on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place white paper flat on the table. Position the desk lamp to one side of the paper at a fixed angle. Fix the camera above or at an oblique angle and lock focus.Outline Drawing: Use a graphite pencil to lightly draw a cube with clear edges, ensuring perspective is stable.Lighting Observation: Observe which face of the cube faces the light and which face turns away from it.Core Shadow Drawing: Gradually darken the face opposite the light source to form the core shadow, keeping edges soft and tonal transitions smooth.Cast Shadow Drawing: Extend a shadow from the cube onto the paper surface in the direction opposite the light, darker near the cube and lighter outward.Completion: Refine tones, maintain consistent lighting, and allow the camera to record the full process as a time-lapse.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cube outline appears flat with no depth before shading.2. Final Effect: The cube appears solid and grounded, with clear distinction between lit area, core shadow, and cast shadow.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA single fixed side light creates predictable light and shadow patterns. The core shadow forms on the surface turning away from the light, while the cast shadow is projected onto the surface beneath. Proper tonal hierarchy and consistency enhance spatial realism and depth perception in drawing.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Economies of Scale and the Falling Average Cost CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of Economies of Scale Using an Average Cost Curve2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the feature of economies of scale by showing that average cost decreases as output increases, and to help learners understand the economic mechanism behind a falling average cost curve.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsCoordinate axis template or digital graphing interface, time-lapse plotting tool or animation software, pointer or cursor (for demonstration), label markers for axes.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Display a blank coordinate axis. Clearly label the horizontal axis as Output and the vertical axis as Average Cost.2. Initial Plotting: Mark a point at low output with relatively high average cost to represent small-scale production.3. Core Operation (Time-Lapse Demonstration): Gradually increase output along the horizontal axis. At each increase, plot a new point with a lower average cost than the previous one. Use time-lapse or accelerated animation so the curve appears to be drawn progressively.4. Curve Formation: Connect the plotted points smoothly to form a downward-sloping average cost curve.5. Final Observation: Pause on the completed graph, emphasizing the overall downward trend as output increases.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: At low output levels, the average cost is high, shown by a point high on the vertical axis.2. During the Demonstration: As output increases, each new plotted point appears lower on the average cost axis, forming a declining pattern.3. Final State: The completed curve slopes downward from left to right, clearly indicating falling average cost with increased output.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis demonstration is based on the economic principle of economies of scale. As production output increases, fixed costs are spread over a larger number of units, and operational efficiencies improve. As a result, the average cost of producing each unit decreases. This relationship is visually represented by a downward-sloping average cost curve on a graph where output increases along the horizontal axis and average cost is measured on the vertical axis.VI. Notes and Precautions1. Ensure axis labels are clear and correct before plotting.2. The curve should be smooth and continuous, avoiding upward fluctuations that contradict economies of scale.3. Time-lapse plotting should preserve the correct order of output increases.

Minimum assumptions include a fixed coordinate system, correct axis labeling, and a monotonic increase in output.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – A static coordinate axis appears with output (horizontal) and average cost (vertical). Phase 2 – At low output, a high average cost point is plotted. Phase 3 – As time progresses (accelerated via time-lapse), output increases and successive points appear lower on the average cost axis. Phase 4 – Points connect into a smooth downward-sloping curve, visually confirming economies of scale. Visibility Constraints: The entire graph must remain in view, with no camera movement that obscures axis labels or curve shape.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Gradient Technique on a SphereI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Applying the Gradient Technique to a Sketch Sphere2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Arts (Drawing Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To understand and demonstrate the gradient technique by creating a smooth tonal transition from dark to light on a simple sphere, ensuring light and shadow conform to artistic rules, and recording the process using time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Materials and ToolsDrawing paper (A4 or similar), graphite pencil (HB–4B recommended), eraser, blending tool or tissue (optional), desk lamp (single light source), camera or mobile phone with time-lapse function, tripod or fixed stand.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the drawing paper on a flat surface. Position a single light source to one side to create clear light and shadow. Fix the camera directly facing the paper to ensure a stable, focused frame.2. Sketching the Sphere: Lightly draw a simple circle to represent the sphere. Adjust the outline to ensure roundness and three-dimensional accuracy.3. Determining Light and Shadow: Identify the highlight area, mid-tone area, core shadow, and reflected light according to the light source direction.4. Applying Gradient Technique (Core Operation): Starting from the darkest shadow area, gradually apply pencil strokes toward the lighter areas. Control pressure to ensure a smooth transition with no obvious color block boundaries. Blend tones so that the gradient area appears continuous and natural.5. Refinement: Repeatedly adjust tones to enhance volume, ensuring the light-to-dark transition conforms to sphere form.6. Time-lapse Recording: Throughout the shading process, record continuously using time-lapse mode, keeping the image focused and stable.7. Completion: Stop recording once a smooth, complete gradient sphere is achieved.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sphere outline is light, flat, and without tonal variation.2. During Shading: Dark areas gradually appear on the shadow side; mid-tones transition smoothly toward the light area without sharp boundaries.3. Final State: The sphere shows a clear three-dimensional effect, with smooth gradient areas and realistic light and shadow distribution.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe experiment is based on the artistic principle that gradual tonal change creates volume and depth. By controlling pencil pressure and stroke density, a smooth gradient from dark to light is formed. This gradient conforms to light and shadow rules, allowing a flat circle to visually appear as a three-dimensional sphere.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure a single consistent light source; avoid heavy initial strokes; maintain camera stability and focus; do not over-blend to the point of losing tonal structure.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Law of Supply – Movement Along the Supply CurveI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Price Increase and Quantity Supplied Movement Along the Supply Curve2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Economics3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the law of supply by showing that when price rises, quantity supplied increases, represented as a movement upward and to the right along the same supply curve.II. Experimental EquipmentDigital display screen or whiteboard; coordinate axis template; animation or drawing tool (for time-lapse effect); marker or pointer for labeling points.III. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Setup: Display a two-dimensional coordinate axis with quantity on the horizontal axis and price on the vertical axis. Ensure labels are clear and fixed.2. Drawing the Supply Curve: Draw an upward-sloping supply curve from the lower-left to the upper-right of the graph, indicating a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied.3. Marking Initial State (Point A): Mark point A on the lower-left section of the supply curve, representing low price and low quantity supplied. Label it clearly.4. Price Increase Operation: Indicate an increase in price by moving upward along the vertical axis. Use a time-lapse or smooth animation effect.5. Movement to Point B: Move point A along the same supply curve upward and to the right until it reaches a new position (point B), representing higher price and higher quantity supplied. Mark and label point B.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The graph shows point A at a low price and low quantity on the supply curve.2. During Change: As price increases, the point moves smoothly upward and to the right along the curve.3. Final State: Point B is located at a higher price and higher quantity on the same supply curve.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis demonstration illustrates the law of supply in economics: other factors remaining constant, an increase in price leads to an increase in quantity supplied. Graphically, this is shown as a movement upward and to the right along an existing supply curve, rather than a shift of the curve itself.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure axes labels are not reversed; emphasize that the curve does not shift; keep visual elements stable to avoid confusion between movement along the curve and curve shifts.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Law of Supply – movement along the supply curve.Minimum Assumptions: A standard two-axis economic graph, ceteris paribus conditions, and a positively sloped supply curve.Phased Storyline: (1) Static graph with labeled axes and supply curve; (2) clear identification of point A at low price–low quantity; (3) explicit indication of price increase; (4) smooth, time-lapse movement along the same curve; (5) final marking of point B at higher price–higher quantity. Visibility Constraints: fixed camera, clear labels, no curve shifting, and continuous motion for verification.

Experiment Title: Sexual Dimorphism in African Elephants: Comparison of Male and Female Tusks2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Gender & Sexuality Studies3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand sexual dimorphism in African elephants by comparing morphological differences, especially tusk length and thickness, between a female and a male elephant using visual evidence.II. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAfrican elephants exhibit sexual dimorphism, meaning males and females differ in physical traits. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Voiced vs Voiceless Plosive Sounds Shown by Candle Flame MovementI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Voiced and Voiceless Plosive Sounds Demonstrated by Candle Flame Movement2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Linguistics (Phonetics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the articulatory and aerodynamic differences between voiced and voiceless plosive consonants by observing candle flame movement during speech, and to understand the relationship between airflow, vocal fold vibration, and speech sounds.II. Experimental Equipment1. Lit candle (1, stable base, flame height approximately 2–3 cm)2. Table and chair for the speaker3. Camera or smartphone (capable of video or time-lapse recording)4. Tripod or stable support for the camera5. Quiet indoor environment with minimal air movementIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   Place the candle upright on the table. Seat the speaker comfortably facing the candle. Adjust the distance so that the candle flame is approximately 3–5 cm from the speaker’s mouth. Darken the background slightly if possible to enhance flame visibility.2. Camera Setup:   Position the camera at the side or slightly in front of the speaker so that both the mouth and the candle flame are clearly visible. Fix the focus and exposure; do not use auto-focus during recording. Begin recording or set time-lapse mode.3. Core Operation:   The speaker alternately produces voiceless plosive syllables (e.g., /pa/, /ta/, /ka/) and voiced plosive syllables (e.g., /ba/, /da/, /ga/) toward the candle. Each syllable is produced clearly with a brief pause between syllables. Repeat the alternation at least two cycles.4. Completion:   Stop recording after clear differences in flame movement have been captured. Extinguish the candle safely.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State:   When the speaker is silent, the candle flame burns steadily with minimal movement.2. Voiceless Plosive Production:   During the production of voiceless plosives (such as /p/), the candle flame shows a sudden, strong deflection or flicker away from the speaker, sometimes briefly bending or almost extinguishing.3. Voiced Plosive Production:   During the production of voiced plosives (such as /b/), the candle flame shows weaker movement, with only slight flickering or gentle bending.4. Comparative Observation:   Across repetitions, voiceless plosives consistently cause larger and more abrupt flame movement than voiced plosives.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis demonstration is based on phonetic principles of plosive consonant production. Plosives are produced by building up air pressure behind a complete closure in the vocal tract and then releasing it. Voiceless plosives require a stronger burst of airflow because the vocal folds are open and not vibrating, resulting in higher oral air pressure and stronger aspiration. Voiced plosives involve vocal fold vibration, which reduces airflow intensity. The candle flame visually responds to differences in airflow strength, making the aerodynamic contrast between voiced and voiceless plosives observable.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the candle at a safe distance to avoid burns or fire hazards.2. Ensure no external airflow (fans, open windows) interferes with the flame.3. Fix camera focus in advance to avoid visual instability during recording.4. The speaker should articulate clearly but avoid blowing intentionally, relying only on normal speech production.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Physical Weathering by Rock Abrasion in Moving Water (Rotating Drum Simulation)2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Archaeology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the process of physical weathering through rock abrasion caused by tumbling and collision in moving water, and to understand how angular rock fragments become rounded over time. The experiment also trains observation skills using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment- Clear rotating drum or rock tumbler with transparent wall (1)- Electric or manual rotation device (stable speed)- Water (clean, enough to partly fill the drum)- Angular rock fragments (sharp edges, irregular shapes)- Rounded pebbles (smooth, pre-weathered)- Camera or smartphone with tripod (time-lapse capable)- Fixed light source (optional, for clear imaging)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the rotating drum to ensure transparency. Place the drum securely on the rotating device. Select several angular rock fragments and several rounded pebbles with visible differences in shape.2. Loading the Drum: Put the rock fragments and pebbles into the drum. Add water until the drum is approximately one-third to one-half full, ensuring rocks can tumble freely.3. Camera Setup: Place the camera on a tripod facing the clear wall of the drum. Fix the focus, frame the central tumbling area, and set time-lapse mode. Do not adjust focus or angle during the experiment.4. Core Operation: Start rotating the drum at a steady, moderate speed. Ensure rocks tumble, roll, and collide rather than sticking to the wall.5. Time-Lapse Recording: Allow the drum to rotate continuously. Record the process using time-lapse photography to compress long-term abrasion into a short visual sequence.6. Ending the Experiment: Stop the rotation after sufficient tumbling. Turn off the camera and carefully open the drum. Remove rocks for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Angular rock fragments have sharp edges and corners; rounded pebbles are smooth. Water is clear.2. During Tumbling: Rocks roll, slide, and collide with each other and the drum wall. Angular fragments visibly chip and lose sharp corners. Fine sediment may appear in the water.3. Final State: Angular fragments become noticeably smoother and more rounded. Differences between original angular rocks and pebbles are reduced.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates physical weathering by abrasion. In moving water environments such as rivers and coastlines, rocks are transported and repeatedly collide with other rocks and surfaces. These mechanical impacts cause edges to break off and surfaces to become smoother. The rotating drum simulates continuous water-driven motion, while time-lapse photography reveals gradual shape changes within a short observation period.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not overfill the drum; sufficient space is required for tumbling.2. Maintain a stable rotation speed to avoid unnatural motion.3. Ensure the camera focus remains fixed throughout recording.4. Handle rocks carefully when removing them after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: physical weathering through rock abrasion in moving water, simulated by a rotating drum. Minimum assumptions: rocks are solid, water enables motion, and repeated collisions cause mechanical rounding without chemical change.Phased storyline: (1) initial state shows angular fragments and rounded pebbles in clear water; (2) drum rotation initiates continuous tumbling and collisions; (3) sustained motion leads to visible smoothing and fine sediment; (4) final comparison highlights reduced angularity. Visibility constraints: camera focus and framing remain fixed on the transparent drum wall to verify continuous motion and gradual change.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Single Scene Lighting Shift from Romantic Comedy to HorrorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Visual Genre Transformation through Lighting in a Single Scene2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Literature & Comparative Literature3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how lighting alone can transform genre perception within a continuous narrative scene, moving from romantic comedy to horror without changing setting, characters, or camera position.II. Experimental EquipmentFixed camera on tripod (locked focus), small apartment dining area, small table and two chairs, two actors, adjustable lighting system (warm key lights, neutral fill lights, cold and directional lights), dimmer or lighting control software.III. Experimental Procedure1. Scene Setup: Arrange a small table in an apartment dining area. Seat two actors facing each other as if on a dinner date. Lock the camera position and focus; no zoom or reframing is allowed.2. Initial Lighting (Romantic Comedy): Use warm, soft, evenly distributed lighting with minimal shadows. Actors maintain relaxed, friendly body language.3. Continuous Recording: Begin recording and maintain a single uninterrupted shot. Actors continue natural dinner-date interaction without changing blocking.4. Lighting Transition: Gradually and continuously reduce warm light, introduce cooler tones, increase contrast, and add directional shadows over time. No cuts or camera movement.5. Final Lighting (Horror): End with low-key, high-contrast lighting, cooler color temperature, and pronounced shadows that partially obscure faces and background.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial Phase: Scene appears light-hearted, intimate, and comedic due to warm, balanced lighting.2. Transition Phase: Mood becomes ambiguous as lighting cools and shadows deepen, despite unchanged dialogue and actions.3. Final Phase: Scene reads as tense and threatening, characteristic of horror, created solely through lighting changes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates a core principle in literature and visual storytelling: genre perception is not inherent in narrative events alone but is co-produced by formal elements such as lighting. By manipulating lighting variables (color temperature, contrast, shadow), the same scene can shift interpretive frameworks from romantic comedy to horror, revealing how readers and viewers rely on visual cues to construct meaning.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Urban Heat Island Effect Using Concrete and Grass Under a Heat LampI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urban Heat Island Effect Using Concrete and Grass Under a Heat Lamp2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Geography3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the urban heat island effect by comparing heat absorption and temperature change between concrete and grass surfaces under identical heating conditions.II. Experimental EquipmentConcrete slab (flat, dry), grass tray or sod in a shallow tray (moist but not flooded), two identical ice cubes, heat lamp (same height and power for both surfaces), tabletop, camera or mobile phone with tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the concrete slab and grass tray side by side on a flat tabletop, ensuring similar size and exposure.2. Placement of Ice: Put one identical ice cube at the center of the concrete slab and one at the center of the grass tray at the same time.3. Heating: Position a heat lamp directly above the midpoint so that both surfaces receive equal light and heat; turn on the lamp simultaneously.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position, then start time-lapse recording to capture the melting process.5. Observation End: Continue heating until a clear difference in melting speed is observed, then turn off the lamp.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both ice cubes are solid and similar in size; concrete and grass appear at room temperature.2. During Heating: The ice cube on the concrete slab melts faster, forming water sooner, while the ice on grass melts more slowly.3. Final State: The concrete surface appears warmer and drier, while the grass remains relatively cooler and moist.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleConcrete has a lower albedo and higher heat absorption than grass, causing it to heat up faster under the same radiation. Grass cools its surface through moisture and evapotranspiration. This difference demonstrates the urban heat island effect, where built-up urban surfaces become hotter than vegetated areas under the same sunlight.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Rubber Strip Elasticity vs. Brittle Plastic FractureI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Elastic Rubber Strip and Brittle Plastic Strip Under Repeated Stretching2. Subject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Architecture & Urban Planning (Material Behavior Demonstration)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare elastic and brittle material behaviors by observing the deformation and recovery of a rubber strip versus the cracking of a brittle plastic strip under repeated stretching.II. Experimental Equipment1. Red rubber strip (elastic material)2. Clear brittle plastic strip (e.g., acrylic or brittle plastic)3. Two clamps or a dual clamp fixture4. Stable support frame or table edge5. Protective gloves and safety gogglesIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fix the red rubber strip on the left side and the clear brittle plastic strip on the right side, each clamped firmly at one end to the same support. Ensure both strips hang freely.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial shape and condition of both strips (no deformation or cracks).3. Core Operation: Grasp the free end of the red rubber strip and stretch it horizontally to a moderate, consistent length, then release it. Repeat this action several times.4. Repeat the same stretching and releasing action on the clear brittle plastic strip, aiming for a similar stretch length each time.5. Continue the repeated stretching cycles while observing changes in both materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Rubber Strip: During stretching, the rubber elongates noticeably; upon release, it quickly recoils and returns close to its original length without visible damage.2. Brittle Plastic Strip: During stretching, the plastic shows limited deformation; after repeated stretching, visible cracks, whitening, or sudden fracture appear, and it does not return to its original shape.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Elasticity Principle: Rubber is an elastic material. Under external force, its polymer chains stretch and store elastic energy; when the force is removed, the material recoils and largely recovers its original shape.2. Brittleness Principle: Brittle plastic has limited capacity for elastic deformation. Repeated tensile stress causes micro-cracks to form and propagate, leading to cracking or fracture rather than recovery.3. Architectural Relevance: Understanding elastic versus brittle behavior is essential in material selection for structures, as elastic materials can absorb deformation, while brittle materials fail suddenly under stress.

Minimum assumptions: two visually distinct strips (red rubber, clear plastic), each clamped at one end, subjected to similar stretch–release actions.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase – camera shows left red rubber strip and right clear plastic strip clamped at one end. (2) Action phase – each strip is repeatedly stretched to a similar length and released, in clear sequence. (3) Outcome phase – rubber recoils and remains intact; plastic shows cracking or fracture. Visibility constraints: clamping point, stretching direction, and material deformation must remain in frame to verify causal relationships.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Inflation Feature Demonstration Using Price Index CurveSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EconomicsObjective: To visually demonstrate inflation by showing a price index that rises continuously over time as average prices increase.II. Experimental MaterialsBlank coordinate axis template (digital or paper); time labels (Period 1, Period 2, Period 3…); price index scale; data points representing average prices; drawing or animation tool capable of time-lapse display.III. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Draw or display a coordinate axis with time on the horizontal axis and price index value on the vertical axis.2. Initial State: Plot the initial period’s average price as the first index point.3. Sequential Update: For each subsequent period, assume a higher average price due to inflation and plot a new data point higher than the previous one.4. Curve Formation: Connect data points sequentially to form a rising curve.5. Time-Lapse Display: Accelerate the plotting process so points appear one after another, clearly showing the curve updating over time.IV. Observation of Phenomena1. At the start, the graph shows a single low index point.2. As time advances, new points appear at higher positions on the vertical axis.3. The connected points form a curve that rises continuously along the time axis.V. Experimental Principle SummaryInflation refers to a sustained increase in the general price level. A price index measures average prices over time. When average prices rise each period, the index value increases, and plotting these values against time produces a continuously rising curve. This visualizes the core feature of inflation.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Inflation as a sustained rise in the general price level, represented by an increasing price index over time. Minimum assumptions: time progresses in discrete periods; average prices increase each period; the index accurately reflects these averages.Phased storyline: (1) Static graph with labeled axes; (2) first index point plotted; (3) successive periods add higher points due to rising prices; (4) points connect into an upward curve; (5) time-lapse emphasizes continuity. Visibility constraints: axes labels must remain readable; the curve update must stay in frame; no perspective shifts that obscure the rising trend.

subject: Gender & Sexuality Studies
selected_point: Mandarin Duck Sexual Plumage Dimorphism: Male Asian mandarin ducks have bright plumage (red beak, green head, yellow belly), females have gray-brown plumage and gray beaks, typical of East Asian wetland populations
posted_prompt: Display two columns: the left column shows a female Mandarin duck from an East Asian wetland population, and the right column shows a male Mandarin duck from the same population. The image focuses on the differences in plumage color and morphology between the two ducks.

pg_specification.2 points: Two columns are present but sex assignment is wrong or only one duck is clearly identifiable; major plumage features are incorrect.
pg_specification.3 points: Two columns correctly show a female on the left and a male on the right, but some key plumage colors or morphological traits are missing or unclear.
pg_specification.4 points: Left female and right male Mandarin ducks are correctly placed with most key plumage differences visible; minor non-core details (background clarity or posture) are weak.
pg_specification.5 points: Clear two-column layout with left female and right male from East Asian wetlands; all core plumage and morphology differences are accurate and visually salient.

scc_specification.1 point: Plumage colors and traits contradict biological knowledge; causal explanation of dimorphism is absent or incorrect.
scc_specification.2 points: Some correct traits appear, but core male–female differences are confused or causality is poorly presented.
scc_specification.3 points: Core differences (bright male vs dull female) are correct, but explanations lack completeness or clarity.
scc_specification.4 points: Correct and coherent depiction of sexual dimorphism with accurate traits and a reasonable biological explanation; minor omissions exist.
scc_specification.5 points: Fully correct depiction and explanation of Mandarin duck sexual plumage dimorphism, with clear, concise causal logic linked to sexual selection and ecology.

sc_specification.5 points: Perfectly stable two-column spatial arrangement and continuous, realistic presentation throughout.

manual: Experiment Title: Observation of Sexual Plumage Dimorphism in Mandarin DucksSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – Gender & Sexuality Studies (Biological Sex Differences)Experiment Objective: To visually compare and identify sexual plumage dimorphism between female and male Mandarin ducks from East Asian wetland populations by observing differences in plumage color and morphology.Experimental Materials: High-resolution reference images or specimens of Mandarin ducks; display interface capable of two-column layout; neutral wetland background.Experimental Procedure:1. Preparation: Select representative images/specimens of one adult female and one adult male Mandarin duck from the same East Asian wetland population.2. Layout Setup: Arrange the display into two vertical columns; place the female duck in the left column and the male duck in the right column.3. Core Observation: Ensure both ducks are shown in similar posture and scale to allow direct comparison. Focus the frame on head, beak, chest, and body plumage.4. Observation Recording: Observe and note differences in beak color, head coloration, body plumage brightness, and overall morphology.5. Conclusion: Confirm sex-based differences and end the observation.Observation of Experimental Phenomena:- Female (left): Gray-brown plumage, subdued coloration, gray beak, overall camouflaged appearance.- Male (right): Bright red beak, green head, yellow belly, and highly decorative multicolored plumage.Summary of Experimental Principle: Mandarin ducks exhibit clear sexual plumage dimorphism. Males evolve bright, conspicuous plumage due to sexual selection for mate attraction, while females retain cryptic gray-brown plumage that enhances camouflage during nesting. These consistent differences allow reliable visual sex identification within East Asian wetland populations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Sexual plumage dimorphism in Mandarin ducks. Minimum assumptions: two adult ducks of the same species and population, correctly sexed, displayed side-by-side with clear visibility of plumage.Phased storyline: (1) Establish a stable two-column view with the female on the left and male on the right; (2) Visually emphasize contrasting plumage colors and morphology; (3) Enable direct comparison without camera movement or layout changes. Visibility constraints: frontal or three-quarter views, consistent scale and lighting to verify color and morphological differences.

posted_prompt: The footage shows a student learning in a classroom by observing the teacher's actions. The teacher moves and stacks blocks step by step. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Visual Characteristics of Observational Learning – Gaze FollowingI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Gaze Following in Classroom Demonstration LearningSubject: Humanities and Social Sciences – EducationObjective: To observe and verify the visual characteristic of observational learning in which a student’s gaze follows a teacher’s demonstrative actions during a step-by-step task.II. Experimental Materials and EnvironmentClassroom setting with desks and chairs; one teacher; one student observer; a set of colored wooden blocks (uniform size); table for demonstration; video recording device capable of close-up shots and time-lapse or accelerated recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Arrange the classroom so the student sits facing the teacher and the demonstration table. Place blocks neatly on the table.2. Demonstration: The teacher slowly picks up blocks and stacks them one by one in a fixed sequence, pausing briefly after each placement.3. Observation Recording: Use close-up shots to record the student’s head orientation and eye direction while the teacher moves each block.4. Time Compression: Apply time-lapse or accelerated playback to condense the full process into a short, continuous sequence while preserving action order.5. Completion: End recording after the final block is stacked and the student’s gaze settles on the completed structure.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Student’s gaze is neutral or directed at the teacher.During demonstration: As the teacher’s hands move and blocks are stacked, the student’s head and gaze shift correspondingly toward each movement and placement.Final state: After completion, the student’s gaze remains focused on the stacked blocks.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on observational learning theory, which states that learners acquire information by watching others. A key visual characteristic is gaze following: the observer’s visual attention tracks the demonstrator’s actions. The student’s synchronized head and gaze movements indicate attention allocation and cognitive processing of the demonstrated task.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Observational learning with gaze following, assuming a basic classroom context, a demonstrator performing sequential actions, and an observer capable of shifting visual attention.Minimum assumptions: One teacher demonstrates block stacking; one student observes; gaze direction can be inferred from head and eye orientation; actions precede gaze responses.Phased storyline: (1) Classroom setup and neutral gaze; (2) teacher initiates block movement; (3) student’s gaze shifts toward the moving hand and block; (4) repeated action–gaze coupling across steps; (5) final fixation on completed stack. Visibility requirements: clear close-ups of head and eye direction, stable camera perspective, and preserved action order even under time-lapse acceleration.
